# 📍 Locality Research Guide
## County Cork, Ireland — 1830s–1840s

**Standard place:** Cork, Munster, Ireland | **Type:** County | **Established:** 1606
**Provincial authority:** Munster | **National authority:** United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland (post-1800 Acts of Union)

No boundary changes affected County Cork during this period. Records were created at the **townland**, **civil parish**, **barony**, and **county** levels. Poor Law Unions were established in 1838, creating a new administrative layer relevant to the 1840s.

---

## ⚠️ Defining Constraints: Know These First

Two facts shape everything about Cork research in this window:

1. **The 1922 Four Courts Fire** destroyed most pre-1901 census returns, the great bulk of pre-1858 wills and probate bonds, and many government records held in Dublin. Church and land records held *outside* Dublin are the primary surviving substitutes.
2. **Civil registration did not exist** for this period. There are no government-issued birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1830s–1840s.

*(Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))*

---

## 1. Civil Registration (Vital Records)
**❌ Does NOT exist for this target window**

| Event type | Registration began | Level |
|---|---|---|
| Non-Catholic (CoI) marriages | 1845 | National |
| All births, deaths, RC marriages | 1 January 1864 | National |

**For the 1830s–1840s, there are no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates.** Church registers are the essential substitute for all families in this period.
*(Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))*

---

## 2. Church Records ⭐ PRIMARY SOURCE
**✅ Partially available — access varies by parish**

Roman Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, and occasionally burials) are the **core genealogical source** for the period. The great majority of County Cork's population was Roman Catholic.

- **Start dates vary widely by parish.** Many Cork RC parishes begin their registers in the **1810s–1830s**, placing at least some within the target window; earlier registers are rarer.
- **National Library of Ireland (NLI):** Free online digital images of RC registers up to 1880 — accessible at [registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie). This is your first stop.
- **IrishGenealogy.ie:** Free transcriptions and images of RC and Church of Ireland registers.
- **Church of Ireland (Anglican) registers:** Held at the **Representative Church Body Library** (Dublin) and sometimes in local custody. Cover the Protestant minority.
- Presbyterian, Methodist, and Quaker registers also exist for relevant communities.

> **Critical quirk:** Registers are organized by **RC parish**, not civil parish — and the boundaries differ substantially. You must identify the correct RC parish for the specific townland before searching. The NLI's parish map tool helps with this.

*(Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))*

---

## 3. Census and Census Substitutes
**⚠️ Original censuses destroyed — substitutes available**

The 1841 and 1851 census returns for Cork were destroyed in the 1922 fire. Two key substitutes bracket your window:

### Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) ✅ Indexed, free online
- Lists **occupiers of tithe-liable agricultural land** by name, townland, and acreage
- The **key census substitute for the 1830s** — every agricultural occupier, not just heads of household
- Available free at [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org) and IrishGenealogy.ie
- **Coverage gap:** Does not include urban dwellers, landless labourers, or cottiers without a recorded plot

### Griffith's Valuation (published for Cork, early 1850s) ✅ Indexed, free online
- Lists **every householder** — landholders, occupiers, and some urban tenants — with location and land/property value
- The **major substitute for the destroyed 1841/1851 censuses** — slightly postdates your window but captures many of the same families
- Searchable free at [askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/) and on Ancestry

*(Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))*

---

## 4. Emigration Records ⭐ HIGH PRIORITY
**✅ Available — Cork is a major departure port**

Cork ports — principally **Cobh (then called Queenstown)** — were among Ireland's primary embarkation points for emigrants to North America and Australia.

- **Passenger manifests** from Famine-era departures list **complete family groups including young children** — making these among the most family-rich records available when Irish civil records don't exist.
- Emigration was already active in the 1830s–early 1840s, well before the Famine's onset in 1845.
- U.S. arrival manifests searchable on **Ancestry.com** (ports: New York, Boston, Philadelphia, Baltimore, New Orleans, Quebec).
- **Tip:** If your ancestor emigrated from Cork, passenger lists are a priority — they may supply ages, townlands, and family composition lost in destroyed Irish records.

*(Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))*

---

## 5. Land and Property Records
**✅ Available (beyond census substitutes)**

- **Registry of Deeds** (Dublin, 1708–present): Records land transactions — deeds, leases, mortgages — including Cork properties. Accessible in person or via microfilm/Ancestry. Indexes are searchable.
- **Estate papers:** Many large Cork estates (e.g., Ponsonby, Devonshire, Boyle/Cork) produced rent rolls, tenancy lists, and eviction records. Held at the **National Archives of Ireland**, National Library, and some county collections. Largely unindexed — you need to know the landlord or estate name first.

---

## 6. Probate Records
**⚠️ Largely destroyed — fragments survive**

Pre-1858 probate was administered by ecclesiastical courts (diocesan and prerogative). The 1922 fire destroyed most pre-1858 wills and administration bonds.

- **Betham Abstracts** (National Archives of Ireland): Sir William Betham's pre-1800 will abstracts — limited Cork coverage, skews earlier than your window
- **Will calendars (indexes) from 1858 onward** survive at the National Archives of Ireland
- For the 1830s–1840s, probate survival is very sparse; treat any finding as a bonus

---

## 7. Military Records
**✅ Partial — held in the UK**

- Cork men served in the **British Army**; muster rolls, description books, and pension records are at **The National Archives (Kew, UK)**, partly accessible via Ancestry and Findmypast.
- The **Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC)**, established 1836, has surviving service records at TNA Kew — searchable on Findmypast.

---

## 8. Newspapers
**✅ Available — useful for middle and upper families**

Cork had active newspapers in this period:
- *Cork Examiner* (founded 1841)
- *Cork Constitution*, *Southern Reporter*, and others
- Carry birth, marriage, and death notices (mainly for Protestant and merchant-class families), local news, famine reports

Accessible via the **British Newspaper Archive** (Findmypast) and **Irish Newspaper Archives** (irishnewsarchive.com).

---

## 9. Poor Law Union Records (from 1838)
**✅ Some survive — important for poorer families**

Poor Law Unions were established across Cork in 1838, creating workhouse admission registers, minute books, and out-relief lists. These document the **poorest families** — those invisible in land and church records.

- Surviving records held at the **National Archives of Ireland** and local county archives
- Coverage is patchy; not all unions have surviving registers for the 1830s–1840s

---

## Online Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Key holdings for Cork 1830s–1840s | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie) | RC parish register images to 1880 | Free |
| [irishgenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) | RC + CoI register transcriptions/images | Free |
| [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) | Tithe Books; some registers; passenger lists | Free |
| [askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/) | Griffith's Valuation | Free |
| [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com) | Griffith's Valuation; passenger lists; registry of deeds | Subscription |
| [Findmypast.com](https://www.findmypast.com) | Cork newspapers; RIC records; British Army | Subscription |
| National Archives of Ireland (Dublin) | Estate papers; post-1858 probate; civil records | In-person / some online |
| Representative Church Body Library (Dublin) | Church of Ireland registers | In-person |
| The National Archives, Kew (UK) | British Army + RIC service records | In-person / some online |

> **Note on external links:** The external_links_search tool returned 6 generic curated links for the Cork / 1830–1849 window (Ancestry US Census, FamilySearch Wiki, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) — these are not Ireland-specific curated collections. FamilySearch appears to have limited curated external links specifically tagged to County Cork at these dates; use the repository table above for targeted access.

---

## Adjoining Counties

The Cork County Genealogy wiki page was not returned separately by the tools. Cork's neighboring counties are **Kerry** (west), **Limerick** (north), **Tipperary** (north-east), and **Waterford** (east). If your ancestor lived near a border, search those counties' Tithe Books, Griffith's Valuation, and church registers as well — families routinely crossed county lines for markets, marriages, and churches.

---

## Key Research Quirks

1. **No civil vital records for this period** — church registers are the only vital-record equivalent; start with the NLI.
2. **Tithe Books (1823–1837) vs. Griffith's (early 1850s)** — neither falls squarely in the 1840s; use both as brackets around your decade.
3. **Identify the RC parish first** — civil parish ≠ RC parish; get the correct parish for the townland before searching registers.
4. **The 1922 fire is the defining constraint** — assume wills, pre-1901 censuses, and many government records are gone; always check what survived (Registry of Deeds, estate papers, church registers held outside Dublin).
5. **Cork ports (Cobh/Queenstown)** — if your ancestor emigrated through Cork, passenger manifests are a high-priority source and may supply family details lost in destroyed Irish records.
6. **Poor Law Union records from 1838** — workhouse registers can document the poorest families, otherwise invisible in land and church sources.
7. **RC register gaps are common** — if a Cork parish register begins after your target date, check neighboring parishes; families often used the nearest open church.

---

# Berkshire County, Massachusetts — Locality Research Guide
**Period: 1820–1850 | Focus: Births, Marriages, Deaths**

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Berkshire County was formed in **1761** from Hampshire County, with its county seat at **Pittsfield**. No boundary changes occurred during the 1820–1850 window, so all records for this period fall cleanly under Berkshire County jurisdiction. The county spans Massachusetts's westernmost edge, bordered by **New York State** (Columbia and Rensselaer Counties) to the west and **Bennington County, Vermont** to the north — a critical cross-border consideration addressed at the end of this guide.

> ⚠️ The FamilySearch Wiki page for *Berkshire County, Massachusetts Genealogy* returned only generic content — the county-specific page is absent. Neighboring county names above are drawn from known geography rather than the wiki's Neighboring Counties table.

---

## Vital Records — Births, Marriages, Deaths

### How the Registration System Worked

From the **FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Vital Records page** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records):

- **Town-level recording** was mandated as early as **1639**, though compliance varied town by town. For 1820–1840, the individual **town clerk** is your primary source.
- **Statewide registration** began in **1841** — Massachusetts was the first state to implement a unified system. The state-level series runs from 1841 onward; original records remained with the town clerk.
- **Marriage intentions** were recorded in the **bride's hometown** and may also appear in the groom's hometown and their current residence — always check both.
- The original records are **still held by each town or city clerk** to this day.

### Where to Find Them

**🔍 Indexed + Images (name-searchable online)**
- **[Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)** — FamilySearch Collection 2061550. The primary indexed collection for this period. Covers births, marriages, and deaths reported at the town level across Massachusetts, including Berkshire County towns. ~3.4 million records as reported by FamilySearch.

**⚠️ Browse-Only Images (no name index — must be paged through image by image)**
- **FamilySearch Volume 004500891** — "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," Berkshire County, 1761–1850: 512 images. **0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable.** This Berkshire-specific digitized volume is invisible to name searches — you must open it and browse page by page. It is one of only 2 digitized volumes FamilySearch holds for Berkshire County in this period.

**📚 Published Compilations (often the easiest entry point)**
- The **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series: Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial), over 200 Massachusetts towns have published printed vital-records volumes covering all recorded births, marriages, and deaths through 1850. Check whether your specific Berkshire town has a volume — NEHGS and the Internet Archive hold many of these, and they often transcribe records not yet digitized on FamilySearch.

**🏛️ Physical Repositories**
- **Individual town clerks** (each Berkshire County town): The original registers still sit here. For 1820–1840 especially — before the 1841 state system — a town clerk contact may be the only route to an unindexed record.
- **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston): Holds state-level vital registrations from 1841 forward.

---

## Church Records

Churches were recording baptisms, marriages, and burials in Berkshire County long before the 1841 civil system — and continued alongside it. For missing civil records, church registers are the primary substitute.

**🔍 Indexed + Images**
- **[Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)** — FamilySearch Collection 1921657. ~987,000 records across multiple denominations. Name-searchable.

**⚠️ Browse-Only Images**
- **FamilySearch Volume 004500892** — "Church Records (Congregational)," Pittsfield, 1791–1850: 274 images. **0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable.** Congregational churches were the dominant denomination in western Massachusetts. This volume is a key primary source for Pittsfield-area families but requires page-by-page browsing.

**Denominations to pursue for Berkshire County:**
- **Congregational** — dominant; the Pittsfield volume exists; check other towns
- **Methodist and Baptist** — grew rapidly in this period; records at denominational archives or local churches
- **Episcopal** — check diocesan archives (Diocese of Western Massachusetts)
- **Quaker (Friends)** — if applicable, records held by the New England Yearly Meeting archives at the Rhode Island Historical Society

---

## Federal Census Records

All four federal censuses in this window covered Berkshire County:

| Year | What It Lists | Key Value |
|------|--------------|-----------|
| **1820** | Head of household + age/sex tallies | Documents household presence |
| **1830** | Head of household + age/sex tallies | 10-year gap filler |
| **1840** | Head of household + age/sex tallies | Last pre-name census |
| **1850** | **Every person named**, with age, sex, birthplace, occupation | First census naming all members — invaluable for birth years and origins |

- The **1850 Mortality Schedule** (available on Ancestry.com) lists every person who died in the 12 months before the June 1850 enumeration date. It is a de facto death record for that window and should always be checked.
- FamilySearch and **Ancestry.com** (confirmed in external-links results) both hold the U.S. Federal Census Collection.

---

## Probate Records

- **[Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)** — FamilySearch Collection 1678901. ~567,000 records. **Indexed with images.** Covers wills, inventories, letters of administration, and guardianships.
- Physical originals at the **Berkshire County Probate Court** (Pittsfield). The FamilySearch indexed collection draws from these records.
- Probate files frequently name spouses, children, and neighbors — often the richest single document for reconstructing a family when vital records are thin.

---

## Land Records

- Deeds were recorded at the **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds** (Pittsfield) from the county's formation in 1761. The run through and beyond 1850 is substantially complete.
- The FamilySearch Wiki notes Massachusetts land/deed records were recorded at the county level from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial).
- **No dedicated digitized Berkshire County land volume appeared in the volume_search results** for 1820–1850 — this is a gap. Physical records at the Registry or microfilm at NEHGS/FamilySearch are the access routes.
- Grantor/grantee deed indexes can be used as a substitute address record, tracking when a family arrived or left a town.

---

## Military Records

Two conflicts fall squarely in the 1820–1850 window:

- **War of 1812 (1812–1815):** Service records and pension files at NARA; searchable on **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) and Ancestry. Massachusetts state militia records at the **Massachusetts Archives**.
- **Mexican-American War (1846–1848):** Service records and pension files at NARA via Fold3. Bounty Land Warrants issued under the 1847 and 1855 acts can place a veteran in a land transaction.

Pension files are among the most genealogically rich military records — they frequently contain birth dates, marriage details, and widow's testimony.

---

## Newspapers

Berkshire County had active local papers by the 1820s, including the *Pittsfield Sun*. These published marriage notices, death notices, legal notices, and sheriff's sale announcements that can substitute for missing vital records.

- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) — confirmed in external-links results; holds historical Massachusetts newspaper digitizations.
- The **Massachusetts Historic Newspapers** collection at the Massachusetts Digitization Initiative and Readex (America's Historical Newspapers) are additional routes.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds |
|------------|---------------|
| **Town Clerks** (each Berkshire County town) | Original birth, marriage, death registers |
| **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds** (Pittsfield) | Deeds and land records |
| **Berkshire County Probate Court** (Pittsfield) | Wills, estates, guardianships |
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | State vital records 1841+; state and colonial records |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** (Boston) | Largest regional genealogical library; holds "Vital Records to 1850" series and microfilm |
| **National Archives / NARA** (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal military records, pension files, passenger lists |
| **FamilySearch** | Indexed state-level collections + browse-only Berkshire volumes |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, military pensions, newspapers, passenger lists |
| **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military service and pension records |

---

## Cross-Border Search — Do Not Skip

Families near Berkshire County's western and northern edges routinely generated records in neighboring states. Always extend your search across the line.

### New York (western border — Columbia & Rensselaer Counties)
- New York **did not have statewide civil registration until 1880**. For 1820–1850, rely on: church records (FamilySearch has indexed NY church collections), the **New York State Censuses of 1825 and 1835** (which fill gaps between federal enumerations), and county clerk records.
- The Hudson River valley (Columbia County) and Troy area (Rensselaer County) were economically connected to western Massachusetts — migration across the line was common.

### Vermont (northern border — Bennington County)
- Vermont **town-level recording dates from 1760**; statewide civil registration began in **1857**. For 1820–1850, town clerk registers are the primary Vermont source.
- FamilySearch holds Vermont vital records collections. The Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) holds state-level records.

> ℹ️ The Berkshire County Genealogy wiki's Neighboring Counties table was unavailable (the page returned generic content). The New York and Vermont neighbors identified above are from known county geography.

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | Access Level | Where |
|-------------|-------------|-------|
| Town Vital Records (MA state collection) | ✅ **Indexed + images** | FamilySearch Collection 2061550 |
| Town Clerk Vital Records (Berkshire volume) | ⚠️ **Browse-only** (0% indexed, 512 images) | FamilySearch Vol. 004500891 |
| Church Records (MA state collection) | ✅ **Indexed + images** | FamilySearch Collection 1921657 |
| Pittsfield Congregational Church | ⚠️ **Browse-only** (0% indexed, 274 images) | FamilySearch Vol. 004500892 |
| Probate Records | ✅ **Indexed + images** | FamilySearch Collection 1678901 |
| Federal Census 1820–1850 | ✅ **Indexed** | FamilySearch, Ancestry.com |
| 1850 Mortality Schedule | ✅ **Indexed** | Ancestry.com |
| Land / Deed Records | ⚠️ **Physical or microfilm** | Berkshire Registry of Deeds; NEHGS |
| Military / Pension Records | ✅ **Indexed** | Fold3, Ancestry.com, NARA |
| Newspapers | ✅ **Full-text searchable** | Newspapers.com |
| Published "Vital Records to 1850" series | ✅ **Searchable** (where printed) | NEHGS, Internet Archive |

---

## Research Quirks to Keep in Mind

1. **Before 1841, vital records are town-level only.** The 1639 recording mandate existed but compliance varied. If an indexed search comes up empty, go directly to the browse-only Town Clerk volume (004500891) or contact the individual town clerk.
2. **The Berkshire-specific Town Clerk volume (004500891) cannot be name-searched** — its 512 images covering 1761–1850 must be paged through manually.
3. **Marriage intentions were dual-filed** — recorded in the bride's hometown and potentially also in the groom's town. Always check both.
4. **The "Vital Records to 1850" published series is often the fastest route** — many Berkshire County towns have a printed volume transcribing all records to 1850. Check NEHGS's catalog for your town before treating a gap as real.
5. **Cross-border families:** The NY state censuses of 1825 and 1835 fill the intercensal gaps not available in the federal record — a family that crossed into Columbia or Rensselaer County, NY between 1820 and 1830 may only appear there.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — 1840s–1860s

## Jurisdictional Context

Schuylkill County was formed in **1811** from Berks and Northampton Counties (FamilySearch standardPlace: *Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States*). By the 1840s–1860s, the county was fully established and experienced rapid growth driven by the anthracite coal industry, drawing large immigrant communities of Welsh, Irish, and German workers. No boundary changes affect the record trail during the target period — all county-level records for 1840–1870 were generated and filed under Schuylkill County.

> **Wiki coverage note:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania (all four sections: home, getting\_started, online\_records, research\_tips), Pennsylvania Vital Records, and Schuylkill County Genealogy all returned generic, non-Pennsylvania-specific content. All specific facts below are grounded in FamilySearch tool results only. Gaps where the wiki would normally provide detail are flagged explicitly.

---

## Record Types Available

### 1. 🟢 Federal Census — *Indexed + images*

The strongest digitized resource for the target period. FamilySearch holds **one digitized volume** (imageGroupNumber **007621224**):

- **Coverage:** Schuylkill County, U.S. Federal Census, **1850–1860**
- **Images:** 412
- **Indexing:** 96% name-indexed **and** full-text searchable — fully accessible by name search
- **Languages:** English

Ancestry.com also holds a curated Schuylkill County 1850 census collection: [Pennsylvania, U.S. 1850 Federal Census – Schuylkill County](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/)

> ⚠️ **Gap — 1840 census:** The 1840 federal census for Schuylkill County did **not** appear in the FamilySearch volume search for this window. Search FamilySearch and Ancestry separately for 1840 access.
>
> **Mortality schedules** accompanied the 1850 and 1860 censuses, recording deaths in the prior year — an important substitute for civil vital records in this period.

---

### 2. 🟡 Probate Records — *Full-text searchable (4% name-indexed)*

Two FamilySearch resources cover Schuylkill County probate:

**Statewide collection:**
- *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* (collection ID **1999196**)
- **2,304,118 images** statewide — includes Schuylkill County
- [Search this collection](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)

**County-level digitized volume** (imageGroupNumber **004812990**):
- **Coverage:** 1845–1880
- **Images:** 286
- **Indexing:** Only **4% name-indexed** — most names will not surface in a standard name search
- **Full-text searchable:** Yes — keyword/surname searches are possible
- **Language:** English

> ⚠️ **Search strategy:** Because indexing is only 4%, use the full-text keyword search rather than the name index. Supplement by browsing the volume image by image for the relevant time window.

Probate records (wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, letters of administration) are also held physically at the **Schuylkill County Courthouse** in Pottsville and at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** in Harrisburg.

---

### 3. 🔴 Church Records (Lutheran) — *Browse-only images, partial German*

FamilySearch holds **one digitized volume** of Schuylkill County Lutheran church records (imageGroupNumber **004288771**):

- **Coverage:** 1840–1875
- **Images:** 198
- **Indexing:** **0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable**
- **Languages: English and German** ⚠️
- **Access:** Must be browsed **image by image** — no search capability of any kind

> ⚠️ **This volume must be paged through manually.** Researchers must be able to read German for portions of the register.

Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are critical substitutes for civil vital registration in the 1840s–1860s. Schuylkill County had substantial German Reformed, Catholic (Irish and German), and Welsh Calvinist Methodist communities in addition to Lutheran congregations — but **no additional FamilySearch volumes** for those denominations appeared in the search results for this time window. Check denominational archives directly.

---

### 4. ❌ Vital Records (Civil Registration) — *Gap: no civil registration collection found*

No FamilySearch collections or digitized volumes for civil vital registration appeared for Schuylkill County in the 1840s–1860s window. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content, so the specific start date for Pennsylvania vital registration cannot be confirmed from tool results.

- Consult: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania\_Vital\_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)
- **Primary substitutes for this period:** church records (baptisms/marriages/burials), census mortality schedules, probate records, and cemetery records.

---

### 5. ❌ Land Records — *Physical/microfilm likely required*

No FamilySearch digitized volumes for Schuylkill County land or property records (deeds, mortgages, tax lists) appeared in the 1840–1870 search window. The one Ancestry external link for Pennsylvania tax records covers only **1768–1801** — well before the target period and useful only as background.

Physical holdings are likely at:
- **Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds**, Pottsville, PA — deed books, mortgage records
- **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg — copies or indexes
- **Family History Library microfilm** — check the FamilySearch catalog for county-level holdings

---

### 6. ❌ Military Records — *National Archives / State Archives*

The 1860s saw heavy Civil War participation from Schuylkill County. No FamilySearch digitized volumes for county military records appeared in the search results for this period. Records are held at:

- **National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)**, Philadelphia region — compiled military service records and pension files for Pennsylvania volunteers
- **Pennsylvania State Archives** — state adjutant general records, enrollment lists

---

### 7. ❌ Naturalization Records — *County courthouse (physical/microfilm)*

The anthracite coal boom drove heavy immigration to Schuylkill County in the 1840s–1860s. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — in Schuylkill County, that means the **Court of Common Pleas** in Pottsville. No FamilySearch digitized volumes for naturalizations appeared in the search results. Check:

- **Schuylkill County Courthouse**, Pottsville
- **FamilySearch catalog** for any microfilmed naturalization records

## Searcher Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No civil vital registration found for this period** — Church records and census mortality schedules are the primary birth/marriage/death sources. Confirm Pennsylvania's registration timeline at the FamilySearch Wiki before assuming records exist.
2. **Lutheran church records are bilingual and browse-only** — Volume 004288771 (1840–1875, 198 images) has zero indexing and no full-text search; it must be paged image by image. Some entries are in German.
3. **Probate volume is only 4% name-indexed** — Standard name searching will miss most records. Use the full-text keyword search and plan to browse by year range.
4. **Heavy multiethnic immigrant community** — Welsh, Irish, and German miners are well represented. Look beyond Lutheran records to Catholic, Welsh Calvinist Methodist, and German Reformed denominational archives for vital events.
5. **Neighboring counties** — The Schuylkill County Genealogy wiki page returned generic content; the neighboring counties list was not available from tool results. Schuylkill County borders Berks, Lebanon, Dauphin, Northumberland, Columbia, Carbon, and Luzerne Counties. Families near those borders likely generated records in adjacent jurisdictions — search those counties' records as well.
6. **1840 census not returned** — The 1840 federal census did not appear in FamilySearch's volume search for this window. Search FamilySearch and Ancestry independently for 1840 Schuylkill County census access.

---

**Bottom line for the 1840s–1860s:** The strongest starting points on FamilySearch are the **1850–1860 federal census** (96% indexed, fully searchable) and the **Pennsylvania Probate Records** collection (full-text searchable). Lutheran church records are digitized but require image-by-image browsing in both English and German. For births, marriages, and deaths, church records and mortality schedules are the workhorses in the absence of civil registration. Land, naturalization, and military records for this period will generally require a courthouse visit, microfilm, or a NARA request.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (circa 1780–1819, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed as a state:** December 14, 1819 (22nd state). The target period entirely predates statehood.
- **Governing jurisdictions during the target period:**
  - **Mississippi Territory (1798–1817):** Present-day Alabama formed the eastern portion. Created from land ceded by Georgia and territory previously claimed by Spain.
  - **Alabama Territory (1817–1819):** Carved from the eastern half of the Mississippi Territory when its western half became the state of Mississippi.
  - **Mobile District, Spanish West Florida (1780–1813):** The southwestern corner of present-day Alabama — Mobile and the coastal strip — remained under Spanish sovereignty until U.S. forces seized Mobile in April 1813.
- **Administrative center:** Natchez was the Mississippi Territory capital (in present-day Mississippi). St. Stephens (Washington County) served as Alabama Territory capital 1817–1819.
- **Population during period:** The region was thinly settled by Euro-Americans around 1800. The interior was largely Creek and Cherokee Nation territory until the Creek War of 1813–1814 opened it to American settlement. A significant settlement wave from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia followed that war. (*place_population* returned no data for this period — population figures are not available from FamilySearch for pre-statehood Alabama.)
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fur trade; cotton cultivation emerged in river valleys (Tennessee Valley, Mobile-Tombigbee basin) after 1810.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee Nations in the interior; Euro-American settlers (primarily of English, Scots-Irish descent from the Southeast seaboard states) on the frontier; French Creole and Spanish colonists in and around Mobile; enslaved African-descended people brought by Euro-American settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuits, Baptist associations on the frontier; Catholic Church centered in Mobile (dating to the French and Spanish colonial periods).
- **Key historical events:** Organization of Mississippi Territory (1798); Washington County formed (1800); U.S. seizure of Mobile from Spain (1813); Creek War 1813–1814; organization of Alabama Territory (1817); statehood (1819).

---

## Boundary changes

This is one of the most complex jurisdictional histories in early American genealogy. Records for the same family may span three distinct sovereign systems.

| Period | Authority | Notes |
|--------|-----------|-------|
| Pre-1763 | France (coastal/Mobile) | French settlement since 1702 |
| 1763–1780 | Britain | Mobile and Gulf Coast |
| 1780–1813 | Spain (Mobile District) | Coastal/southwestern Alabama only |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory | American-controlled interior and north |
| 1813–1817 | U.S. (Mobile County added) | After Spain expelled from Mobile |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory | Eastern portion of former Miss. Territory |
| 1819– | State of Alabama | Statehood Dec. 14, 1819 |

**County formation note:** Washington County (formed 1800 in the Mississippi Territory) was the first county covering present-day Alabama. It is the parent jurisdiction for most pre-1810 county-level records in the region. Other counties were carved from it and from formerly Creek/Spanish territory after 1813.

**Key quirk:** Records generated under the *Spanish* administration of Mobile (before 1813) are filed under the Spanish colonial system, not the Mississippi Territory. Searching FamilySearch or U.S. county records will not surface them — you must go to Spanish and French repositories (see Repository Guide below).

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in this jurisdiction during the target period (pre-1819) at any level — territorial, county, or statewide. Alabama did not begin statewide vital registration until the twentieth century.
- **What exists:** No territorial requirement for recording births or deaths. Marriage records are the exception: county clerks began recording marriages when counties were formally organized under territorial law. The FamilySearch collection **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (collection 1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images) covers the earliest county marriages from approximately 1809.
- **Where held:** County probate courts hold original marriage registers. FamilySearch has indexed county marriage records beginning 1809. Pre-1809 marriages in the territory are generally undocumented in civil records.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration in this period. Earliest county marriages on FamilySearch begin in 1809 (Washington County area). Marriage records before 1809 essentially do not exist in civil form.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (Catholic in Mobile; Methodist/Baptist circuit records elsewhere) are the primary substitute for vital events. See Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic Church (Mobile, continuous since French colonial period); Methodist circuits (active in Alabama frontier from ~1808); Baptist associations (active ~1808 onward).
- **Record types:** Catholic sacramental registers — baptisms, marriages, burials (dating from the Spanish period in Mobile). Methodist and Baptist records — minutes, membership lists, some baptism/marriage entries.
- **Where held:**
  - **Catholic/Mobile:** The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception (Mobile) holds sacramental registers dating to the Spanish colonial period. The Archdiocese of Mobile Archives holds colonial-era Catholic registers, some of which were microfilmed. Spanish-period Mobile church records are also described in the Archivo General de Indias holdings (see Colonial Records below).
  - **Methodist/Baptist:** Records are scattered across local churches and denominational archives. Many early circuit records have not been centrally archived or digitized.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950** (collection 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) — begins 1803, overlapping the territorial period.
- **Language:** Catholic records from the Spanish and French periods will be in Spanish or French. Later American-period Catholic records may be in English.

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** The FamilySearch wiki (["Alabama Genealogy," Territorial Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)) states that the Mississippi Territory took censuses in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery. They are not available as indexed FamilySearch records.
- **Federal census — 1810:** The first federal decennial census to include the Alabama region was the **1810 census**, which enumerated the Mississippi Territory (covering what would become Alabama). The FamilySearch collection **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890** (collection 2016756; 287,634 records, no images) begins with 1810.
- **Federal census — 1820:** The first census taken after statehood. By 1820 much of the Creek cession had been settled rapidly; this census captures the initial land rush.
- **No 1790 or 1800 federal census** covers this region — the territory was not part of an enumerated U.S. jurisdiction in those years (or the interior was still Native American territory).
- **Access:** The 1810 and 1820 federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) are physical/microfilm only at ADAH.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories; territorial court minutes; early county court records.
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins with county formation. Washington County (formed 1800) has the earliest surviving records.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985** (collection 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) — begins 1809.
- **Digitized browse-only volumes on FamilySearch:**
  - **Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808–1819** — imageGroup 004512889 (214 images). **Browse-only: 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image.
  - **Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820** — imageGroup 004512890 (96 images). **Browse-only: 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (Washington County Courthouse in Chatom for pre-1810 records); ADAH holds microfilm of many territorial-era court records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a **public domain (federal land) state** — land was distributed through the federal government, not through Alabama as a state-land state. This is a critical distinction: land patents are in federal, not state, records.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office (GLO) administered land entries. The Huntsville Land Office (opened 1811) was the first federal land office in present-day Alabama, handling entries in the Tennessee Valley. Additional offices followed as Creek cession lands opened.
- **Types:** Federal land patents and entries (the primary land-grant record); county deed books (for resale of already-patented land); Spanish and British colonial land grants in the Mobile area.
- **Federal patents:** Searchable free online at **glorecords.blm.gov** (BLM General Land Office Records). This is the essential starting point for any land research in Alabama.
- **Pre-American land grants:** Spanish colonial land grants (Mobile District, pre-1813) and British colonial grants (1763–1780) were not part of the federal GLO system. They are found in European archives (see Colonial Records below) and in some American confirmations of prior grants.
- **Digitized browse-only:** The territorial court and land records volume (imageGroup 004512889, 1808–1819) includes land records — browse-only, see above.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (federal patents, online free); county deed books at county courthouses and ADAH microfilm; Spanish/British grant confirmations in NARA and ADAH.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813–1814 (decisive for opening the Alabama interior); War of 1812 (Mississippi Territory militia units saw service); earlier territorial militia musters.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (War of 1812 service often generated bounty land claims in Alabama).
- **Where held:** **NARA** (Washington, D.C. / National Personnel Records Center) holds compiled military service records and pension files. Fold3.com has many War of 1812 and Revolutionary War pension records digitized and indexed (accessible via the external_links_search result for Fold3). **ADAH** holds some militia records for the territorial period.
- **War of 1812 bounty land warrants** are particularly relevant — many veterans settled in Alabama using bounty land patents, making military records and land records interlinked for this period.

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** For circa 1800, formal cemetery records are sparse. Catholic cemeteries in Mobile have the oldest organized burial records. Protestant frontier cemeteries were informal; many headstones are lost.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) is available per the external links returned. Coverage of pre-1820 Alabama burials is highly incomplete.
- **Physical records:** The Mobile Cathedral cemetery is the oldest organized burial record in the region (Spanish colonial period). ADAH holds some transcription projects.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Newspapers in the Mississippi Territory/Alabama region began ca. 1811–1813 (the *Mobile Centinel* was among the earliest in the territory's Alabama portion). Coverage for exactly 1800 is essentially zero — no papers existed in present-day Alabama at that date.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com is available for later territorial newspapers (per external links returned). The **Alabama Department of Archives and History** holds early Alabama newspaper microfilm. Chronicling America (Library of Congress) has some early Alabama territorial newspapers digitized.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** Most migrants to the Alabama region circa 1800 were internal domestic migrants from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia — not international immigrants. Standard international passenger lists are not the relevant source class here.
- **Relevant records:** Migration-era documents include: land entry paperwork, frontier pension applications, and removal records (for Creek/Cherokee neighbors). For Mobile, which had an international port, Spanish-period passenger and residency records exist in the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Where held:** NARA for federal records; Archivo General de Indias (Seville) for Spanish colonial Mobile.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial tax lists; county personal property and land tax digests.
- **Substitute value:** Critical substitute for the missing 1800 federal census and for years between territorial censuses. Tax lists from 1800–1810 can place a person in the territory and identify neighbors.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds Mississippi Territory and early Alabama Territory tax records. Some have been published/transcribed by genealogical societies. The FamilySearch collection **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890** (collection 2016756) includes some tax-list substitutes from 1810 onward.
- **Access:** Primarily physical/microfilm at ADAH; some transcriptions published by the Alabama Genealogical Society.

### Colonial records (a record class unique to this jurisdiction)
For the Mobile area specifically, a distinct colonial record series predates any American territorial records:
- **Spanish period (1780–1813):** Census returns, church registers, land grants, and notarial records of the Mobile District. Held at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) — physical access or hire a researcher. Copies of some records are at the **Library of Congress** (Washington, D.C.). Microfilm copies are at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**. Per the FamilySearch wiki ["Alabama Genealogy," Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **French period (1702–1763):** Records at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** (Aix-en-Provence, France) and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Per the same FamilySearch wiki section.
- **British period (1763–1780):** Records in British colonial archives (The National Archives, Kew, London) and NARA.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place & period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1809–1950 (collection 1598408); Probate Records 1809–1985 (collection 1537764); Compiled Census & Substitutes Index 1810–1890 (collection 2016756); Church Records 1803–1950 (collection 1986396); 2 browse-only image volumes (territorial court/land 1808–1819; Washington Co. deeds/probate 1803–1820) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Alabama — the primary source for land grants in this federal-land state | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (1810, 1820) | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Military service records, pension files (War of 1812, Creek War era) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave.com | Cemetery transcriptions (coverage thin for pre-1820) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of **2 digitized volumes** matching Alabama for 1780–1819 — this is the complete set returned (no nextPageToken). Both are browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). FamilySearch's indexed collections all start at 1803 or later; no indexed records exist on FamilySearch for the Alabama region before 1803.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery, AL | Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); territorial tax lists; militia records; early county records on microfilm; published transcriptions | In-person; some microfilm via interlibrary loan; adah.alabama.gov |
| **NARA (National Archives)**, Washington, D.C. | Federal territorial records; military service records; pension files; War of 1812 bounty land warrants; General Land Office correspondence | In-person; many records on Fold3 or Ancestry |
| **Washington County Courthouse**, Chatom, AL | Original deed books and probate records from county formation (1800) | In-person or mail request |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records of the Mobile District — censuses, church registers, land grants, notarial records (pre-1813) | In-person or hire a researcher; some digital facsimiles via Portal de Archivos Españoles (PARES) |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer**, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (1702–1763) | In-person or hire a researcher |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives**, Mobile, AL | Microfilm copies of French and Spanish colonial records; early Mobile city records | In-person; contact for reproduction requests |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C. | Copies of Spanish colonial records from the Mobile District | In-person; some digitized via loc.gov |
| **The National Archives**, Kew, London | British colonial records (1763–1780) | In-person or online (some digitized via nationalarchives.gov.uk) |

---

## Records NOT online

- Mississippi Territory censuses of **1801, 1805, and 1808** (the 1810 is partly indexed via FamilySearch collection 2016756) — physical/microfilm at ADAH only.
- Territorial tax lists pre-1810 — physical/microfilm at ADAH.
- Territorial militia muster rolls — physical at NARA and ADAH.
- Spanish colonial Mobile records (census, land grants, church registers, notarial) — physical in Seville; some microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives and Library of Congress.
- French colonial records — physical in Aix-en-Provence; some microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- Early Methodist circuit and Baptist association records — scattered in local church archives; not centrally digitized.
- The two FamilySearch image volumes (imageGroup 004512889, 004512890) are **digitized but not indexed or full-text searchable** — they must be browsed image by image with no name-search capability.

---

## Known record losses

- **Interior Alabama pre-1813:** For areas that remained Creek Nation territory until after the Creek War (essentially everything east and north of the Tombigbee/Black Warrior river system), **no Euro-American civil records were created** for the period ending 1813. These communities simply were not under U.S. jurisdiction.
- **County courthouse fires:** Several Alabama county courthouses suffered fires in the 19th century, destroying original deed, probate, and court records for counties formed from the Creek cessions. Washington County (the oldest) has the most intact early record set; records for counties formed 1810–1819 should be checked individually for losses.
- **No statewide birth/death registration:** There are no systematic birth or death records for the entire pre-statehood period, and this gap extends well into the 19th century for Alabama.

---

## Research tips

1. **Work backward from statehood, not forward from colonial records.** The most productive sequence for circa 1800 is: start with the 1810 federal census (first to enumerate the region), then use tax lists and territorial censuses at ADAH to push back to 1800–1805, then use land entry records (BLM GLO) to pin location and arrival date.

2. **Identify which side of the Mobile District boundary your ancestor was on.** If your ancestor was in the Mobile/Tombigbee coastal area before 1813, they were under Spanish jurisdiction — U.S. territorial records will not exist for them before that date. Search Spanish colonial records instead. If they were in the interior (Tombigbee frontier, Tennessee Valley), they were under U.S. Mississippi Territory authority from 1798 and the ADAH is the primary repository.

3. **Federal land records are essential for this period.** Alabama is a federal land state. The BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) is free and searchable; land patents name the patentee, the land office, the date, and the legal description. Many settlers first appear in the documentary record through their land entry. Land offices opened across Alabama from 1811 onward as Creek cession lands opened.

4. **Territorial censuses are not federal censuses.** The Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) at ADAH are separate from the federal decennial census. They are the only population enumeration for the Alabama region before 1810. These are physical records — request microfilm or in-person access at ADAH.

5. **The FamilySearch wiki pages for Alabama-specific record types (Vital Records, Land and Property, Census, Church Records, Probate Records, Genealogy overview) all returned only generic content** during this survey — none of the Alabama-specific wiki articles resolved. Check [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy) directly for the most current guidance; some sections (Territorial Records and Colonial Records) are confirmed to exist per the wiki_search results.

6. **The two browse-only FamilySearch volumes must be worked image by image.** ImageGroup 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808–1819, 214 images) and imageGroup 004512890 (Washington County deed/probate, 1803–1820, 96 images) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Use the search-images skill to browse them page by page, or order the microfilm through ADAH.

7. **For Mobile-area ancestors, Spanish is a required research language.** Spanish colonial records — the primary source for Mobile before 1813 — are in Spanish. The Archivo General de Indias holds the definitive collection. The Library of Congress has copies of some Mobile District materials.

8. **Check adjoining jurisdictions.** Families on the territorial frontier straddled the Georgia–Mississippi Territory and Tennessee–Mississippi Territory borders. Records for families who moved into Alabama just before 1800 may be found in **Georgia** (for settlers from the east) and **Tennessee** (for settlers coming down the Tennessee River valley). The territorial census rolls and early land entries often name the state of origin.

---

# Locality Research Guide: Arkansas, Spanish Colonial Period (ca. 1686–1800)

## Jurisdictional Context

The territory now called Arkansas was never an independent colonial administrative unit before 1800. It belonged to a succession of French and Spanish colonial jurisdictions:

| Period | Controlling Power | Administrative Unit |
|---|---|---|
| 1686–1763 | France | La Louisiane (Lower Louisiana) |
| 1763–1800 | Spain | Provincia de Luisiana (Upper & Lower Louisiana) |
| 1800 (Oct.) | France | Re-ceded secretly by Treaty of San Ildefonso |
| 1803 | United States | Louisiana Purchase |

**Arkansas Post** (established 1686) was the only significant European settlement in the region throughout this period and the administrative hub where virtually all colonial records were created. Records for this place were generated under Louisiana colonial governance, administered from New Orleans, and the researcher must work *both* Arkansas-specific and Louisiana-level sources together as a single connected research trail.

> **Critical quirk:** Arkansas was not a U.S. territory until 1819 and did not become a state until 1836. FamilySearch's Arkansas collections begin no earlier than 1819. All genealogical sources for the pre-1800 period come through colonial church, military, civil, and land record systems — not U.S.-era county infrastructure.

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 1. Church / Sacramental Records ⭐ *Primary source for vital events*

Civil registration did not exist. The only records of births (baptisms), marriages, and deaths (burials) were maintained by Roman Catholic clergy at Arkansas Post.

**FamilySearch digitized volume — BROWSE-ONLY (Spanish)**
- **Image Group 008814402** — *Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)*, Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, 1763–1800
  - 64 images | 0% name-indexed | not full-text searchable | language: **Spanish**
  - Must be browsed image by image with no search capability. Researcher must read Spanish.
  - [Browse on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/image/index?owc=008814402)

**Physical / microfilm holdings**
- **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** (Little Rock, AR) — holds original French Catholic missionary registers from the early 1700s onward, predating Spanish control
- **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) — holds transcribed versions of the French Catholic registers; also a key repository for Spanish-era church documents
- **Louisiana Church Records, 1718–1925** (FamilySearch collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905), ~987,654 records, indexed + images) — the Diocese of Louisiana et des Deux-Florides administered Arkansas Post; this Louisiana-level collection may hold connected sacramental records covering the same community

> *Sources: [FamilySearch Wiki — Arkansas Genealogy, Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records); FamilySearch volume_search result, image group 008814402*

---

### 2. Civil & Military Records (Spanish Colonial Administration)

Under Spanish rule, the commandant at Arkansas Post kept civil and military records, including:
- **Padrones** — household census lists naming heads of household, family members, and sometimes enslaved individuals. An irregular series was taken throughout the Spanish period.
- **Military post records** — muster rolls, correspondence, and administrative lists of soldiers stationed at Arkansas Post.

**Repositories:**
- **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock, AR — primary U.S. repository for surviving Spanish colonial civil records; holds padrones and post records
- **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)**, Seville, Spain — the original repository for Spanish colonial administrative records from Louisiana. Records relating to Arkansas Post are found in the Papeles de Cuba section (the administrative records of Spanish Cuba, which had jurisdiction over Louisiana)
- **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C. — holds microfilm copies of selected Papeles de Cuba / AGI records relating to the Louisiana–Arkansas region

> *Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)*

---

### 3. Land Records

Spain issued formal land concessions (*concesiones*) to settlers throughout the colonial period. After the Louisiana Purchase, U.S. land commissioners confirmed (or rejected) Spanish and French land grants, creating a paper trail that names original grantees and their heirs.

**Access paths:**
- **Arkansas History Commission** — holds transcripts and copies of Spanish land concessions for the Arkansas Post district
- **Bureau of Land Management — General Land Office (GLO)** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) — post-1803 U.S. confirmations of Spanish land grants; searchable by grantee name and often links back to the original colonial grant
- **NARA (National Archives)** — records of the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners for Louisiana/Arkansas, which adjudicated Spanish-era land claims after 1803; these records name original colonial-era grantees

---

### 4. Notarial / Legal Records (French Colonial Period, pre-1763)

For the French period specifically, notarial acts (contracts, inventories, wills) were kept by the Superior Council of Louisiana:

- **FamilySearch Image Group 004330992** — *French Colonial Notarial Acts (Superior Council Records)*, Louisiana, 1699–1769
  - 149 images | 0% indexed | not full-text searchable | languages: **French and Spanish**
  - Browse-only; covers the broader Louisiana colony including Arkansas Post pre-1763
  - [Browse on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/image/index?owc=004330992)

---

### 5. Probate Records

- **Louisiana Probate Records, 1756–1984** (FamilySearch collection [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341), ~456,789 records, indexed + images) — date range begins 1756, within the colonial period; covers the broader Louisiana colonial jurisdiction and may include estates probated at New Orleans for individuals connected to Arkansas Post

---

### 6. Colonial Sacramental Registers — New Orleans Diocese

Since Arkansas Post fell under the Diocese of Louisiana et des Deux-Florides (headquartered in New Orleans), the New Orleans sacramental register series is a parallel source:

- **FamilySearch Image Group 004330991** — *Sacramental Registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans*, Orleans, Louisiana, 1720–1803
  - 264 images | 0% indexed | not full-text searchable | languages: **French and Spanish**
  - Browse-only; covers the colonial diocesan territory that included Arkansas Post
  - [Browse on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/image/index?owc=004330991)

---

## What Does NOT Exist for This Period

| Record Type | Status |
|---|---|
| U.S. Federal census | First enumeration covering Arkansas: 1830; Arkansas Territory first included 1820 |
| State/territorial vital registration | No civil registration at any level before statehood (1836); no statewide registration until the 20th century |
| County courthouse records | No county infrastructure existed before U.S. territorial period (post-1803) |
| Name-indexed FamilySearch records | Zero indexed records on FamilySearch overlap with the pre-1800 Arkansas period |

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock, AR | Spanish padrones, land concessions, transcribed church registers, colonial post records | On-site; some digitized finding aids at [ark-ives.com](https://www.ark-ives.com) |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original French & Spanish-era sacramental registers | Contact diocese archivist |
| **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)**, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial administrative records (Papeles de Cuba section) | On-site; [PARES portal](https://pares.cultura.gob.es) for partial digital access |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of AGI / Papeles de Cuba records for Louisiana–Arkansas | On-site; some finding aids online |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | U.S. land commission records confirming Spanish grants (post-1803) | On-site and Ancestry.com |
| **FamilySearch** | Image group 008814402 (64 browse-only Spanish images, 1763–1800); Louisiana collections 1612905 and 2078341 (indexed) | Free at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Confirmed Spanish land grant patents | Free at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) |

---

## Key Research Guidance

1. **Start at FamilySearch with image group 008814402.** It is the only digitized collection specifically covering Arkansas Post 1763–1800. It is 64 images in Spanish, browse-only — work through it page by page.
2. **Spanish is required.** All surviving Spanish-era records — sacramental registers, padrones, land concessions — are written in 18th-century Spanish. French-era records (pre-1763) are in French. Plan for translation or bring a specialist.
3. **Follow the record trail through Louisiana.** Arkansas Post was administered from New Orleans. The FamilySearch Louisiana Church Records (collection 1612905) and the New Orleans sacramental register volume (004330991) are direct complements to the Arkansas Post register and should be searched alongside it.
4. **For land ownership, work forward into the U.S. period.** Spanish land grant confirmations filed with U.S. land commissioners after 1803 are often the most accessible entry point — they name the original colonial-era grantee and can anchor earlier research.
5. **Contact the Arkansas History Commission directly.** It is the primary custodian of surviving Spanish colonial civil records for this region, and its holdings extend beyond what is available digitally.
6. **The Archivo General de Indias is the ultimate source.** For any individual connected to the military garrison or civil administration at Arkansas Post, the AGI's Papeles de Cuba section (accessible through the PARES portal or on-site in Seville) is where the original administrative records reside.

---

*Coverage note: The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas (home, getting started, online records, research tips) returned only generic content for this place; the Arkansas Genealogy and Arkansas Vital Records wiki pages also redirected to a generic page. The findings above are grounded in FamilySearch tool results and the wiki search excerpts from [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) and [Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records). Consult those wiki pages directly for any updates.*

Now launching the full Step 3 parallel survey batch:

Here is the compiled locality guide based on everything the tools returned:

---

# 📍 Locality Research Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory, c. 1780–1803

**Place:** Ohio (pre-statehood) · **Period:** 1780–1803 · **Compiled:** 2026-09-22

---

## Jurisdictional History & Boundary Changes

In 1790, the land now called Ohio did not yet exist as a state or even a named territory in its own right — it was administered as part of the **Northwest Territory**, established by the **Northwest Ordinance of 1787**. That territory encompassed present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. Ohio achieved statehood on 1 March 1803, the first state carved from the Northwest Territory. *(Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio)*

**County formation was rapid and boundaries constantly shifted.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki *(https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)*:
- **Washington County (1788)** — the first county organized; covered most of eastern Ohio, centered on Marietta.
- **Hamilton County (1790)** — organized next; covered the southwestern corner, centered on Cincinnati.

Because boundary changes were frequent throughout the territorial and early statehood period, researchers must determine *which county held jurisdiction at the precise time of the event* before searching any record set. A place that appears under one county name after 1803 may have been in Washington or Hamilton County in 1790.

**Two special land districts add a geographic split:**

| District | Location | Survey System | Record Repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers | Metes-and-bounds | **Virginia State Library** |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio | Township grid | **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland |

These are *geographic* splits, not temporal ones. Which repository holds a given record depends entirely on where within Ohio the land was located — you cannot assume Ohio courthouses or FamilySearch Ohio collections cover these zones. *(FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)*

---

## The Pre-Statehood Search Trail: Two Place Name Labels

**Critical quirk:** FamilySearch's digitized volumes for this era are filed under **two different place labels**, not one:
- **"Northwest Territory, United States"** — for records created before county formation or at the territorial level (1788–1799)
- **Individual county names** (Washington County, Hamilton County) — for records created once counties were organized

You must actively search *both* labels to cover the full 1787–1803 research window as one continuous trail. Failing to check the Northwest Territory label will leave territorial land records invisible.

---

## Record Types: What Survives, What Doesn't

### 🔴 Vital Records (Births, Deaths) — MAJOR GAP

No civil registration of births or deaths existed in Ohio or the Northwest Territory in 1790. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ohio Vital Records and Ohio Land and Property were requested but returned only generic content — Ohio-specific registration start dates were not stated in any tool result. Do not assume certificates exist. *(Verify directly at: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records)*

**Primary substitute:** Church registers (see below).

---

### 🟢 Land Records — STRONGEST SURVIVING SOURCE

Land records are the best-documented record class for this period.

**FamilySearch Indexed Collection:**
- **Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840** · Collection ID 1542187 · 234,567 records · 117,283 images
  Starting date of 1787 puts this squarely in the territorial era.
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187

**Digitized Volumes (from volume_search — 2 volumes returned, 2 total in system):**

| Volume | Place Filed Under | Record Type | Dates | Images | % Indexed | Full-text? | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 005112233 | Northwest Territory, United States | Territorial Land Records | 1788–1799 | 51 | **0%** | No | **Browse-only** |
| 005112240 | Washington County, Ohio | County Tax Records | 1799–1803 | 73 | 12% | No | Mostly browse-only |

- **Volume 005112233** (Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799): 51 images, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image-by-image with no search capability.
- **Volume 005112240** (Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803): 73 images, only 12% name-indexed — partial search possible; majority must be browsed.

**Off-FamilySearch:**
- **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov): Federal land patents for Ohio as a public-land state.
- **Virginia Military District warrants** → Virginia State Library (not in Ohio or FamilySearch Ohio collections).
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** → Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.
- **Ohio History Connection**, Columbus: Holds early territorial court and land records. *(FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)*

---

### 🟢 Marriage Records — EARLIEST INDEXED SOURCE

- **Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013** · Collection ID 1803785 · 1,523,678 records · 761,839 images
  Begins **1789** — Washington County marriage records overlap the target period directly.
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785

---

### 🟡 Church Records — VITAL SUBSTITUTE

Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are often the **only surviving source for vital events** in the territorial period. Settlement in 1790 was largely Methodist, Presbyterian, and Congregationalist at Marietta and Cincinnati.

- **Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950** · Collection ID 2246917 · 678,234 records · 339,117 images
  Begins 1787. Coverage for 1790 will be sparse given the tiny settler population.
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917

---

### 🟡 Tax Records — PARTIAL COVERAGE

- **Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850** · Collection ID 1987542 · 345,890 records · 172,945 images
  Begins **1800** — just after the target window of 1790. *(https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542)*
- Volume 005112240 (Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803) covers the very end of the territorial period but is largely browse-only.
- **Pre-1800 tax records are a gap** — no FamilySearch collection was found with earlier coverage.

---

### 🔴 Death Records — OUT OF PERIOD

- **Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001** · Collection ID 1417891 · 2,156,789 records
  Begins **1840** — provides zero coverage for 1790. Church burial registers are the only substitute.

---

### 🔴 Census Records — 1790 DOES NOT COVER OHIO

The 1790 Federal Census did **not** enumerate the Northwest Territory — Ohio was absent. The **1800 Federal Census** is the first to include Ohio residents (covering the territory in its final years before statehood). No territorial census was found in any tool result. If your ancestor settled Ohio before 1800, the 1800 census is your first federal enumeration, supplemented by tax lists and land records.

---

### 🟡 Military Records

- **Fold3** (fold3.com): U.S. service records. Relevant for **Revolutionary War veterans** (who settled Ohio under land grant programs) and the **Northwest Indian Wars (1790–1795)**, including the Battle of Fallen Timbers.
- **NARA** (archives.gov): Federal pension files, bounty land warrants, muster rolls. Revolutionary War pension files in particular may document families who relocated to Ohio shortly after 1790.

---

### 🔴 Newspapers — Very Limited Pre-1800

The *Centinel of the North-Western Territory* (Cincinnati, 1793) was Ohio's first newspaper, but pre-1800 territorial newspaper coverage is minimal. **Newspapers.com** (newspapers.com) holds historical newspapers but coverage at this date should be verified directly. Not a reliable primary source for 1790.

---

### Cemetery Records

**Find A Grave** (findagrave.com): Transcribed cemetery records. Coverage for 1790 burials will be very sparse — early settlers often had informal grave sites. Worth checking but expect gaps.

---

## Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holdings Relevant to 1790 |
|---|---|
| **Ohio History Connection**, Columbus | Early territorial court and land records; county records |
| **FamilySearch.org** | County marriages (1789+), church records (1787+), land records (1787+), tax records (1800+), territorial land volumes (browse-only) |
| **Virginia State Library** | Virginia Military District land warrants |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land & settlement records |
| **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Military records, pension files, bounty land warrants |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Census (1800 is first for Ohio), military collections |

---

## Key Quirks & Warnings

1. **Search "Northwest Territory" AND county names.** FamilySearch volumes for 1788–1799 are filed under "Northwest Territory, United States" — volume 005112233 (territorial land records) will not surface under an Ohio county search alone.

2. **Determine the county of jurisdiction first.** In 1790, virtually all Ohio settlement fell under Washington County (Marietta area) or Hamilton County (Cincinnati area). Searching later county names for 1790 events will fail.

3. **Virginia Military District records live in Virginia, not Ohio.** Any land west of the Scioto and east of the Little Miami must be pursued at the Virginia State Library.

4. **Connecticut Western Reserve goes to Cleveland.** The Western Reserve Historical Society holds records for northeastern Ohio — separate search from the Ohio History Connection.

5. **Both pre-statehood digitized volumes are effectively browse-only.** Volume 005112233 is 0% indexed (51 images to browse manually); volume 005112240 is only 12% indexed (73 images, mostly manual).
