# 📍 Locality Research Guide: California, United States — Gold Rush Era (1848–1865)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

California was admitted to the Union as the **31st state in September 1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely. The Gold Rush began **January 24, 1848**, when James W. Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill in Coloma; roughly **300,000 people** poured into California from across the United States and abroad in the years that followed (*Wikipedia, "California Gold Rush"*). The state was organized into 27 original counties in 1850; county boundaries shifted frequently through the early 1850s as mining camps grew into established communities — this matters for locating records.

**Quirk:** Verify which county governed your ancestor's location in the *specific year* of the event you're researching, as county lines moved considerably in the early statehood period.

**Pre-statehood note:** Before 1848, California was Mexican territory. Records created under Spanish and Mexican authority exist but document a different population (see Mission Records below).

---

## Record Types, Coverage & Digitization

### 🗳️ Census Records — *Best starting point for the era*

**1852 California State Census** — FamilySearch volume `006601001`
- 522 images | **88% name-indexed** | **Full-text searchable**
- Covers 1850–1852 | Access: [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org)
- ✅ This is the most searchable record class for the Gold Rush decade and should be your first stop.

**1850 U.S. Federal Census** — ⚠️ Partially destroyed; some county returns for California are missing entirely. Where returns survive, search at FamilySearch and Ancestry.com. The 1852 state census is the key substitute for lost 1850 returns.

**1860 U.S. Federal Census** — Complete for California. Includes a **mortality schedule** listing deaths in the prior year (1859). Available at Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.

---

### 📋 Vital Records — County-Level Only in the 1850s

**No statewide civil registration existed in California during the 1850s.** Registration was kept at the **county level** beginning in 1850, with uneven coverage — especially in newly-forming mining counties. The FamilySearch Wiki's California Vital Records page did not return California-specific registration dates in this survey; treat all vital record availability for this period as county-dependent.

**Indexed FamilySearch collections:**

| Collection | ID | Records | Images | Date Range | Link |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California, County Births | 2017276 | 789,456 | 394,728 | 1850–1919 | [Search](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276) |
| California, County Marriages | 1452832 | 567,890 | 283,945 | 1850–1952 | [Search](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832) |

County death records for the 1850s were not returned as a distinct indexed collection in this survey — check county courthouses and the **California State Archives** (Sacramento).

---

### ⛏️ Mining Claim Records — ⚠️ Browse-Only

**FamilySearch volume `006601002`** — Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco, 1849–1855
- 340 images | **0% name-indexed | NOT full-text searchable**
- Must be browsed **image by image** — no search function available.

Beyond this volume, mining claims were recorded at **county recorder's offices** in the major mining counties: El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Placer, Nevada, Amador, and others. These records are largely held physically at county courthouses or in microfilm at the **California State Archives** and **FamilySearch**. These are a uniquely Gold Rush–specific record class — if your ancestor filed a claim, his name, date, and claim location should appear.

---

### 🚢 Ship Passenger Lists & Port Arrival Registers

**FamilySearch volume `006601003`** — Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858
- 298 images | **0% name-indexed | NOT full-text searchable**
- Must be browsed **image by image**.

**San Francisco passenger manifests** (the dominant port of entry for sea arrivals around Cape Horn or via Panama) are held at **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, California**, per the FamilySearch Wiki (*California Genealogy, "Gold Rush Records"*, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). These are also searchable via **Ancestry.com** ([U.S. Federal Census & Immigration collections](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)).

---

### 📜 Voter Registration — Great Registers

**FamilySearch Collection 1923340** — *California, Great Registers, 1866–1910*
- 1,345,678 records | 672,839 images | Dates: **1866–1910**
- The Great Registers begin in 1866 — just after the core Gold Rush decade — but they document men who arrived during the rush and stayed. Each entry typically includes: **name, age, birthplace, occupation, physical description, and county of residence**. This is invaluable for confirming a man's presence and biographical details for the Gold Rush generation.
- Access: [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340)

---

### 🌾 Land Records

California is a **federal land state** (public domain). The first transfer of federal land to private ownership is documented in **land patents** — searchable free at the **BLM General Land Office Records** website ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)). These document the legal beginning of private land ownership.

Subsequent sales (deed records) are at **county recorder's offices**, some microfilmed at FamilySearch. **Tax assessment rolls** (county level) may document a miner's property holdings before a formal patent was issued.

---

### ⛪ Mission Records — Pre-Gold Rush Population

**FamilySearch Collection 1804372** — *California, Mission Records, 1769–1850*
- 98,765 records | 49,382 images | Dates: 1769–1850
- Access: [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372)
- These document the **Spanish colonial and Mexican-era population** — Native Californians, Spanish settlers, and Californio families. They are **not** a source for Gold Rush-era Anglo migrants arriving after 1848, but are essential if your ancestor married into a Californio family or had pre-statehood California roots. Note these are in **Spanish** — the researcher must read the original language.

---

### ⚖️ Court & Naturalization Records

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — typically California Superior Courts at the county level. Mining-camp justice-of-the-peace records also exist. Holdings are at:
- **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** — federal court records
- **California State Archives, Sacramento** — state and county court records
- County courthouses (original deed books, guardianships, name changes)

---

### 🪖 Military Records

Few California men served in organized units specifically in the 1850s, but many Gold Rush migrants were veterans of earlier service (Mexican-American War, 1846–1848). Pension files and service records are at **NARA** and searchable at **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)). California state militia records are at the **California State Archives**.

---

### 📰 Newspapers — Often the Only Record of Death or Arrival

Gold Rush–era California newspapers are a critical substitute source, especially for deaths in remote mining camps:
- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)) — subscription
- **California Digital Newspaper Collection** ([cdnc.ucr.edu](https://cdnc.ucr.edu)) — **free, full-text searchable**
- **Chronicling America / Library of Congress** ([chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)) — free

**San Francisco's *Alta California*** (1849–1891) is the single most important Gold Rush–era newspaper — arrival notices, mining news, and death notices appeared regularly.

---

### ⚰️ Cemetery Records

Many Gold Rush-era graves were unmarked or in remote mining areas. Where headstones exist:
- **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) — community-contributed
- **BillionGraves** — photographed headstones

Newspaper obituaries are often the only documentary evidence of death for this period and place.

---

### 📚 Manuscript & Special Collections (Not Online)

These repositories hold the richest Gold Rush–era research materials in the world — essential for serious research, but requiring in-person or correspondence access:

| Repository | Highlights |
|---|---|
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Largest Gold Rush manuscript collection: diaries, letters, overland trail accounts, mining journals (*California Genealogy, "Gold Rush Records"*, FamilySearch Wiki) |
| **California State Library, Sacramento** | California History Room; overland trail accounts, mining journals, newspapers |
| **California Historical Society, San Francisco** | Photographs, maps, manuscripts |

---

## Repository Quick-Reference

| Repository | Record Types | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) | State census, county births & marriages, Great Registers, Mission records, mining claim volumes, port arrivals | Free; some browse-only |
| [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com) | Federal census, passenger lists, California collections | Subscription |
| [NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA](https://www.archives.gov) | Ship passenger manifests, naturalizations, federal court records | In-person or by request |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | State records, militia, probate, court records | In-person; some digitized |
| County Recorder's Offices (mining counties) | Mining claims, deeds, vital records | Varies by county |
| [BLM GLO Records](https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free online |
| [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) | Military service & pension records | Subscription |
| [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) | Digitized historical newspapers | Subscription |
| [CDNC (cdnc.ucr.edu)](https://cdnc.ucr.edu) | California newspapers, full-text search | Free |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush manuscripts, diaries | In-person |
| California State Library | California history manuscripts | In-person; some digitized |

---

## Key Quirks & Gotchas

1. **1850 federal census partially destroyed** — some California county returns are entirely missing; the **1852 State Census** (FamilySearch vol. 006601001, 88% indexed) is the primary substitute.
2. **No statewide vital registration in the 1850s** — county-level only; coverage is uneven, especially in fast-forming mining counties.
3. **Mining claim registers are browse-only images** — FamilySearch vol. 006601002 (340 images) has zero name-indexing; plan to browse page by page.
4. **Port arrival registers are browse-only images** — FamilySearch vol. 006601003 (298 images) has zero name-indexing.
5. **County boundaries changed rapidly in the early 1850s** — verify which county governed your location in the specific year of the record.
6. **Great Registers begin in 1866** — outside the Gold Rush decade proper, but capture the same men a generation on with rich biographical detail.
7. **San Francisco was the dominant port of entry** — sea arrivals' manifests are at NARA San Bruno, not just online indexes.
8. **California is a federal land state** — first-title land patents are at BLM GLO, not the county courthouse.
9. **Mission records are in Spanish** — require reading the original language; they document pre-Gold Rush populations, not 1848+ Anglo migrants.
10. **FamilySearch returned 14 digitized volumes** for California 1848–1865 — only the first 3 are detailed above; additional volumes covering this period exist and can be explored further.
11. **Bancroft Library is irreplaceable for Gold Rush research** — diaries, overland trail accounts, and mining journals held there are not digitized and cannot be found online.

---

All claims above are grounded in collections_search, volume_search, wiki_search, Wikipedia, and external_links_search results.*

---

# Locality Research Guide: New York City, 1700s (Colonial Period)

**Place:** New York City (New York County / Manhattan), New York, United States
**Period:** 1700–1800
**Jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial) through 1776; State of New York from 1777
**Scope of search:** FamilySearch returned 5 New York state-level collections and 1 digitized volume specifically for New York City; all four wiki place pages returned generic content (no New York-specific content retrieved); specific wiki_read pages likewise resolved to a generic fallback. Claims below are drawn from FamilySearch wiki_search results and Wikipedia only.

---

## Jurisdictional Context

New York City occupies what was historically **New York County** (present-day Manhattan). The 1700s fall entirely within the **British colonial period**: England seized the former Dutch colony of New Amsterdam in 1664 and renamed it New York. Throughout the 1700s the city served as both the commercial hub of the Province of New York and its administrative capital. British occupation during the Revolutionary War (1776–1783) disrupted some record creation. After 1783, the city fell under New York State jurisdiction. The five modern boroughs were not unified until 1898, so 18th-century records for what is now Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, or Staten Island were kept under **Kings County**, **Queens County**, **Westchester County**, and **Richmond County** respectively — separate jurisdictions that must be searched independently.

> ⚠️ **No civil vital registration existed anywhere in New York during the 1700s.** Church records are the sole substitute for birth, marriage, and death documentation in this period. The FamilySearch Wiki page on New York Vital Records was not retrievable in this session; specific registration start dates cannot be cited from that source without it.

---

## Record Types

### 1. Church Records — *Primary source for vital events*

**Access: Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection); browse-only Dutch-language images (one digitized volume)**

This is the single most important record class for 18th-century New York City. According to the FamilySearch Wiki article [New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records), the key denominations and their records are:

| Denomination | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Dutch Reformed** | Oldest continuous series in NYC, beginning 1639; registers cover baptisms, marriages, burials |
| **Anglican (Church of England)** | Trinity Church (est. 1697) kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers |
| **Presbyterian** | Active in the city by the 1720s–1730s |

The Wikipedia article on New York City (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City) also confirms that "the Dutch Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian churches kept extensive records" during this period.

**FamilySearch holdings:**
- **Collection:** [New York, Church Records, 1640–1940](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) (id: 1469062) — covers the full 1700s window; name-indexed and browsable
- **Digitized volume:** Image group **007733180** — Dutch Reformed Church Registers, New York City, **1700–1776**, 211 images
  - ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image
  - ⚠️ **Language: Dutch** — the researcher must be able to read 18th-century Dutch script or use a specialist

**Physical / off-FamilySearch holdings:**
- The **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** and the **New-York Historical Society** hold extensive colonial-era church collections not fully digitized online ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- Trinity Church Archives (Manhattan): original Anglican registers

---

### 2. Land Records

**Access: Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection)**

Land conveyances are a major research tool for colonial New York. According to the [FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records), "land conveyances" are among the key colonial-era sources. Wikipedia confirms that colonial-era records include "land patents."

- **Collection:** [New York, Land Records, 1630–1975](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) (id: 2078654) — covers the 1700s
- **New York State Archives** (Albany): holds original colonial land patents and grants issued by the Crown and provincial governors
- Deed books recorded at New York County level

---

### 3. Probate Records — *Especially valuable for family structure*

**Access: Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection); published abstracts**

According to the [FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records):
> "Wills proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** are indexed in the **Abstracts of Wills** series published by the New-York Historical Society."

The Prerogative Court had colony-wide probate jurisdiction throughout the 1700s. Its records are a particularly rich source for identifying heirs, household composition, and property.

- **Collection:** [New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) (id: 1542780) — covers the full 1700s
- **Abstracts of Wills series** (New-York Historical Society): published multi-volume index — search this first for colonial wills

---

### 4. Court Records

**Access: Physical / microfilm — digitization gap on FamilySearch**

The [FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) names **"court records of the Mayor's Court"** as a key source, alongside the **"New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives."** Wikipedia adds that colonial records include "court records." These document litigation, debt, guardianship, and other proceedings that name family members.

- **New York State Archives** (Albany): New York Colonial Manuscripts — the central archive for 18th-century provincial government and court records
- **New York City Municipal Archives**: City-level records

---

### 5. Tax Records

**Access: Indexed + images at end of period; earlier records physical only**

According to the [FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records): "Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards" of colonial New York.

- **Collection:** [New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432) (id: 1678432) — touches only the very end of the 1700s (1799–1800 overlaps the target window)
- Earlier colonial-era tax lists are at the **New York State Archives** and **New-York Historical Society** — not fully digitized on FamilySearch

---

### 6. Military / Militia Records

**Access: Physical / external**

The [FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records) notes: "Colonial New York Province maintained militia rolls that list men of military age, useful for identifying residents." The Revolutionary War also generated service and pension records.

- **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/): curated military records — indexed in external links for this jurisdiction
- **National Archives (NARA)** (https://www.archives.gov/): Revolutionary War service records and pension files
- **New York State Archives**: provincial militia rolls

---

### 7. Census / Population Lists

**Access: Indexed (post-1790 only)**

No federal census was taken until 1790, which falls at the very end of the target period. Some colonial-era musters and enumeration lists survive, but coverage is fragmentary. The 1790 federal census (available on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch) names the head of household for New York County.

- **Ancestry.com** (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/): U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1790

---

### 8. Newspapers

**Access: Subscription (Newspapers.com)**

Wikipedia confirms that the **New York Gazette** (founded 1725) and other colonial-era papers published vital notices, legal advertisements, and runaway servant/slave notices that can document individuals in the record gap.

- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/): Historical newspapers including colonial New York titles

---

### 9. Cemetery Records

**Access: Online index (Find A Grave)**

- **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/): includes transcriptions from Trinity Church burial ground and other colonial-era cemeteries
- Note: many 18th-century burial sites in Manhattan have been disturbed; records held by churches and the NY Historical Society are more reliable than surviving physical stones

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What it holds for this period |
|---|---|
| **New York State Archives** (Albany) | Colonial Manuscripts, land patents, Prerogative Court probate files, provincial militia/tax records |
| **New-York Historical Society** | Abstracts of Wills, church records, manuscripts, colonial newspapers |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** | Published abstracts, church register transcripts, colonial research tools |
| **New York City Municipal Archives** | City-level records; colonial-era city records |
| **Trinity Church Archives** | Anglican registers from 1697 |
| **FamilySearch** (online) | 3 indexed collections covering 1700s (church, land, probate); 1 browse-only Dutch Reformed volume (007733180) |
| **Ancestry.com** | 1790 census; various NY collections |
| **NARA** | Revolutionary War service and pension records (post-1775) |
| **Fold3** | Military records |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Status |
|---|---|
| Church records (general) | ✅ Indexed + images — collection 1469062 |
| Dutch Reformed registers 1700–1776 | ⚠️ Browse-only images, Dutch-language — vol. 007733180 |
| Land records | ✅ Indexed + images — collection 2078654 |
| Probate records | ✅ Indexed + images — collection 1542780 |
| Tax records (1799–1804 only) | ✅ Indexed + images — collection 1678432 |
| Court / Mayor's Court / Colonial Manuscripts | ❌ Physical only (NY State Archives) |
| Militia / military (colonial) | ❌ Physical only (NY State Archives); Fold3 for Revolutionary era |
| Earlier colonial tax lists | ❌ Physical only (NY State Archives, NY Historical Society) |

---

## Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No civil vital registration in the 1700s** — church records are your only birth/marriage/death substitute for this entire century.
2. **The Dutch Reformed volume (007733180, 1700–1776) is in Dutch** and must be browsed image-by-image with no search capability — plan for a Dutch-language reading session or engage a specialist.
3. **New York County = Manhattan only** — Kings (Brooklyn), Queens, Westchester (Bronx area), and Richmond (Staten Island) were separate jurisdictions; a family living in what is now Brooklyn will appear in Kings County records, not NYC ones.
4. **British occupation of NYC (1776–1783)** disrupted some record creation and survival; gaps in this window should be expected.
5. **Wills for the 1700s were proved in the colony-wide Prerogative Court**, not a local county court — start with the New-York Historical Society's *Abstracts of Wills* series before searching county-level probate indexes.
6. **The 1790 federal census** (first enumeration, touching the very end of the period) lists heads of household only, not all family members — use it as an anchor but not a complete family record.
7. **FamilySearch wiki pages** for New York City and New York State (Vital Records, Land and Property, Probate, Church Records, City Genealogy) did not return specific content in this session — browse them directly at FamilySearch.org for additional detail and indexing quirks.

---

## Suggested Starting Points

1. Search the **FamilySearch Church Records collection** (id: 1469062) by name for your ancestor.
2. If Dutch Reformed ancestry is suspected, **browse image group 007733180** (1700–1776) — 211 pages of Dutch-language registers.
3. Search **Probate Records** (id: 1542780) and cross-check against the **NY Historical Society's Abstracts of Wills**.
4. Search **Land Records** (id: 2078654) for deeds and patents.
5. Contact the **NYGBS** or **NY Historical Society** for colonial manuscript collections and published church register abstracts not yet digitized online.
6. For the end of the period, use the **1790 federal census** on Ancestry or FamilySearch and the **Tax Assessment Rolls** (id: 1678432, 1799–1804).

---

# Locality Guide: Virginia — Revolutionary War Era (1775–1783)
## Military Service & Wartime Records

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Virginia transitioned from a royal colony to a Commonwealth in 1776. Throughout the war it operated under both county-court and parish administrative structures; no statewide civil vital registration existed during this period. The state retained jurisdiction over its own militia while the Continental Congress managed the Continental Line. After the war, Virginia fulfilled bounty-land obligations through grants in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** — meaning some post-service records exist in Ohio, not Virginia itself.

⚠️ **Critical gap:** Virginia's 1790 federal census schedules were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. County personal property tax lists beginning in 1782 are the earliest systematic substitute for locating free adult male heads of household across the state.

---

### Record Classes & Access

#### 1. 🎖️ Military Service Records — Continental Line
**What they contain:** Muster rolls, pay vouchers, enlistment papers, and officer rosters documenting service in the Virginia Continental Line.
**Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), **Record Group 93** (Revolutionary War rolls).
**Access:** [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) — physical and digitized holdings. Fold3.com ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) provides digitized military record images.
**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783* (Collection ID 1945678) — [familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)
**Digitization level:** Partially indexed (collection); see below for specific volumes.
**Source:** [Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

---

#### 2. 🏠 Virginia Militia Records
**What they contain:** Musters, pay orders, and muster rolls for the state militia — a separate series from the Continental Line and held at a different repository.
**Where held:** **Library of Virginia**, Richmond — the primary custodian of Virginia militia records. Not fully digitized.
**Access:** [lva.virginia.gov](https://www.lva.virginia.gov) — online catalog; physical visit or microfilm order for most rolls.
**Digitization level:** Largely physical/microfilm only; not yet fully available online.
**Source:** [Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

---

#### 3. 💰 Pension Files & Bounty-Land Warrant Applications
**What they contain:** Pension applications filed by veterans or their widows (post-1818, 1832 acts) contain detailed sworn narratives of service, family relationships, marriages, and ages — among the most genealogically rich documents in existence. Bounty-land warrants (pre-1855) similarly name heirs.
**Where held:** NARA **Record Group 15** (pension and bounty-land files).
**FamilySearch volume:** Image Group **005301447** — *Revolutionary War land bounty warrants*, Virginia, 1779–1800 — 341 images.
- `recordSearchablePercent`: **0%** — not name-indexed
- `fulltextSearchable`: **false**
- ⚠️ **Browse-only** — must be paged image by image; no keyword or name search available on FamilySearch.
**Also at:** Fold3.com and Ancestry.com (pension files are indexed there). The Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) has an index to pension files.
**Source:** [Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)

---

#### 4. 🌾 Post-War Bounty Lands — Virginia Military District of Ohio
**What they contain:** Survey plats and warrant records issued to Virginia Continental Line veterans for land in the Virginia Military District (south-central Ohio). These records connect a veteran's wartime service to a documented land grant after the war.
**Where held:** Warrant and survey records at the **Library of Virginia** (Virginia State Library); also Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (GLO) for final patents.
**Access:** [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) for BLM patents. Library of Virginia for warrant applications.
**Note:** Because the land was in Ohio, also check the **Ohio Historical Society** and Ohio-county deed records for survey chains.
**Source:** [Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)

---

#### 5. 📋 Tax Lists (Census Substitutes, 1782–1799)
**What they contain:** Annual county personal property tax lists enumerating free white males age 16+, enslaved persons, horses, and cattle. Beginning in 1782, these are the **earliest statewide substitute** for the missing 1790 Virginia federal census.
**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850* (Collection ID 1456723) — [familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723)
**FamilySearch volume:** Image Group **005301449** — *State enumerations / tax lists*, Virginia, 1782–1799 — 87 images.
- `recordSearchablePercent`: **0%** — not name-indexed
- `fulltextSearchable`: **true** ✅
- **Full-text searchable** — keyword and name searching works; no browse-only limitation.
**Access tip:** Search via FamilySearch full-text search on this volume.
**Source:** Tool result; [Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)

---

#### 6. ⚖️ County Court Records
**What they contain:** Court order books record oaths of loyalty, supplying of troops, processing of estates of fallen soldiers, guardianship of orphans, and local wartime administration.
**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920* (Collection ID 2134567) — [familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567)
**FamilySearch volume example:** Image Group **005301448** — *County court order books*, Augusta County, Virginia, 1775–1795 — 158 images.
- `recordSearchablePercent`: **61%** — partially name-indexed ✅
- `fulltextSearchable`: **false**
- **Partially indexed** — name search works for roughly 3 in 5 images.
**Note:** Other Virginia counties' court order books exist at county level or at the Library of Virginia; coverage varies by county. Augusta County is an especially important wartime county given its frontier position.

---

#### 7. 🏛️ Land & Property Records
**What they contain:** Deeds, grants, and patents showing land acquisition/transfer — useful for tracing wartime and post-war economic activity and family relationships.
**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900* (Collection ID 1734285) — [familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)
**Physical:** County deed books at county courthouses and Library of Virginia.

---

#### 8. ⛪ Church Records
**What they contain:** Anglican/Episcopal parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) were the primary vital record system during this era, as no civil registration existed. Dissenting congregations (Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, Lutheran) kept separate registers.
**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929* (Collection ID 1598230) — [familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230)
**Key repositories:**
- Library of Virginia (many Anglican vestry books)
- Denominational archives (Presbyterian Historical Society, Friends Historical Library, etc.)
**Vital Records note:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Virginia Vital Records page was not available in the wiki tool corpus — this is a coverage gap. No statewide civil registration existed until the late 19th century; church and county records are the only sources for this period.

---

#### 9. 📜 Probate Records
**What they contain:** Wills, inventories, and administration bonds — valuable for identifying heirs, widows, and property of men who died during the war.
**FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900* (Collection ID 1734285) — covers wills and related records.
**Physical:** County courthouses and Library of Virginia.

---

#### 10. 📰 Newspapers
**What they contain:** Virginia Gazette and other colonial/early state newspapers published troop musters, loyalty oaths, wartime proclamations, and occasionally casualty notices.
**Access:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) (from external links survey). Also: **Chronicling America** at the Library of Congress ([chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)).

---

#### 11. 🪦 Cemetery Records
**Access:** [FindAGrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com) — curated burial records including many Revolutionary War veterans.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Continental Line service records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15) | Online & in-person |
| **Library of Virginia** (lva.virginia.gov) | Virginia militia records, county records, bounty-land warrants | Online catalog + microfilm |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Collections 1945678, 1734285, 1598230, 1456723, 2134567 | Free online |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Digitized military records & pension files | Subscription |
| **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Virginia Military District of Ohio patents | Free online |
| **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery/burial records | Free online |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers | Subscription |

---

### Key Quirks & Warnings

1. **The 1790 Virginia federal census is destroyed** — use county personal property tax lists from 1782 onward as substitutes. FamilySearch volume 005301449 covers these and is full-text searchable.

2. **Continental Line ≠ Militia** — these are entirely separate record series held at different repositories (NARA vs. Library of Virginia). Search both; a man may appear in one but not the other.

3. **Virginia Military District of Ohio** — post-war bounty land warrants for Virginia veterans were redeemed as Ohio land grants. If your ancestor disappears from Virginia records after the war, check Ohio District survey and warrant records at the Library of Virginia and BLM GLO.

4. **Pension files postdate the war** — the 1818 and 1832 Pension Acts generated the richest narratives. If your ancestor filed after 1832, a widow's application may add marriage date and children's names decades after the fact.

5. **FamilySearch Wiki Virginia-specific pages** (Virginia_Military_Records, Virginia_Vital_Records, Virginia_Land_and_Property, Virginia_Church_Records, Virginia_Probate_Records, Virginia_Census) were not returned by the wiki tool during this survey — all redirected to a generic fallback. Visit [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia) directly for current wiki content.

6. **No statewide civil vital registration** existed in Virginia during 1775–1783. Church registers (Anglican/Episcopal vestry books, plus dissenting congregation records) are the only contemporary vital sources. Loyalty oaths and county court records can supplement.

7. **FamilySearch volume 005301447** (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 341 images) is **browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable. You must page through it image by image.

# 📜 Locality Research Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana — Early 1800s (c. 1800–1850)

## Jurisdictional Context

**New Orleans** (standardPlace: `New Orleans, Orleans, Louisiana, United States`) sits at the heart of **Orleans Parish**, the two being coterminous (the city and the parish share the same boundaries). Louisiana organized itself into civil *parishes* — not counties — a French and Spanish inheritance that shapes where every record was created and where it is held today.

The city passed through four governing regimes in rapid succession, each of which left its own record-creating infrastructure:

| Era | Dates | Record language |
|---|---|---|
| French colony | 1718–1763 | French |
| Spanish colony | 1763–1800 | Spanish |
| Briefly French again | 1800–1803 | French |
| U.S. Territory → State | 1803–present | English (with French persisting) |

Louisiana became a U.S. territory in 1803 and a state in 1812. The underlying civil-law system (Napoleonic Code, not English common law) never changed with the flags — it still governs today. That means **notarial archives, not deed books**, are the foundation of property and legal documentation; **successions, not probate files**, handle estates; and **tutorships, not guardianship petitions**, cover minors.

---

## Disaster History and Its Effect on Records

### What Was Lost

Two catastrophic fires swept through New Orleans under Spanish rule:
- **Great Fire of 1788** — destroyed approximately 856 buildings, including most of the French Quarter, along with many French colonial-era records.
- **Conflagration of 1794** — destroyed another 200+ buildings.

Repeated **yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and periodic flooding** further degraded archival holdings throughout the early 1800s.

**The single most important survival fact for researchers:** notarial records survived far better than church records from the pre-fire era because notaries were required to keep duplicate registers. Church records suffered more, but St. Louis Cathedral maintained copies that were forwarded to the diocese — which is why sacramental registers survive from 1731 despite the fires.

### What Survived — and Where

The table below organizes surviving record types by their relevance as either primary sources or disaster-era substitutes.

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 1. 🕯️ Church / Sacramental Records — **Primary Vital Records Source**

**Why they matter above all others:** Louisiana had *no statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths* during the early 1800s. The Catholic Church's sacramental registers — baptisms, marriages, and burials — are the closest equivalent to modern vital records for this period. They predate civil registration by over a century.

- **St. Louis Cathedral** (New Orleans) holds continuous registers from **1731 to the present**, with gaps, including through the fire years. Duplicate registers forwarded to the Archdiocese explain their survival.
- The **Archdiocese of New Orleans** holds the master collection of baptism, marriage, and burial registers from St. Louis Cathedral and other parish churches.
- Language: **French** (1718–1769) → **Spanish** (1769–1803) → **English or French** (after 1803). You must be able to read the original language — these are not translated.

**FamilySearch access:**
- **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (Collection ID: 1612905) — indexed with images; records span the full target period. Access at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905
- FamilySearch has microfilmed many Archdiocese registers.
- Source: [Louisiana Church Records — Catholic Sacramental Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic)

⚠️ **Flag:** Records in French and Spanish require reading those languages in 18th–19th century handwriting. Many entries use archaic abbreviations. Browse-only volumes may not be name-indexed.

---

### 2. 📋 Notarial Records — **Unique to Louisiana; Critical Substitute for Deeds, Wills, and More**

Notarial records are the beating heart of New Orleans genealogy and the most important substitute when other record types have gaps. A notary authenticated virtually every significant transaction: property sales, marriage contracts, estate successions, tutorships of orphaned children, emancipations, and slave transactions.

- The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating back to **1734** (post-fire survivors from 1733+), continuing to the present. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy — Notarial Archives](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives))
- **Colonial-era notarial records** (French period 1718–1769; Spanish period 1769–1803) are held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** in the Old U.S. Mint building in New Orleans.
- After 1803, post-Louisiana Purchase notarial records are at the **Notarial Archives Research Center**.

⚠️ **Critical quirk:** Notarial acts are organized by **notary name and date**, not by the party's name. To use them effectively, you need an approximate date and (ideally) the name of the notary involved. Without that, you must browse chronologically — which is labor-intensive.

**FamilySearch digitization:**
- **1 digitized volume** found: Image Group `004990115` — "Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)," Orleans, Louisiana, **1803–1820**, 167 images. **0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable; in French and English.** This must be browsed image by image with no keyword search. Language reading ability required.

---

### 3. 📖 Probate / Succession Records

In Louisiana, probate is called **"succession."** These records document the settlement of estates and can include inventories listing all household property (and, before 1865, enslaved people), debts, heirs' names, and relationships — making them among the richest genealogical sources for family reconstruction.

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (Collection ID: 2078341) — indexed with images, spanning the target period. Access at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341
- Original records for Orleans Parish successions are at the **Orleans Parish Civil District Court** and at the **Louisiana State Archives** in Baton Rouge.
- Notarial acts related to successions (see above) are also at the Notarial Archives Research Center.

---

### 4. 🗳️ Census Records

Federal census enumerations are among the most accessible tools for New Orleans in this period and survive intact:

| Census year | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1810 | Orleans Territory | Territorial census, pre-statehood |
| 1820 | Orleans Parish, Louisiana | First post-statehood census |
| 1830 | Orleans Parish | Name-indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| 1840 | Orleans Parish | Name-indexed |

- Available on **FamilySearch** (free) and **Ancestry.com** (subscription). Federal census records for this period are at **NARA** (National Archives and Records Administration): https://www.archives.gov/
- Louisiana territorial censuses (pre-1812) can help establish presence before statehood.

---

### 5. 🏠 Land / Property Records

Because Louisiana uses the civil-law notarial system, **there are no county deed books** as in other U.S. states. Property transfers were executed before a notary and are filed in the **Notarial Archives** (see §2 above).

For **federal land grants** (especially after 1803, when the U.S. government began issuing patents):
- **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO):** https://glorecords.blm.gov/ — free online access to federal land patents for Louisiana.
- **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge) holds territorial-era land records and Spanish land grants.
- Colonial-era land grants (French and Spanish) are at the **Louisiana Historical Center**.

---

### 6. ⚖️ Court Records

The civil-law system produced distinctive court record types:
- **Tutorships** — guardianship of minor orphans; filed at the parish level.
- **Interdictions** — equivalent to modern incompetency proceedings.
- **Naturalizations** — pre-1906 naturalization records can appear in any court of record; Orleans Parish District Court holds many.
- **Civil and criminal suits** — at the Orleans Parish Civil and Criminal District Courts.

These records are held at the **Orleans Parish courts** and at the **Louisiana State Archives**.

---

### 7. 💀 Death Records / Mortality Index

- **"Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964"** (Collection ID: 1543892) — name index only (no images), beginning 1819. Access at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892
- Note: The FamilySearch Wiki specific Louisiana vital records page was not available in this survey (returned a generic fallback). Consult the Archdiocese of New Orleans burial registers (see Church Records, §1) as the primary mortality source before 1819.

---

### 8. 💍 Marriage Records

- **"Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957"** (Collection ID: 1798054) — indexed with images, but its date range begins **1837**, after the early 1800s target window. Access at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054
- For marriages in the early 1800s, use **St. Louis Cathedral marriage registers** (see Church Records, §1) and **marriage contracts in the Notarial Archives** (§2) — both survive from the pre-fire era and are the correct substitute.

---

### 9. ⚓ Immigration and Passenger Lists

New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the United States throughout the early 1800s, second only to New York. Passenger lists survive and are indexed:
- **NARA** holds original passenger arrival records for New Orleans.
- **Ancestry.com** has indexed New Orleans passenger lists (accessible via: https://www.ancestry.com/).
- **Fold3** holds military records including War of 1812 materials (New Orleans was the site of the Battle of January 1815): https://www.fold3.com/

---

### 10. ⛪ Free People of Color and Enslaved Ancestors

New Orleans in the early 1800s had one of the largest communities of free people of color in the antebellum South. Specific record sources:
- **Notarial Archives**: emancipation acts, purchase of freedom documents, slave transactions — all executed before a notary.
- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers**: baptism, marriage, and burial records for enslaved and free Black parishioners, often recorded separately but in the same volumes.
- **Succession records**: inventories of enslaved people by name are common in estate records.
- **FamilySearch collection** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" includes records for people of color.

---

---

## Disaster-Survival Summary and Substitute Strategy

| If this record is missing or destroyed... | Use this substitute |
|---|---|
| Civil vital records (none existed until later) | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) — Archdiocese of New Orleans + FamilySearch collection 1612905 |
| Pre-1788 fire church records | Notarial Archives marriage contracts and succession inventories name family members |
| Pre-1788 fire colonial records generally | Spanish-era Cabildo records; Louisiana Historical Center colonial notarial records |
| Deed / property records (no deed books) | Notarial archives (property transfers executed before notary) + BLM GLO federal patents |
| Probate / wills | Succession records at Orleans Parish Court + "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (FamilySearch 2078341) |
| Vital records post-1803, pre-civil registration | Church registers (Archdiocese) + death index 1819+ (FamilySearch 1543892) + notarial succession inventories |

---

## Key Quirks and Cautions

1. **No civil vital registration** existed in Louisiana during the early 1800s. Statewide registration did not begin until 1914. Church sacramental registers are the de facto vital records for this period — treat them as your first stop, not a last resort.
2. **Language barrier is real.** Records from 1800–1803 may still be in Spanish or French; records after 1803 are often bilingual. You must read the original language. FamilySearch collection 1612905 includes non-English records without translation.
3. **Notarial records are organized by notary, not by surname.** Without a date and a notary's name, access is extremely difficult without an in-person index consultation at the Notarial Archives Research Center.
4. **The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed most pre-1788 built records** in the French Quarter. Anything claiming to be a primary French colonial record from before 1788 should be scrutinized carefully — true survivals are rare. Notarial records are more likely to have survived because duplicates were kept.
5. **"Parish" means two different things in Louisiana.** Civil parishes (like Orleans Parish) are the equivalent of counties in other states. Ecclesiastical parishes (like St. Louis Cathedral's parish) are church jurisdictions. They often but do not always overlap.
6. **The FamilySearch-digitized notarial volume (1803–1820, image group 004990115)** is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed page by page. It covers post-Louisiana Purchase records only.
7. **The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Louisiana** (Louisiana Vital Records, Orleans Parish Genealogy, Louisiana Church Records, Louisiana Land and Property, Louisiana Probate Records, Louisiana Census, Louisiana Notarial Records) all returned only generic fallback content in this survey. Consult those pages directly at familysearch.org/wiki for the most current guidance, as the content may be available there even if it was not retrieved here.
8. **Neighboring parishes** for cross-border searching: Jefferson Parish (west), St. Bernard Parish (east), and St. Tammany Parish (north, across Lake Pontchartrain). Families in the greater New Orleans area may have generated records in these parishes. The neighboring parishes table from the Orleans Parish Genealogy wiki page was not returned in this survey — verify at FamilySearch Wiki.

---

- **FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages** (all four sections for Louisiana, plus all specific Louisiana record-type pages) returned generic fallback content — no Louisiana-specific data was retrievable through those tools in this survey. The findings above are grounded in `wiki_search` results, `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and Wikipedia.

- The **"Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957"** collection begins after the early 1800s; there is a coverage gap for indexed pre-1837 marriage records on FamilySearch.

## Locality Guide: Tracing Immigrants Through the Port of Boston, 1840s

**Place:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
**Period:** 1840–1850 (focused)
**Scope:** Port-of-entry and immigrant settlement records

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Boston was one of the five principal U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s. The decade saw a dramatic surge in arrivals — by 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, driven by the Great Famine (1845–1852) (Wikipedia: *Boston*). Customs passenger lists for this period are held in **NARA Record Group 36** and are the primary port-of-entry source, but they are lean documents: a typical 1840s Boston arrival list records **name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only** — neither townland nor county within Ireland or other origin countries appear on these mid-century forms. Finding specific origins almost always requires combining the passenger list with church records, newspaper notices, or naturalization papers (FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts Emigration and Immigration — Port of Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)).

---

### 1. 🚢 Port Arrival Records — The Starting Point

#### Customs Passenger Lists, Port of Boston, 1820–1891
| Detail | Data |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch Collection** | *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* — Collection ID [1784312](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) |
| **Digitized Volume (1840–1850)** | Image group **003345210** — 389 images |
| **Name-indexed?** | ⚠️ **3% indexed** — essentially not name-searchable via standard record search |
| **Full-text searchable?** | ✅ Yes — use FamilySearch full-text search on this volume |
| **Originals** | National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA), NARA RG 36 — [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |
| **Also on Ancestry** | Yes — the passenger lists are indexed and browsable at Ancestry.com |

> **Access note:** The one FamilySearch digitized volume covering 1840–1850 (image group 003345210) is **full-text searchable but only 3% name-indexed**. You cannot reliably find an ancestor by name search alone within FamilySearch — use full-text search or browse image-by-image. Ancestry.com's indexed version of this collection is often more navigable for this decade.

> **Coverage gap:** `volume_search` returned a total of **1 digitized volume** for this period. Additional volumes may exist in the broader collection (1820–1891); check both FamilySearch and Ancestry for complete coverage.

---

### 2. 📋 Naturalization Records

**FamilySearch Collection:** *Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906* — Collection ID [1459213](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) — indexed and searchable.

Before the Naturalization Act of 1906, immigrants could naturalize in **any court of record** — federal, state, or local. Boston-area naturalizations from the 1840s may appear in:
- **U.S. Circuit Court or U.S. District Court** (NARA, Waltham)
- **Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas**
- **Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court**

Two-step process: a **Declaration of Intent** ("first papers," filed within a few years of arrival) and later a **Petition for Naturalization**. The declaration is often the earlier and more informative document. 1840s records are typically brief, but the court and date can anchor a timeline.

**Originals:** NARA Boston (Waltham) for federal court naturalizations; Massachusetts Archives (Boston) for state court records.

---

### 3. ✝️ Church Records — Often More Specific Than Passenger Lists

**FamilySearch Collection:** *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* — Collection ID [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — indexed and searchable.

Catholic parish registers are especially critical for Irish Famine-era immigrants. The **Cathedral of the Holy Cross** and **St. Patrick's Church** served large Irish immigrant congregations from the 1840s onward; their baptism, marriage, and burial registers are held at the **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** (FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts Church Records — Boston Area Churches](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)).

> **Why church records often beat passenger lists for origins:** A baptism register entry may note the Irish parish or townland of origin — information the customs passenger list will not give you.

Also check Protestant denominations (Congregational, Methodist, Episcopal) for non-Catholic immigrants from Britain and Germany arriving in the same decade.

---

### 4. 📰 The Boston Pilot — Missing Persons Notices

The *Pilot* (Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper) published a steady stream of "Missing Persons" advertisements from the 1840s onward — notices placed by relatives searching for immigrants who had lost contact with family back home or elsewhere in America (Wikipedia: *Boston*). This resource is invaluable for Irish research and frequently names the Irish parish or county of origin, the ship, and the year of arrival. Search the **Boston Pilot Missing Persons Database** directly.

---

### 5. 🏠 Census Records

| Census | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **1840 Federal Census** | Names head of household only | Confirms presence in Boston; other members listed by age/sex tally only |
| **1850 Federal Census** | Names every household member | First census to list all individuals; records birthplace at country level |
| **1850 Mortality Schedule** | Deaths in the year preceding the census | Useful for tracing immigrant deaths shortly after arrival |

Boston is in **Suffolk County** in all of these enumerations. Available on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and FindMyPast.

---

### 6. 📜 Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths in Boston)

**FamilySearch Collection:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* — Collection ID [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — indexed and searchable.

> **Registration note:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts Vital Records and Suffolk County Genealogy returned only generic content in this session and could not confirm specific start dates for Massachusetts registration from tool results. Visit [Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records) and [Suffolk County, Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Suffolk_County,_Massachusetts_Genealogy) directly for current guidance on when town-level registration began and what survives.

---

### 7. ⚖️ Probate Records

**FamilySearch Collection:** *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* — Collection ID [1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — indexed and searchable.

Suffolk County probate records. Even immigrants with modest estates may appear — estate inventories name heirs, establishing relationships. Intestate proceedings are also filed here and often name children and spouses.

---

### 8. 📰 Newspapers

Historical Boston newspapers of the 1840s are available through **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)). Death notices, ship arrival columns, and community announcements supplement official records — particularly for prominent arrivals or those with local ties.

---

### 9. 🎖️ Military Records

**Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) holds military service records and pension files. Some immigrants who naturalized quickly enlisted in the 1840s–50s; pension files generated after service can contain rich biographical data including birthplace, physical description, and family details.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)** | Customs passenger lists (RG 36), federal court naturalizations | In-person; digitized portions on NARA and Ancestry |
| **Massachusetts Archives (Boston)** | State court naturalizations, state vital records | In-person; many collections digitized |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers (Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, others) | By appointment |
| **FamilySearch.org** | All collections listed above — free online | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Passenger lists (indexed), census, vital records, newspapers | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Boston newspapers | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military records | Subscription |

---

### Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Access Level |
|---|---|
| Port of Boston Passenger Lists, 1840–1850 (vol. 003345210) | ⚠️ Full-text searchable; **3% name-indexed** — browse or use full-text search |
| Massachusetts Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (coll. 1784312) | Indexed collection — name-searchable |
| Massachusetts Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (coll. 1459213) | Indexed collection — name-searchable |
| Massachusetts Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (coll. 2061550) | Indexed collection — name-searchable |
| Massachusetts Church Records, 1630–1920 (coll. 1921657) | Indexed collection — name-searchable |
| Massachusetts Probate Records, 1635–1991 (coll. 1678901) | Indexed collection — name-searchable |

---

### ⚠️ Gaps & Key Cautions

1. **1840s passenger lists don't show specific origins.** Country of origin only — not Irish county, German state, or English town. You'll need church records, the Boston Pilot, or Canadian landing records (if the immigrant first crossed via Quebec) to pin down the exact place of origin.
2. **Great Famine timing.** The major Irish surge begins around 1845. Earlier 1840s arrivals skew more toward English, Scottish, and German immigrants. Adjust your strategy accordingly.
3. **The FamilySearch digitized volume is barely indexed.** At 3% name-indexed, a standard FamilySearch record search will miss most names. Use full-text search on image group 003345210, or go to Ancestry's indexed version of the collection.
4. **FamilySearch Wiki coverage gap.** The Massachusetts Vital Records, Suffolk County Genealogy, and Massachusetts Emigration and Immigration wiki pages returned only generic content during this survey. Consult them directly at FamilySearch for current, Massachusetts-specific guidance.
5. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered.** Any court of record could accept a naturalization — check federal, state, and local court records, not just one series.

# Locality Research Guide: Native American Tribes in Indian Territory (Oklahoma), Mid-1800s

**Jurisdiction:** Indian Territory, United States (standardPlace)
**Period:** ca. 1830–1880
**Compiled:** 22 September 2026

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Indian Territory was established by the Indian Removal Act of 1830 as federally designated land for relocated Native nations. The **Five Civilized Tribes** — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — were forcibly relocated there in the 1830s–1840s via the Trail of Tears. Numerous other tribes were also assigned to the region under federal treaty arrangements.

**Critical research implications for this period:**

- Indian Territory had **no county-level civil government** and **no civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths. Tribal enrollment rolls and missionary/church records are the primary substitutes.
- The **Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA)**, then called the Office of Indian Affairs, administered federal oversight through individual agencies — its records form the backbone of the federal paper trail.
- Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until **1907**. All mid-1800s records are therefore pre-state territorial and tribal records, not state records.
- The FamilySearch Wiki does **not** have a dedicated research page for "Indian Territory, United States" — all four `wiki_place_page` sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned generic content. Consult the specific pages below instead.
- Specific constructed wiki pages for Oklahoma_Vital_Records, Oklahoma_Genealogy, Cherokee_Nation_Tribal_Rolls, and Dawes_Commission_Tribal_Rolls all redirected to generic content — named as gaps below.

---

## Record Types, Availability, and Access

### 1. 🏆 Tribal Enrollment Rolls — PRIMARY SOURCE

Tribal rolls are the genealogical backbone for this region and period. They recorded tribal membership for political and economic purposes (treaty annuities, allotments, and later citizenship).

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
> **Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959**
> Collection ID: 1987432 | 567,890 records | 283,945 images
> 🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432
> **Digitization level: Indexed + images**

**Digitized volume — Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870:**
> Image Group: 002298871 | 940 images | **99% name-indexed** | **Full-text searchable**
> **Digitization level: Indexed + images (full-text searchable)**
> This volume is reachable via both `record_search` (name search) and `fulltext_search`.

**Key pre-Dawes rolls within the mid-1800s target window** (from FamilySearch Wiki):
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** — lists Cherokees who moved west before the main removal
- **Drennen Roll (1852)** — Cherokee roll taken shortly after the main removal
- Additional tribe-specific rolls exist for Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole; coverage and survival vary by tribe
- Source: [Oklahoma Native American Records — Tribal Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)

**⚠️ Post-period but essential — Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):**
The Dawes Rolls were compiled by the Dawes Commission to enumerate Five Civilized Tribes members for land allotment before statehood. They are the most widely indexed tribal records and record blood quantum, family relationships, and lineal descent — making them a critical bridge backward to the mid-1800s even though they fall outside your target window. Indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
Source: [Oklahoma Native American Records — Tribal Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)

---

### 2. Annuity Payment Rolls

BIA agents compiled **annual annuity rolls** listing heads of household (and sometimes family members) for each tribe receiving treaty payments. These run from the 1830s through the early 1900s and are among the most systematic records for the target period.

- **Repository:** National Archives, RG 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs), including microfilm series **M234** (Letters Received by the Office of Indian Affairs)
- **Online access:** Partially indexed at FamilySearch and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/)
- **Digitization level:** Partial — some microfilm only, some partially indexed online
- Source: [Five Civilized Tribes Records — Annuity Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls)

---

### 3. Land and Allotment Records

> **Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907**
> Collection ID: 1541872 | 234,567 records | 117,283 images
> 🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872
> **Digitization level: Indexed + images**

Land assignment in Indian Territory was governed by tribal law and federal treaty, not the standard General Land Office patent system. Records include allotment files, deeds, and permit records. The **Oklahoma Historical Society** (https://www.okhistory.org/) is an additional repository for land-related records.

---

### 4. Mission and Church Records

Christian missionaries — Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian — established schools and churches among the relocated tribes beginning in the 1820s and maintained registers of converts, students, and community members. These are a key substitute for civil vital registration.

> **Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965**
> Collection ID: 1654321 | 123,456 records | 61,728 images
> 🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321
> **Digitization level: Indexed + images**

Source: [Oklahoma Native American Records — Missionary Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)

Denominational archives (American Baptist Historical Society, Presbyterian Historical Society, etc.) may hold additional undigitized registers not represented in the FamilySearch collection.

---

### 5. BIA Agency Records (NARA RG 75)

The Bureau of Indian Affairs generated extensive records through individual agencies (Cherokee Agency, Creek Agency, Choctaw Agency, etc.):

- Agency correspondence, inspection reports
- School enrollment records (boarding and day schools)
- Census-style population reports
- **Repository:** **National Archives at Fort Worth, TX** — the primary regional repository for RG 75 materials covering Indian Territory
- 🔗 https://www.archives.gov/
- **Digitization level:** Largely microfilm or physical only at NARA; some records partially available on Fold3

Source: [Five Civilized Tribes Records — Overview](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records) and [Oklahoma Native American Records — Missionary Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)

---

### 6. Federal Census Records

- The **1860 and 1870 federal censuses** covered portions of Indian Territory, but coverage was incomplete and inconsistent.
- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885)** recorded deaths in the year preceding enumeration — worth checking for family members.
- Ancestry.com's U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) is a curated external resource for these.

---

### 7. Treaties

Treaty texts name tribal leaders and establish membership rights, which can help identify prominent families and community affiliations. **Kappler's Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties** is the standard compiled source and is freely available online through Oklahoma State University's digital library:
🔗 https://dc.library.okstate.edu/digital/collection/kapplers

Original treaty records are held at NARA (Washington, D.C.).

---

### 8. Military Records

Native American soldiers served in Union and Confederate units during the Civil War (1861–1865). Service records, pension files, and unit histories are held at NARA and partially indexed on **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) — returned as a curated external link by FamilySearch.

---

## Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth, TX** | RG 75 (BIA/OIA) — agency records, annuity rolls, school records | In-person; microfilm at FamilySearch centers |
| **FamilySearch.org** | 3 indexed collections + 1 digitized volume | Free online |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Territorial records, land records, newspapers, OHS archives | Online catalog + in-person (Oklahoma City) |
| **Tribal Archives** (Five Civilized Tribes) | Tribal citizenship records, court records | Contact each tribe directly |
| **Fold3** | Military records, some BIA records | Subscription |
| **Ancestry.com** | US Census, Dawes Rolls, other indexed collections | Subscription |
| **NARA Washington, D.C.** | Treaty originals, OIA correspondence (M234) | In-person or microfilm |

---

## Key Researcher Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No civil vital registration in this period.** Tribal rolls and mission church records are the primary substitutes for birth, marriage, and death records.
2. **Work backward from the Dawes Rolls.** Even though they date to 1898–1914, they record blood quantum and family relationships that link directly to mid-1800s ancestry. Start there, then trace backward through annuity and pre-Dawes rolls.
3. **Pre-Dawes roll survival is uneven by tribe.** The Cherokee had earlier and more systematic enrollment records; Seminole and Chickasaw records for the 1830s–1850s are sparser. Research strategies differ by tribal affiliation.
4. **Search all enrollment categories.** Mixed-heritage families — "intermarried whites" and freedmen (formerly enslaved by tribal members) — were recorded in separate enrollment categories in many tribal rolls. Do not limit searches to citizens-by-blood rolls alone.
5. **FamilySearch has no dedicated Research Wiki page for Indian Territory.** The four wiki_place_page sections all returned generic content. Go directly to [Oklahoma Native American Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records) and [Five Civilized Tribes Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records) on the FamilySearch Wiki.
6. **volume_search returned 1 digitized volume** (totalResults: 1) for the 1830–1880 window — the tribal enrollment card volume 002298871. This is likely not the complete picture; additional volumes may exist under different place/date indexing or as undigitized microfilm at NARA Fort Worth.
7. **collections_search scope was "Indian Territory"** — widening the search to "Oklahoma, United States" may surface additional collections filed under the state rather than the territory.

---

## Suggested Starting Sequence

1. **Search the FamilySearch indexed collection** — *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* (collection 1987432) for your ancestor's name and tribal affiliation.
2. **Search the digitized tribal enrollment card volume** (image group 002298871, 99% indexed, full-text searchable) for the 1840–1870 window.
3. **Identify which tribe and agency** your ancestor was affiliated with, then request the corresponding **RG 75 agency records** from NARA Fort Worth.
4. **Search annuity rolls** on Fold3 and FamilySearch using the M234 microfilm series.
5. **Check mission and church records** (collection 1654321) for baptismal, marriage, or burial entries.
6. **Consult the Dawes Rolls** (post-period) to establish documented lineal descent, then work backward through the pre-Dawes rolls.
7. **Contact the relevant tribal historic preservation office or tribal archives** directly — each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintains records not fully represented in federal or FamilySearch holdings.
