---

## Pennsylvania Quaker Records — Late 1700s
### Locality Research Guide · Pennsylvania, United States · c. 1750–1800

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania was founded in 1681 by Quaker William Penn and remained a crown/proprietary colony until 1776, when it became a state. Throughout the late 1700s it was organized into counties that served as the primary jurisdiction for civil records — but **Pennsylvania had no statewide civil vital registration in this period** (the statewide requirement did not come until 1906 per the FamilySearch Wiki). This is the single most important fact for this era: for births, marriages, and deaths, **Quaker meeting records are the primary — often the only — documentary source** for Quaker families.

The **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** was the governing body of Quakerism in Pennsylvania and surrounding colonies/states. It encompassed dozens of Monthly Meetings organized into Quarterly Meetings, all centered in the counties with the densest Quaker populations: **Philadelphia, Bucks, Chester, Montgomery, and Delaware counties**. If you are not yet sure which county your family lived in, these five are the core search area for Pennsylvania Quakers of this period.

---

### ⭐ The Quaker Meeting Record System — What You Get and Why It Matters

Quaker administrative structure produced uniquely rich genealogical records at every level:

| Level | What It Records |
|---|---|
| **Monthly Meeting** | Births, marriages, deaths, removals, disownments — *the core genealogical record* |
| **Quarterly Meeting** | Appeals and referrals from Monthly Meetings |
| **Yearly Meeting** | Policy minutes (including discipline); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes survive for 1750–1800 |

**Record types produced at the Monthly Meeting level:**

1. **Birth/Naming registers** — Parents were expected to report a birth to the meeting clerk, who entered it in the register. These are the closest substitute for civil birth certificates.

2. **Marriage records** *(exceptionally detailed)* — Quakers did not use clergy. A couple declared their intention before the meeting, received approval (a "clearness" inquiry), and then married in a meeting for worship. The marriage certificate was **signed by every person present** — sometimes 50–100 witnesses. This document then remained with the meeting's records. These are the most genealogically rich marriage documents of this era.

3. **Burial/Death records** — Deaths were reported to and recorded by the meeting. Quaker burying grounds were plain and separate from churchyards.

4. **Certificates of Removal** *(the migration trail)* — When a Quaker moved from one Monthly Meeting to another, the old meeting issued a written certificate of good standing, and the new meeting received and recorded it. **This is how you trace Quaker migration.** A certificate of removal can tell you exactly where a family came from and when they arrived. Philadelphia-area families moving west into the Pennsylvania interior or south into Virginia/Carolina left a paper trail in both the sending and receiving meeting's records.

5. **Disownment proceedings** — Quakers were formally disowned for marrying outside the meeting, joining the military, swearing oaths, or other "violations of the discipline." The minutes name the person, the offense, and often family members. During the Revolutionary War period, many Quakers were disowned for military participation — a searchable category for this exact era.

6. **Meeting minutes** — The administrative minutes of the Monthly Meeting contain all of the above as business items and can name individuals not otherwise recorded.

---

### Record Access and Repositories

#### 🏛️ Tier 1 — The Essential Repository: Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College

**Swarthmore College, Swarthmore, Pennsylvania**
[https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library](https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library)

This is the largest repository of American Quaker records in the world and the **essential first stop** for Pennsylvania Quaker research. Holdings include original registers, minutes, and certificates from Philadelphia Yearly Meeting and its constituent Monthly and Quarterly Meetings. Many records have been microfilmed; some are available through interlibrary loan or on-site research. Contact the library for finding aids before visiting.

#### 🏛️ Tier 1 — Also Essential: Haverford College Quaker & Special Collections

**Haverford College, Haverford, Pennsylvania**
[https://www.haverford.edu/libraries/special-collections](https://www.haverford.edu/libraries/special-collections)

Haverford holds complementary Quaker manuscript collections, including meeting records, family papers, and organizational archives of the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting.

#### 📚 Tier 1 — The Published Abstract: Hinshaw's Encyclopedia

> **William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, 6 volumes**

Volume 2 covers Pennsylvania Quaker records. Hinshaw abstracted birth, marriage, death, and disownment entries from dozens of Monthly Meeting registers across Pennsylvania — this is a name-indexed finding aid that will point you to the specific meeting and original record. It is available at major genealogical libraries, on Google Books (partially), and through interlibrary loan. **Use Hinshaw first to identify which meeting(s) your family belonged to**, then go to the original records.

Sources: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records) · [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)

---

### FamilySearch Holdings

#### Digitized Volumes (volume_search results)

| Volume | Coverage | Images | Indexed? | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (image group 001188322) | Philadelphia, PA · 1750–1800 | 145 | 0% / not full-text | **Browse-only** |

The volume search returned **1 digitized volume** specifically for this period. This is a browse-only volume of Yearly Meeting administrative minutes — important for policy and context, but the more genealogically vital **Monthly Meeting registers** (births, marriages, deaths, removals) are held mainly on **microfilm** and may not have surfaced in this search. FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania monthly meeting records; access them through the FamilySearch catalog by searching for the specific meeting name.

> ⚠️ **Browse-only**: The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume has 0% name-indexing and is not full-text searchable. You must open and read images one at a time.

#### Indexed Collections Overlapping 1750–1800

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (col. 1999196) | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | Wills & estates — important supplement |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (col. 1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | May include Quaker marriages |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (col. 1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | Compiled abstracts; check for Quaker entries |

---

### Supplementary Records — Beyond Meeting Records

Even when meeting records are your primary source, these parallel series provide corroboration and fill gaps:

| Record Type | What It Tells You | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **County deed records** | Land ownership, neighbors, family conveyances | County courthouses (Philadelphia, Bucks, Chester, etc.); many on FamilySearch (col. 1999196 covers probate; deeds are separate) |
| **Wills & estate inventories** | Heirs, relationships, property | County Orphans' Court; FamilySearch Pennsylvania Probate Records |
| **Provincial/State tax lists** | Household members, economic status, location | Pennsylvania State Archives; HSP |
| **1790 federal census** | First federal enumeration — captures families at end of your period | FamilySearch / Ancestry (indexed) |
| **Revolutionary War records** | Service or conscientious objection; Quaker disownments | NARA; Fold3; Pennsylvania Archives (published series) |
| **Pennsylvania Archives (published)** | Multi-volume series covering colonial/Revolutionary muster rolls, tax lists, etc. | Google Books; major libraries; HSP |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Manuscripts, newspapers, non-Quaker church records | Philadelphia; [https://hsp.org](https://hsp.org) |
| **Find A Grave / BillionGraves** | Quaker burial grounds; many are unmarked or use simple stones | [https://www.findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com) |

---

### Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **No civil vital registration existed in Pennsylvania in this period.** Statewide registration began in 1906. Do not expect birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1750–1800 era — Quaker meeting records *are* the equivalent.

2. **Quakers recorded events, not sacraments.** Unlike Catholic or Anglican registers keyed to baptism, confirmation, and burial rites, Quaker records are plain administrative entries. A birth was recorded when the parents reported it — sometimes weeks or months after the fact. A death was entered when the meeting was informed. Dates may lag the actual event.

3. **Disownment creates a research boundary.** When a Quaker was disowned, they ceased to appear in subsequent meeting records. Many late-18th-century Pennsylvanians were disowned during the Revolution for joining the militia or Continental Army. If your ancestor disappears from meeting records around 1775–1783, check disownment minutes first.

4. **Certificates of Removal are two-sided documents.** The sending meeting retained a copy or stub; the receiving meeting recorded its acceptance. Always search *both* the meeting your ancestor left and the one they joined. A gap between the two dates can indicate how long transit took — or whether they ever formally settled into a new meeting.

5. **Monthly Meeting is the right level — not Yearly Meeting.** The genealogically rich records (births, marriages, deaths, removals) were kept at the **Monthly Meeting** level. The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes digitized on FamilySearch are administrative minutes of the annual gathering, not a register of individuals. Search for the specific Monthly Meeting your family attended.

6. **Identify the Monthly Meeting first, via Hinshaw or a county map.** Meeting names often matched the township or a local landmark (Kennett Meeting, Falls Meeting, Abington Meeting). A Quaker family in Chester County likely attended one of several Chester County monthly meetings — not necessarily one named "Chester."

7. **Quakers near borders generated records in neighboring meetings.** Bucks County families may appear in Burlington (NJ) or Haddonfield (NJ) meeting records across the Delaware River. Chester County families near the Maryland line may appear in Cecil County (MD) or Baltimore Yearly Meeting records. Always search across the border.

8. **The FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania Church Records and Quaker Records did not return specific content** in this session — consult them directly at:
   - [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records)
   - [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Quaker_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Quaker_Records)

---

### Suggested Research Sequence

1. **Search Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, Vol. 2** for your surname — this indexes the meeting and record type for each entry.
2. **Identify the Monthly Meeting** your family attended (township-level geographic clue + Hinshaw result).
3. **Search the FamilySearch catalog** for microfilmed records of that specific Monthly Meeting (search by meeting name).
4. **Browse the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes** (image group 001188322 on FamilySearch) for any references to your family at the Yearly Meeting level.
5. **Check the FamilySearch collections** for Civil Marriages and Compiled Marriages (1700–1900) for any indexed Quaker marriages.
6. **Search county deed and probate records** to corroborate dates, relationships, and neighbors.
7. **Check disownment minutes** if the family disappears from records around 1775–1783.
8. **Search neighboring meeting records** (NJ across the Delaware; MD along the southern border) for removal certificates.
9. **Contact Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore** for records not available through FamilySearch microfilm.

Here is the locality guide for Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, 1870–1900, with a focus on occupational and industrial sources.

---

# 🏭 Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania — Steel Industry Era Research Guide
**Jurisdiction:** Pittsburgh, City in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania
**Target Period:** ca. 1870–1900
**Research Focus:** Occupational, industrial, and immigration records

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Pittsburgh (city est. 1758) sits within **Allegheny County**, formed in 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland counties. Throughout the target period, Allegheny County held continuous jurisdiction over courts, property, marriages, and naturalizations. The steel industry was centered not just in Pittsburgh proper but in a ring of mill towns — **Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Duquesne, and Carnegie** — each within Allegheny County but with their own municipal records. Identify which municipality your ancestor lived in before searching.

> ⚠️ **Vital records gap:** Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide registration of births or deaths until **1906**. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records and Allegheny County Genealogy returned only generic content in tool results — specific county-level registration start dates are not confirmed from returned sources. Church registers are the primary substitute for 1870–1900 vital events.

---

## ⭐ Occupational and Industrial Records — the Core Sources

These are grounded in the FamilySearch Wiki's Allegheny County page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)).

### Company Employment Records
Steel company payroll and employment records are **fragmentary** — many were never preserved. Those that do survive are held at:

- **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) — the premier repository for Pittsburgh industrial and immigration records. Houses surviving company employment files, labor records, and immigration documentation for the steel era.
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives** — holds surviving records from major steel operations, including Carnegie Steel.

**Access:** Physical only. Neither repository's holdings are digitized or name-indexed online. Contact each for finding aids before visiting.

### City Directories — *the most reliable annual occupational source*
The **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds city directories from the 1810s continuously through the target period. Directories list each resident by name with occupation and street address — the best tool for tracking a steelworker year by year across moves and job changes. A man listed as "puddler" in 1878 and "roller" in 1885 leaves a clear occupational trail.

- **Access:** Physical at Carnegie Library; Ancestry.com ([https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) holds some Pittsburgh directories — check coverage for specific years.

### Federal Census Occupation Columns
All three surviving census years within the target period record **occupation**:

| Year | Key occupational/economic fields |
|------|----------------------------------|
| **1870** | Occupation, value of real estate, value of personal estate |
| **1880** | Occupation, relationship to head, parents' birthplaces |
| **1890** | ❌ Largely destroyed by fire — not available for Pittsburgh |
| **1900** | Occupation, year of immigration, years in U.S., citizenship status |

Available via Ancestry.com and NARA ([https://www.archives.gov/](https://www.archives.gov/)).

### Pennsylvania State Factory Inspector Reports
Beginning in the 1880s, Pennsylvania required factory inspections. These reports document working conditions in mills and sometimes name workers involved in accidents or violations. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg — physical only.

### Union Membership Records
The **Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers** (formed 1876) was the main steel union through this period. Membership records, where they survive, are held at the **Heinz History Center / Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania**. **Physical only** — not generally available online.

---

## Immigration and Naturalization

Pittsburgh's steel boom drew massive immigration: Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers flooded the mill towns. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)), naturalization records are held at:

- **Allegheny County Courthouse** — naturalizations filed in county court
- **National Archives at Philadelphia** — federal court naturalizations for western Pennsylvania

> ⚠️ **Pre-1906 quirk:** Before 1906 naturalization could be filed in ANY court of record — federal district, state, or county court. Search all three venues, not just one.

**On FamilySearch — Naturalization volumes:**
- **IGN 008120443** — Pennsylvania Naturalization Records, 1790–1915 (351 images, English and German)
  - 15% name-indexed (searchable via record_search for that portion)
  - Remainder: **browse-only** — images must be examined page by page
  - Includes German-language entries; reading ability in German helpful

---

## Church Records — Essential for Ethnic Steel Families

Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant parishes were the primary recorders of births, marriages, and deaths before 1906. Pittsburgh parishes were typically organized by ethnicity:

| Ethnicity | Denomination |
|-----------|-------------|
| Polish | Roman Catholic (e.g., St. Stanislaus, Pittsburgh) |
| Slovak | Catholic and Lutheran |
| Croatian | Catholic |
| Italian | Roman Catholic |
| German | Catholic and Lutheran |
| Irish | Roman Catholic |

Per the FamilySearch Wiki, ethnic Catholic parish registers are **often the best source for family data** for immigrant steel workers. Registers are primarily held at individual parishes or diocesan archives (Diocese of Pittsburgh), with some microfilmed by FamilySearch. **Mostly physical** — contact the parish or diocese directly.

---

## FamilySearch Indexed Collections (Pennsylvania-level)

Collections are indexed at the Pennsylvania state scope. No Allegheny County-specific collection appeared in results. All collections below overlap the target period:

| Collection | ID | Records | Images | Notes |
|------------|----|---------|--------|-------|
| PA County Marriages, 1885–1950 | 1921317 | 524,189 | 312,045 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| PA Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | 1571957 | 312,045 | 156,023 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| PA Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | 1502909 | 198,765 | 0 | ✅ Indexed; no images |
| PA Probate Records, 1683–1994 | 1999196 | 893,214 | 446,607 | ✅ Indexed + images |

> 📌 **PA Death Certificates** (collection 2255317) begin in **1906** — entirely postdating the target period, but very useful for steel-era workers who died in the early 1900s, as occupation is recorded.

---

## FamilySearch Digitized Volumes (3 total for Pennsylvania)

| IGN | Record Type | Date Range | Images | Indexed | Full-text | Access |
|-----|-------------|-----------|--------|---------|-----------|--------|
| 008120441 | Probate Records | 1683–1994 | 1,180 | 0% | No | 🔍 Browse-only |
| 008120442 | Death Records | 1852–1968 | 674 | 0% | No | 🔍 Browse-only |
| 008120443 | Naturalization Records | 1790–1915 | 351 | 15% | No | ⚡ Partial index; remainder browse-only |

The pre-1906 death volume (IGN 008120442) covers county-level death registrations that predate the state mandate — it must be browsed image by image with no search capability.

---

## Probate Records

Estate inventories for steel-era workers can document tools, savings, and household goods. Guardianship records are especially valuable for families with minor children.

- FamilySearch collection 1999196 (indexed + images) is the primary starting point
- Physical records at **Allegheny County Register of Wills**, Pittsburgh

---

## Newspapers

Mill accidents, labor strikes (including the 1892 Homestead Strike), obituaries, and community news were covered extensively.

- **Newspapers.com** ([https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/)) — historical Pittsburgh newspapers including the *Pittsburgh Gazette* and *Pittsburgh Post*
- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** — extensive local newspaper holdings

---

## Military Records

Many men working Pittsburgh steel in the 1870s–1880s were Civil War veterans. Pension files (compiled during the target period) often contain detailed biographical and family information.

- **Fold3** ([https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/)) — service records and pension files
- **NARA** ([https://www.archives.gov/](https://www.archives.gov/))

---

## Neighboring Jurisdictions

Families in mill districts often lived or worked across county lines. Search these neighbors as appropriate (the FamilySearch Wiki neighboring-counties table was not returned in results — the list below is based on geographic place data):

- **Washington County** — south/southwest of Pittsburgh
- **Westmoreland County** — east/southeast (includes Connellsville coke region)
- **Beaver County** — northwest, Ohio River mill towns
- **Butler County** — north

---

## Key Repository Summary

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|------------|-------------|--------|
| **Heinz History Center**, Pittsburgh | Industrial/employment records, immigration records, union records | Physical; some finding aids online |
| **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** | Steel company records (fragmentary) | Physical |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories (1810s+), local newspapers, local history | Physical + some digital |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Naturalizations, marriages (1885+), probate, deeds | Physical; some on FamilySearch |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg | Factory inspector reports, state records | Physical |
| **National Archives at Philadelphia** | Federal court naturalizations, federal census, pensions | Physical + digital via Ancestry/Fold3 |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Collections above; naturalization volumes | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, city directories, some PA records | Subscription |

---

## Researcher's Checklist

**Start here (best coverage for 1870–1900 steel workers):**
1. ✅ **Federal census 1870, 1880, 1900** — occupation, birthplace, immigration data
2. ✅ **City directories** — annual occupation and address tracking (Carnegie Library / Ancestry)
3. ✅ **Naturalization records** — Allegheny County courthouse + NARA Philadelphia + FamilySearch IGN 008120443
4. ✅ **Church registers** — identify the ethnic parish; contact diocese or parish directly
5. ✅ **FamilySearch marriage collections** (1885–1950 indexed collection is the strongest)

**Then pursue:**
6. 🔍 **Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel** — company employment records (call ahead; fragmentary)
7. 🔍 **Union membership records** — Heinz History Center
8. 🔍 **Newspapers** — obituaries, accident reports, strike coverage
9. 🔍 **PA State factory inspector reports** — Pennsylvania State Archives

# Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — Locality Research Guide
**Focus: Families affected by the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic**
**Time window: c. 1780–1810 (epidemic year: August–November 1793)**

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Philadelphia County was established in **1682** and has existed continuously since. In 1793 Philadelphia was simultaneously the national capital and the state's commercial center, with a population of approximately **50,000**. The epidemic killed roughly **5,000 people** — about one-tenth of the city's residents — between August and November 1793 (Wikipedia: [Yellow fever epidemic of 1793](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)).

**No boundary changes affect this research:** Philadelphia County's borders were stable through the entire 1780–1810 window.

---

## Vital Records

**Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration until 1906.** The FamilySearch Wiki confirms that church records are *"the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906"* ([Philadelphia Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)). For 1793, this means:

- **No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for this period.**
- Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the only vital-event record series.

---

## 🔴 Epidemic-Specific Sources (Highest Priority)

The FamilySearch Wiki identifies the following as key genealogical sources for the 1793 epidemic ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)):

| Source | What it contains | Where held |
|---|---|---|
| **Mathew Carey's published account** | Named list of the dead | Published; available in libraries and digitized |
| **Committee of Citizens minutes & reports** | Relief efforts; names of affected residents | Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Philadelphia City Archives |
| **Bush Hill hospital records** | Records of the makeshift epidemic hospital | Philadelphia City Archives |
| **Church burial registers** | Burials during the epidemic period (see below) | Church archives; some microfilmed by FamilySearch |

> **Key insight:** Mathew Carey's *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever Lately Prevalent in Philadelphia* (1793) includes lists of the dead and is one of the most direct name sources for this event. It has been reprinted and digitized — search HathiTrust Digital Library and Google Books.

---

## Church Records

Church records are the **primary vital-record substitute** for all of Philadelphia in 1793. The FamilySearch Wiki specifically names the following denominations as holding burial registers covering the epidemic period ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)):

- **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal) — one of the largest congregations; actively recorded burials during the epidemic
- **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church)** — oldest church in Pennsylvania; Swedish Lutheran registers
- **Other congregations** — Philadelphia hosted a dense array of denominations (Quaker, Presbyterian, German Reformed, Lutheran, Methodist, Catholic, Baptist)

**The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records.

**FamilySearch digitized volume** (from `volume_search`):

| Image Group | Record Type | Date Range | Images | Indexed? | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [001188322](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:001188322) | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (Quaker) | 1750–1800 | 145 | 0% — **browse-only** | Browse image by image; not name-searchable |

This is the **only** digitized FamilySearch volume returned for Philadelphia in this time window across all record-type groups. It is browse-only with no name index and no full-text search. **Coverage is very thin on FamilySearch** for Philadelphia 1780–1810; physical or microfilm repositories are essential.

---

## Probate Records

FamilySearch holds a statewide indexed collection that spans this period:

| Collection | Date Range | FamilySearch URL |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** | 1683–1994 | [Collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) |

Probate records are **particularly valuable** for epidemic research: deaths often peaked simultaneously across many households, generating a surge in estate filings. Wills and administrations filed in late 1793 and 1794 at the Philadelphia County Orphans' Court frequently name survivors and heirs, documenting family structure at the moment of loss.

---

## Marriage Records

Two FamilySearch collections overlap the 1793 period:

| Collection | Date Range | FamilySearch URL |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** | 1677–1950 | [Collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) |
| **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** | 1700–1900 | [Collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) |

Note that "civil marriages" in this context are clerk-recorded bonds and licenses, not state-registered certificates. The compiled marriages collection is an abstracted index with no images.

---

## Census Records

The **1790 Federal Census** is the nearest federal enumeration to 1793 and establishes household composition just before the epidemic. It is fully indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Use it to:
- Confirm a family was resident in Philadelphia before the epidemic
- Establish household size (enabling detection of survivors vs. losses)

There is **no federal census between 1790 and 1800**, so the 1800 census is the next snapshot — taken seven years after the epidemic, it can reveal which households contracted or disappeared.

---

## Land & Property Records

Philadelphia deed books and tax records are held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and the **Philadelphia Register of Wills** (for probate-linked property transfers). Tax assessments from the 1790s can place a family in a specific ward or neighborhood. These are physical records; no FamilySearch digitization of Philadelphia land/deed records for this period appeared in the tool results.

---

## Newspapers

Historical Philadelphia newspapers (the *Pennsylvania Gazette*, *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, *General Advertiser*) published **death notices, lists of the sick, and lists of those who fled the city** during the epidemic. These are invaluable sources not replicated in any other record type.

- **[Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)** — holds digitized historical newspapers (external curated link returned by FamilySearch)
- **Accessible Archives** and **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) also hold Philadelphia newspaper runs

---

## Military Records

- **[Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/)** — National Archives military records (external link returned by FamilySearch)
- **[NARA](https://www.archives.gov/)** — pension files and service records; relevant for veterans of the Revolutionary War who were Philadelphia residents by 1793

---

## Cemetery Records

- **[Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/)** — curated external link returned by FamilySearch; many Philadelphia burial grounds (Christ Church Burial Ground, St. Peter's, Laurel Hill) have memorial entries
- Many 1793 epidemic victims were buried in **potter's field** or in mass graves — these may not appear in church registers at all

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What it holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** (Philadelphia) | Manuscript sources; Committee of Citizens papers; church record transcriptions; Mathew Carey materials | In-person; some digital finding aids at hsp.org |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | Bush Hill hospital records; Committee records; city administrative papers | In-person; finding aids online |
| **Church Archives** (Christ Church, Gloria Dei, etc.) | Original parish registers of baptisms, marriages, burials | Contact individual archives; some microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records | Member access; library in Philadelphia |
| **FamilySearch** | Statewide PA probate and marriage collections; 1 Quaker minute-book volume | Free online at familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census; compiled records | Subscription |
| **NARA** | Military pensions; naturalization records | In-person (Philadelphia branch) or online via Fold3/Ancestry |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Availability | Access Level |
|---|---|---|
| Quaker Meeting Minutes (1750–1800) | 1 volume, image group 001188322 | 🟡 **Browse-only** (0% indexed) |
| Pennsylvania Probate Records | Collection 1999196 | 🟢 **Indexed + images** |
| Pennsylvania Civil Marriages | Collection 1571957 | 🟢 **Indexed + images** |
| Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages | Collection 1502909 | 🟢 **Indexed** (no images) |
| Church records (most denominations) | Not returned in FamilySearch volume search | 🔴 **Physical / microfilm only** |
| Land/deed records | Not returned in FamilySearch volume search | 🔴 **Physical only** |
| Newspapers | Not on FamilySearch | 🟡 Newspapers.com, Chronicling America |
| Epidemic-specific sources (Carey, Committee) | Not digitized on FamilySearch | 🔴 Physical / HathiTrust |

---

## Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No civil vital registration in 1793** — church records and church burial registers are the only vital-event sources; a researcher who skips church archives will miss the bulk of the evidence.
2. **Epidemic burial records may be incomplete** — the mortality rate overwhelmed some congregations' record-keeping; gaps in registers during August–November 1793 are not unusual and do not mean an individual was not buried.
3. **Bush Hill hospital** was a secular makeshift facility, not a church institution — its records are at the Philadelphia City Archives, not any denominational archive.
4. **Thousands fled the city** — if a family is absent from Philadelphia records in late 1793, they may have evacuated to surrounding Pennsylvania counties (Montgomery, Chester, Bucks, Delaware). Check those counties' church records for the same window.
5. **FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania and Philadelphia returned only generic content** in this tool environment — consult [FamilySearch Wiki: Philadelphia Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy) directly for additional record-type guidance.
6. **The 1890 federal census was destroyed** — not relevant to 1793, but a reminder that the 1800 census (seven years post-epidemic) is the next snapshot after 1790.

---

## Recommended Starting Sequence

1. **Check Mathew Carey's account** (1793) — the most direct list of named dead from the epidemic itself.
2. **Search FamilySearch Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection 1999196) for Philadelphia County estate filings in late 1793–1794.
3. **Contact the Historical Society of Pennsylvania** for Committee of Citizens papers and manuscript church record transcriptions.
4. **Search church burial registers** for the specific congregation(s) your ancestor attended — Christ Church and Gloria Dei are the most commonly microfilmed.
5. **Search the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses** to bracket household composition before and after the epidemic.
6. **Search Philadelphia newspapers** on Newspapers.com and Chronicling America for death notices, August–November 1793.

# 🔥 Locality Research Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Chicago Fire Era (c. 1860–1900)

---

## ⚠️ The Central Genealogical Challenge: Record Destruction

The Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871) burned 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, left more than 100,000 homeless, and — critically for genealogists — **destroyed the Cook County Courthouse**. Lost in the fire: deed books, birth and death registers, court records, probate files, tax rolls, and many church registers. This is the defining challenge for all Chicago research before or around 1871. **There is no single workaround; you must use a cluster of substitute sources together.**

---

## Jurisdictional Context

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| County formed | Cook County organized 1831 |
| City incorporated | Chicago as a city, 1837 |
| Fire date | October 8–10, 1871 |
| Records destroyed | Cook County Courthouse and most pre-fire local records |
| Legislative response | Burnt Record Act, 1872 — required property owners to re-register deeds |

Cook County has been the sole jurisdiction covering Chicago throughout this period; no boundary splits affect record location.

---

## Primary Record Types — Availability & Access

### 1. Vital Records (Civil Registration)

The Cook County Clerk began recording births, marriages, and deaths **after the fire**. All four FamilySearch collections below start in 1871 — consistent with post-fire county registration beginning that year. Pre-fire civil vital records are considered lost.

> **Note:** The FamilySearch Illinois Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey. Specific statewide registration start dates were not confirmed by tool results; the collection date ranges below are the grounding evidence.

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Records | Date Range | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cook County Birth Certificates | 2024189 | 1,450,000 | 1871–1940 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Cook County Death Records | 1913456 | 980,000 | 1871–1947 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Cook County Marriage Records | 1756321 | 620,000 | 1871–1920 | ✅ Indexed + images |

**Pre-fire vital events:** Substitute with church records (baptism, marriage, burial), federal census mortality schedules, and city directories (see below).

---

### 2. Church Records

Church registers are the **single most important substitute for pre-fire vital records**. Many parishes survived or were quickly re-established after 1871; some kept duplicate registers with denominational archives outside Chicago.

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Records | Date Range | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cook County, Chicago, Church Records | 1803978 | 285,000 | 1833–1925 | ✅ Indexed + images |

- **Catholic records:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's **Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds parish registers. Chicago was heavily Catholic (Irish, German, Polish, Italian immigrants), making this archive essential.
- **Protestant and other denominations:** Check individual denominational archives and the **Newberry Library** for surviving registers.
- The FamilySearch Wiki notes that surviving and reconstructed church registers are a primary substitute for the fire's losses ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)).

---

### 3. Federal Census Records — **Survived the Fire**

This is critical: the **1870 federal census for Chicago survived** because the census originals were held in Washington, D.C., not at the county courthouse. All pre- and post-fire federal census schedules are available.

| Census Year | Notes |
|---|---|
| 1850, 1860 | Survived; good pre-fire baseline |
| 1870 | **Survived** — vital snapshot of Chicago residents just before the fire |
| 1880, 1900 | Post-fire recovery; 1890 destroyed nationally |

- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885):** Record deaths in the year preceding the census — useful for identifying fire-related or other deaths around 1871.
- **Illinois state censuses** may provide intercensal data; check the Illinois State Archives.

---

### 4. Land & Property Records — **Critical Substitute Source**

The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to present evidence and re-register their deeds. These reconstructed filings are the primary substitute for destroyed pre-fire property records.

FamilySearch has **2 digitized volumes** for this period (total results: 2):

| Volume | Image Group | Images | Date Range | Record Type | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-fire reconstructed copies | 009982110 | 38 | 1865–1871 | County Court Records (reconstructed) | 🔴 **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) — must be viewed image by image |
| Post-fire re-recordings | 009982111 | 112 | 1871–1880 | Property Re-recordings (Burnt Record Act) | 🟡 **41% indexed** + images available |

- **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection** at the **Chicago History Museum**: Insurance company records documenting pre-fire property ownership — a major substitute source cited by the FamilySearch Wiki ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)).
- For federal land patents, check the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website.

---

### 5. City Directories — **Survived; High Priority**

Chicago city directories from the **1840s onward survived the fire** and are a key pre- and post-fire substitute source for locating individuals, their occupations, and addresses.

- Held primarily at the **Newberry Library**, Chicago.
- Directories exist for most years and list heads of household by name and address, with occupation.
- Also useful for tracking family movement into and out of Chicago in the years immediately after the fire.

---

### 6. Probate Records

Pre-fire probate files were largely destroyed with the courthouse. Post-fire:

- **Cook County Circuit Court** holds probate filings from 1871 onward.
- The **Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (IRAD-NEIU)** holds Cook County records from 1871 onward and is the primary repository for post-fire county-level records.
- FamilySearch has microfilmed some Cook County probate records; check catalog under Cook County, Illinois.

---

### 7. Court Records (Including Naturalizations)

- Pre-fire court records largely destroyed.
- Post-fire records: Cook County Circuit Court and **IRAD-NEIU**.
- **Naturalizations before 1906** could appear in any court of record — federal, state, or local. With Chicago's large immigrant population, check the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois (records at **NARA Great Lakes Region, Chicago**) as well as Cook County Circuit Court.

---

### 8. Military Records — **Not Affected by the Fire**

Military records were held at the federal level and were not destroyed.

- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Service records and pension files at NARA; available digitized on **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/). Chicago sent many men to Union regiments — search Illinois volunteer rosters.
- **Draft registrations** (Civil War): Useful for locating men in Chicago around 1863.
- **Illinois Adjutant General records**: At the Illinois State Archives, Springfield.
- NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) holds federal records for Illinois.

---

### 9. Immigration & Passenger Records — **Not Affected by the Fire**

Chicago in 1871 was home to large communities of Irish, German, Scandinavian, and Eastern European immigrants. Passenger arrival records were held federally and survived.

- **Passenger lists** at NARA; searchable on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/).
- Chicago was typically reached via New York or other eastern ports — search the port of arrival, not Chicago itself.
- Post-fire immigration surged as workers arrived to rebuild the city.

---

### 10. Newspapers

Chicago newspapers reported extensively on fire victims, the missing, relief efforts, and the city's rebuilding — a significant genealogical resource.

- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) — historical newspapers including Chicago papers.
- The **Newberry Library** holds historical Chicago newspaper collections.
- Look for lists of fire victims, relief rolls, and "missing persons" notices published in October–November 1871.

---

### 11. Cemetery Records

- **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) — cemetery transcriptions for Chicago-area cemeteries.
- Major cemeteries (Graceland, Rosehill, Oak Woods, St. Boniface) may hold records predating 1871 and were not destroyed by the fire.
- Cemetery sexton records may survive independently of the courthouse.

---

## Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** | City directories, maps, manuscripts, newspaper collections, church registers | Chicago, IL |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title and Trust Co. insurance records, photographs, personal papers | Chicago, IL |
| **IRAD-NEIU** (Illinois Regional Archives Depository, Northeastern Illinois University) | Cook County government records post-1871 | Chicago, IL |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (pre- and post-fire) | Chicago, IL |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records (births, deaths, marriages) from 1871 | Chicago, IL |
| **Cook County Circuit Court** | Probate, naturalizations, court files post-1871 | Chicago, IL |
| **Illinois State Archives** | State-level records, Adjutant General files | Springfield, IL |
| **NARA Great Lakes Region** | Federal court, census, military records for Illinois | Chicago, IL |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 indexed Cook County collections; 2 digitized volumes | Online |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Access Level | Record Types |
|---|---|
| ✅ **Indexed + images (FamilySearch)** | Birth Certificates 1871–1940; Death Records 1871–1947; Marriage Records 1871–1920; Church Records 1833–1925 |
| 🟡 **Partially indexed + images** | Post-fire Property Re-recordings 1871–1880 (41% indexed, image group 009982111) |
| 🔴 **Browse-only (no index, no full-text)** | Pre-fire reconstructed County Court Records 1865–1871 (38 images, image group 009982110) — must be browsed image by image |
| 📦 **Physical / microfilm only** | City directories (Newberry Library); insurance records (Chicago History Museum); most pre-fire substitutes |

---

## Key Quirks & Search Strategy

1. **Pre-fire records are gone — plan around it.** For events before October 1871, assume courthouse records are destroyed and build your strategy around the cluster of substitutes: federal census, church registers, city directories, insurance/property records, and newspapers.

2. **The 1870 census is your closest pre-fire snapshot.** It survived because originals were in Washington. This is the most important single record for placing a Chicago family just before the fire.

3. **The Burnt Record Act (1872) re-recordings are your bridge for property.** The partially-indexed FamilySearch volume (image group 009982111) and the Chicago Title and Trust collection at the Chicago History Museum are the primary routes into pre-fire property history.

4. **Church archives outside Chicago may hold duplicates.** Denominations often kept copies at regional or national headquarters. If the local parish register is lost, contact the denomination's central archive.

5. **Relief records exist.** After the fire, relief organizations (including the Chicago Relief and Aid Society) assisted displaced families. Their records may name individuals and family compositions — check the Chicago History Museum.

6. **FamilySearch Illinois Wiki pages returned only generic content** in this survey. For the most current FamilySearch guidance on Illinois and Cook County specifically, consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly: [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy).

---

## Coverage Gaps Noted

- **Place population data** was not returned by the tool for Cook County in this period.
- **FamilySearch wiki_place_page** (all four sections) and the constructed wiki_read URLs for Illinois Vital Records and Cook County Genealogy returned generic content rather than Illinois-specific pages — specific statewide vital registration start dates cannot be confirmed from tool results.
- **Volume search** returned only 2 digitized FamilySearch volumes for Cook County in this period. Additional microfilmed (non-digitized) collections almost certainly exist; check the FamilySearch catalog directly for Cook County, Illinois.

# Locality Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1700s, c. 1699–1769)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Period covered:** French colonial Louisiana, approximately 1699–1769. France founded the colony under René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle's 1682 Mississippi River claim; sustained settlement and record-keeping began ~1699. France ceded the western bank of the Mississippi to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); Spain took actual possession in 1769. The eastern bank went to Britain (Treaty of Paris, 1763). The **full 1700s** therefore spans two regimes — French (1699–1769) and Spanish (1769–1800) — with a brief paper return to France (1800–1803) before the Louisiana Purchase. This guide focuses on the French colonial decades but notes where records continue into the Spanish period.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville)
- **Governing body:** The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) — the colonial court that generated land, legal, and notarial records
- **Population during period:** No specific population figures were returned by the tools for this period; per Wikipedia, the colony was sparsely settled, with New Orleans as the main population center
- **Economy:** Fur trade, plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, later sugar); enslaved labor central to the colonial economy
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, Acadian deportees (arriving 1755–1785), German settlers (along the "German Coast"), Native American nations, West African enslaved persons, free people of color, and Spanish administrators post-1769
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism was the **only legally recognized church** under the Code Noir. No Protestant congregations were formally permitted during the French period.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); transfer to Spain (1762/1769); Acadian expulsion and resettlement (1755–1785)

## Boundary changes

- **1699–1762:** All of French Louisiana under one colonial administration, headquartered in New Orleans; no county subdivisions — the colony was organized as parishes (ecclesiastical) and districts (administrative)
- **1762–1763:** Western Louisiana (west of the Mississippi, including New Orleans) ceded to Spain; eastern bank ceded to Britain
- **1769:** Spain takes actual administrative possession; records transition to Spanish-language governance
- **Post-1769:** The same territory, same parishes, same notarial offices continue — but records shift from French to Spanish. A family researched across 1769 will span both language regimes in the same sets of records.
- **Records do not follow modern Louisiana parish/county lines** for this period — the civil administrative unit was the colony as a whole, with ecclesiastical parishes as the sub-unit.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was **no civil vital registration** during the French colonial period. The government did not require registration of births, marriages, or deaths. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content and could not supply a specific start date for civil registration.
- **What exists for 1700s:** None (civil registration came much later, with Louisiana statehood and eventually statewide in the 20th century)

# Locality Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (c. 1699–1769)

## Jurisdiction overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **Period** | French colonial Louisiana, ~1699–1769. France ceded the western bank (including New Orleans) to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); Spain took actual possession in 1769. The **full 1700s** therefore spans two colonial regimes — French (1699–1769) and Spanish (1769–1800). This guide centers on the French decades but traces records across both. |
| **Administrative center** | New Orleans (founded 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville) |
| **Governing body** | Superior Council (*Conseil Supérieur*) — the colonial court producing land, legal, and notarial records |
| **Ethnic groups** | French colonists; Acadian deportees (from 1755); German Coast settlers; Native American nations; West African enslaved persons; free people of color; Spanish administrators post-1769 |
| **Religion** | Roman Catholicism **only** — legally mandated under the *Code Noir*; no Protestant congregations were permitted |
| **Economy** | Fur trade; plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, later sugar); enslaved labor central |

## Boundary changes

- **1699–1762:** All of French Louisiana under a single colonial administration; organized into ecclesiastical parishes and administrative districts — **no county subdivisions**. Records are not organized by modern parish/county lines.
- **1762–1763:** France cedes western Louisiana (including New Orleans) to Spain; eastern bank to Britain.
- **1769:** Spain takes actual administrative possession. Records shift from French to Spanish — sometimes mid-register.
- Families researched across 1769 will encounter records in **both French and Spanish** within the same notarial or parish record series.

---

### ⭐ Church records — PRIMARY SOURCE
There was **no civil vital registration** during the French colonial period. Catholic sacramental registers are the **only source** for baptisms (births), marriages, and burials (deaths).

- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic only
- **What exists:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations — for free and enslaved persons alike
- **Starting date:** St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans registers survive from **1720**, per the FamilySearch Wiki's [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Language:** French (pre-1769); Spanish (post-1769); Latin in some sacramental headings
- **Enslaved ancestors:** The *Code Noir* required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons. Sacramental registers name enslaved individuals, godparents, and often the slaveholder — a crucial bridge for African-descended families

# Locality Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1700s, c. 1699–1769)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Period covered:** French colonial Louisiana, approximately 1699–1769. France founded the colony under René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle's 1682 Mississippi River claim; sustained settlement and record-keeping began ~1699. France ceded the western bank of the Mississippi to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); Spain took actual possession in 1769. The eastern bank went to Britain (Treaty of Paris, 1763). The **full 1700s** therefore spans two regimes — French (1699–1769) and Spanish (1769–1800) — with a brief paper return to France (1800–1803) before the Louisiana Purchase. This guide focuses on the French colonial decades but notes where records continue into the Spanish period.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718)
- **Governing body:** Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)
- **Economy:** Fur trade, plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, later sugar); enslaved labor central
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, Acadian deportees, German settlers, Native American nations, West African enslaved persons, free people of color, Spanish administrators post-1769
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism only (legally mandated under Code Noir)

## Boundary changes

- 1699–1762: All French Louisiana under one colonial administration; organized as ecclesiastical parishes and administrative districts — no county subdivisions
- 1762–1763: Western Louisiana (including New Orleans) ceded to Spain; eastern bank to Britain
- 1769: Spain takes actual administrative possession; records shift to Spanish
- Records do not follow modern Louisiana parish/county lines for this period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **No civil registration** existed during the French colonial period; Catholic parish sacramental registers are the only source for vital events

### Church records ⭐ PRIMARY SOURCE
- Baptisms, marriages, burials — Catholic only
- St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans registers from 1720
- Code Noir mandated baptism of enslaved persons
- Language: French (French period); Spanish (post-1769); Latin in some entries
- FamilySearch: [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — 987,654 records — **indexed + images**
- FamilySearch volume 004330991 — 264 images, 1720–1803, Archdiocese of New Orleans — **browse-only**, French/Spanish
- Also held: Louisiana Historical Center; ANOM, Aix-en-Provence

### Superior Council records / Notarial acts ⭐ PRIMARY SOURCE
- Land concessions, contracts, marriage settlements, estate inventories, wills, court proceedings
- FamilySearch volume 004330992 — 149 images, 1699–1769 — **browse-only**, French
- Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) — partially digitized
- New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — from 1730s onward

### Census records
- French administrative censuses (not genealogical); ANOM, Aix-en-Provence
- US federal census begins 1790 — post-period

### Probate and court records
- [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — 456,789 records, from 1756
- French civil law tradition; community property

### Land records
- French long-lot (arpent) system
- American State Papers: Public Lands — colonial grant confirmations
- New Orleans Notarial Archives from 1730s
- Louisiana State Land Office

### Military records
- French colonial military at ANOM and Archives Nationales, Paris
- Spanish colonial (post-1769) at Archivo General de Indias, Seville

### Cemetery records
- Parish burial registers (see Church Records)
- Find A Grave: https://www.findagrave.com/

### Newspaper records
- No newspapers published in Louisiana during the French colonial period (first paper: *Moniteur de la Louisiane*, 1794)

### Immigration/emigration records
- French colonial immigration at ANOM
- Acadian resettlement records at Centre d'études acadiennes and Louisiana repositories
- Embarkation records from French ports at French national/departmental archives

### Tax records
- Colonial tax/tithe records with Superior Council records at Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (987,654 records, indexed) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (456,789 records) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Vol. 004330991 — Sacramental registers, 1720–1803, browse-only | Free |
| FamilySearch | Vol. 004330992 — Notarial acts, 1699–1769, browse-only | Free |
| Library of Congress | American State Papers: Public Lands | Free |
| NARA | Federal-era colonial land confirmation records | Free/in-person |
| Ancestry.com | US Census and other collections (post-1800 primarily) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |

**Coverage:** volume_search returned a complete result set of 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana, 1700–1800. No additional pages exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans | Superior Council records; sacramental registers | In-person; some digitized |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s | In-person; some digitized |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Probate, land, court records | In-person/online request |
| ANOM, Aix-en-Provence, France | Administrative, census, military, immigration records | In-person; some at https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr/ |
| Archives Nationales, Paris | Central French government colonial records | In-person; some digitized |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records (post-1769) | In-person; some at http://pares.mcu.es/ |

## Records NOT online
- ANOM census rolls and administrative censuses
- French colonial military records
- Ship passenger/emigration lists from French ports
- Colonial-period tax and tithe records (browse-only at best)
- Acadian resettlement records (scattered)

## Known record losses
- Multiple transfers of authority (French→Spanish 1769, Spanish→French 1800, French→US 1803) created custody gaps
- St. Louis Cathedral records before 1720 largely lost
- Periodic flooding and fire in New Orleans damaged records
- ANOM is the best backstop for records not surviving locally

## Research tips
- Start with [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — name-indexed, the logical first search
- Records are in French and Spanish — prepare for 18th-century paleography
- Use Superior Council / notarial records for wills, land, and contracts
- Enslaved ancestors: Code Noir baptisms in sacramental registers
- Colonial land grants confirmed in American State Papers: Public Lands (Library of Congress)
- Go to ANOM for what isn't in Louisiana
- Acadian families: check Canadian repositories for pre-Louisiana records
- Sources: [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records); [Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)

quirks: There was NO civil vital registration during the French colonial period — Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the only source for vital events.
Records are in French (1699–1769) and shift to Spanish after Spain took possession in 1769; researchers must read 18th-century French and/or Spanish handwriting.

The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons — sacramental registers record enslaved individuals and are a primary source for researching African-descended ancestors in colonial Louisiana.
French colonial land grants followed French civil law (not English common law); the long-lot 'arpent' survey system was used, not rectangular township survey.
Post-1803 U.S. federal land-grant confirmation files (American State Papers: Public Lands) document colonial-era grantees and their heirs — a backdoor into 18th-century landholding families.

For records not found locally, the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds administrative correspondence, census rolls, and military records for the French colonial period.
Spanish colonial records (post-1769) may also be found at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain.
Acadian deportees arrived in Louisiana from 1755 onward — their pre-Louisiana records are held in Nova Scotia/Acadian repositories, not in Louisiana.
FamilySearch volume 004330991 (Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803, 264 images) is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only, in French and Spanish.
FamilySearch volume 004330992 (French colonial notarial acts/Superior Council records, 1699–1769, 149 images) is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only, in French.

## Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Genealogy Research Guide
### Late 1800s (c. 1870–1910)

---

### Jurisdictional Overview

Pennsylvania's coal mining region divides into two broad zones that were active in the late 1800s:

- **Anthracite (northeastern PA):** Schuylkill County (formed 1811), Luzerne County, Lackawanna County (formed **1878** from Luzerne), Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia counties. The core towns — Pottsville, Scranton, Wilkes-Barre, Mahanoy City, Shenandoah, Hazleton — sit in this zone.
- **Bituminous (western PA):** Cambria, Westmoreland, Fayette, Washington, Allegheny, Indiana, and Somerset counties. Johnstown is the anchor city here.

The Wikipedia Coal Region article ([en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region)) notes that mining expanded dramatically 1820s–1870s, drawing immigrants from Ireland, Wales, and Germany first, then from Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Italy, and Ukraine from the 1880s onward. Ethnic origin shapes which records survive and where.

> ⚠️ **Critical boundary quirk:** Lackawanna County did not exist until **1878**. If your family lived in the Scranton area before that year, their records — deeds, court filings, naturalizations, church registers — were created under **Luzerne County** authority. Search Luzerne first for events before 1878, then Lackawanna for events 1878 and later. These are one continuous research trail despite the differing county names.

---

### Record Types — Availability & Access

#### 1. Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

Pennsylvania did **not** have statewide civil registration of births and deaths during most of the late 1800s. The FamilySearch collection **"Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968"** (collection [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317), 4.2 million records with images — **indexed + images**) begins in 1906, confirming that statewide death registration commenced around that date. For deaths before 1906 within the target period, **church records and cemetery inscriptions are the primary substitutes** — civil death records essentially do not exist at the state level.

For marriages, two collections overlap the late 1800s:
- **"Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950"** (id: [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317)) — 524,189 records, 312,045 images — **indexed + images** — covers 1885 onward at the county level
- **"Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950"** (id: [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)) — 312,045 records — **indexed + images**
- **"Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900"** (id: [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)) — 198,765 records, **no images** — index only

> ⚠️ The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records did not resolve to place-specific content in this survey. Visit [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records) directly to confirm exact registration start dates at the county vs. state level before assuming records exist for a given year.

---

#### 2. Federal Census Records

Federal censuses (1870, 1880, 1900) are your most reliable annual snapshots of coal mining families in this period. The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed (fire). Key features for mining research:

- **1880:** Lists every household member's occupation — search for "miner," "mine laborer," etc.
- **1900:** Lists birthplace of each person *and* parents' birthplaces — critical for immigrant families
- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885)** record deaths in the 12 months preceding the census, sometimes the only death record available before statewide registration

Access: Ancestry.com holds fully indexed images for all surviving federal censuses; FamilySearch also has 1870–1900 censuses searchable online ([ancestry.com/search/collections/census/](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)).

---

#### 3. Church Records ⭐ *Most Important Source for Vital Events*

Ethnic parishes are the single most important source for births (baptisms), marriages, and burials in the late 1800s coal region, because civil registration was largely absent. The FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)) identifies the key denominations by ethnicity:

| Community | Denomination |
|---|---|
| Irish | Roman Catholic |
| Welsh | Congregational, Methodist |
| German | Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic |
| Polish | Roman Catholic (Polish national parishes) |
| Lithuanian | Roman Catholic |
| Slovak | Roman Catholic, Greek Catholic |
| Italian | Roman Catholic |
| Ukrainian | Greek Catholic, Ukrainian Orthodox |

**Where to find them:**
- **FamilySearch** — the collection "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" covers 1708–1985 with images; additional church volumes are among the **23 digitized volumes** found in the FamilySearch volume search (first page returned 3; 20 more pages are available via pagination)
- **Diocese and denominational archives** — Roman Catholic Diocese of Allentown (Schuylkill/Carbon/Luzerne), Diocese of Scranton (Lackawanna/Luzerne after 1868), Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia)
- **Local historical societies** — Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville), Lackawanna County Historical Society (Scranton)
- **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton) — preserves ethnic community records

> ⚠️ Many ethnic Catholic registers are in **Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, or Latin** — plan for translation needs before browsing.

---

#### 4. Mining-Specific Records 🏭 *Unique to This Region*

These records are often overlooked but can be genealogically rich:

**a. State Mine Inspector Reports (published annually from 1870)**
Listed fatal accidents by name, age, nationality, and cause of death. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). The Wikipedia Coal Region article confirms these begin in 1870. ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/))

**b. Mine Worker Employment Cards — Schuylkill County (1870–1900)**
FamilySearch volume IGN **002240015**: 410 images, **95% name-indexed, full-text searchable** — the most searchable mining record set found. Covers Schuylkill County.

**c. Mine Accident Reports — Luzerne County (1870–1895)**
FamilySearch volume IGN **002240016**: 287 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image by image. Contains names, dates, and circumstances of accidents.

**d. Colliery Payroll Ledgers — Lackawanna County (1878–1900)**
FamilySearch volume IGN **002240017**: 199 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable** — browse-only. Useful for confirming employment, estimating wages, and identifying the specific colliery.

> ℹ️ Only the first page (3 of 23 total volumes) was returned by FamilySearch's volume search. Additional volumes covering church records, vital records, census substitutes, and probate for these counties are available — search FamilySearch's catalog directly for Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties to see the full set.

**e. Company Records (fragmentary)**
Employment records, pay ledgers, and accident reports survive at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).

**f. UMWA Union Records (from 1890)**
The United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) membership rolls and grievance files are held at the UMWA archives and some have been microfilmed. Useful for post-1890 research.

---

#### 5. Immigration & Naturalization Records ⭐

The FamilySearch Wiki ([Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)) highlights this as critical for coal region families. Most miners arrived through **Philadelphia** or **New York** and naturalized in **local county courts** near the mines.

**Passenger lists:** NARA holds passenger arrival records; Ancestry.com and FamilySearch have indexed copies. New York arrivals (most common after 1880) are at Ancestry.com's immigration collections.

**Naturalizations (pre-1906):** Before September 1906, any court of record could naturalize immigrants. Search:
- **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906)** — at the Pennsylvania State Archives per the FamilySearch Wiki
- Luzerne and Lackawanna county courts of common pleas — check county courthouse records or Pennsylvania State Archives
- After 1906: uniform federal naturalization records at NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/))

**Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) holds some naturalization and military records; **Ancestry.com** has the bulk of indexed passenger lists.

---

#### 6. Military Records

Civil War veterans in coal towns can be traced through:
- **Pension files** at NARA (Fold3: [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) — pension files are genealogically rich, often containing birth dates, marriage dates, children's names
- **Pennsylvania Adjutant General records** — state service records at Pennsylvania State Archives

Late-period: **Spanish-American War (1898)** draft and service records are at NARA.

---

#### 7. Probate & Court Records

- **"Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994"** (id: [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)) — 893,214 records, 446,607 images — **indexed + images** — covers the full late 1800s window. Wills and estate inventories name heirs, relatives, and creditors.
- County Courts of Common Pleas hold guardianship files, civil suits, and equity cases that often name family members.

---

#### 8. Cemetery Records

**Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) is the largest aggregated cemetery index and covers many coal region cemeteries. Mining towns had both denominational cemeteries (attached to ethnic parishes) and municipal ones. Tombstone inscriptions sometimes give birth dates and birthplaces not found elsewhere.

---

#### 9. Historical Newspapers

**Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) holds digitized Pennsylvania newspapers. Local papers in Pottsville (Miners' Journal, founded 1825), Scranton, and Wilkes-Barre covered mine accidents, union activities, and community news — obituaries and accident notices can substitute for missing vital records.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What They Hold | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Mine Inspector reports, county naturalizations, state-level records | On-site & some online |
| **FamilySearch** | Digitized volumes (23+ for this period), indexed collections | Free at familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census, passenger lists, marriage & probate collections | Subscription |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | Local mining & community records | On-site |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton) | Ethnic community records, mining history | On-site |
| **Lackawanna County Historical Society** (Scranton) | County-level records post-1878 | On-site |
| **NARA / Fold3** | Federal naturalization (post-1906), military records | Online & on-site |
| **Diocese of Allentown / Diocese of Scranton** | Catholic parish registers | By request |

---

### Researcher Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Lackawanna County didn't exist before 1878** — search Luzerne County for all events in the Scranton area prior to that year; treat them as one continuous trail.
2. **No statewide birth or death registration before ~1906** — church baptism/burial registers are the primary substitute for the entire late 1800s window.
3. **Ethnic parish identity matters** — an Irish-Catholic family in Pottsville and a Polish-Catholic family in the same town would have attended different parishes with separate registers. Determine ethnicity first, then find the corresponding parish.
4. **Pre-1906 naturalizations can be in any county court** — don't assume federal records; check the county courthouse where the miner lived.
5. **Mine Accident Reports and Payroll Ledgers on FamilySearch are browse-only** (0% indexed) — you must page through them image by image; no name search is possible.
6. **The 1890 federal census is destroyed** — use state or local sources (tax lists, city directories, church records) to bridge 1880–1900.
7. **Only 3 of 23 FamilySearch digitized volumes for this period were returned** on the first page — search FamilySearch's catalog ([familysearch.org/search/catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog)) for each county directly to see all volumes, including church, court, and vital record microfilm.

---

This guide covers the anthracite coal region most thoroughly (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna), as that is where the densest documentation survives. If your ancestors were in the **western bituminous** counties (Cambria, Westmoreland, Fayette, etc.), the same record *types* apply, but you'd want a separate survey of Cambria County's repositories — Johnstown's history (including the 1889 flood) adds its own documentary complexity.
