## 📜 Locality Research Guide — Massachusetts, Early Colonial Period (1620–1700)

### Jurisdictional Context

The early 1600s in Massachusetts involves **two distinct colonial jurisdictions** — not one — and this split directly shapes where records were created and are now held:

| Colony | Founded | Dissolved | Territory |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plymouth Colony** | 1620 | 1691 | Southeastern Massachusetts (Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol counties) |
| **Massachusetts Bay Colony** | 1630 | 1691 | Boston and the rest of the colony |

In **1691**, both were merged into the **Province of Massachusetts Bay** under a new royal charter. Records for any family before 1691 must be sought in **whichever colony governed their town** — do not assume a family in Scituate or Duxbury appears in Massachusetts Bay records; Plymouth Colony had its own court, land, and vital registration systems. Plymouth Colony records have been published and indexed separately (per the FamilySearch Wiki; see below).

Massachusetts Bay Colony established its first four **counties** in 1643: **Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk** (old, later reorganized), and **Suffolk**. Plymouth Colony formed its own county structure. Probate and land records after 1643 are organized at the county level.

---

### Record Types, Availability, and Access

#### 1. 🗂️ Town Vital Records — **Indexed + Images**

**The most important record class for this period.** The colony mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths starting in **1639** — making Massachusetts unique in having some of the earliest and most complete vital registration in North America. (Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy, Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — name-indexed and searchable
- **Published abstracts:** The multi-volume *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* (the Tanner–Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. These are widely available in libraries and at NEHGS.

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** Recording was at the **town level**, not county or colony level. You must know (or determine) which town a family lived in. Births were often recorded years late or not at all — especially for infants who died young.

---

#### 2. ⛪ Congregational Church Records — **Mixed: Indexed + Browse-Only**

Congregational meetings were the **established church** of the colony. Church registers document admissions to full membership, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary actions (admonishments, excommunications). For families who had not yet achieved full church membership, church records may still document baptisms. These are often the **only surviving record** of a vital event when town records are missing.

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — name-indexed
- **FamilySearch digitized volume** (browse-only image access):
  - **ImageGroup 007612045** — *Congregational church admissions and baptisms, Suffolk County, 1630–1700* — 121 images. **Full-text searchable** but **0% name-indexed** — use FamilySearch's full-text search rather than the name index. Covers Suffolk County (Boston area).
- Many early records published in the *Colonial Society of Massachusetts* series and local historical society volumes — check NEHGS and local town libraries.

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** The Congregational denomination's archives and individual church records are not fully aggregated. If FamilySearch doesn't have a particular congregation, contact the **Congregational Library & Archives** in Boston (14 Beacon St.), which holds thousands of early New England church records.

---

#### 3. 📋 Town Meeting & Proprietors' Records — **Browse-Only Images**

Town proprietors managed the original land distributions, and town meeting records document governance, land grants to settlers, and occasionally family information.

- **FamilySearch digitized volume:**
  - **ImageGroup 007612044** — *Town meeting and proprietors' records, Massachusetts, 1620–1698* — 188 images. **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.** No search shortcut exists; plan for page-by-page review.

---

#### 4. ⚖️ Probate Records — **Indexed + Images**

County probate courts began operating in the **1630s** and produced wills, estate inventories, administration bonds, and guardianship files. These are exceptionally rich for colonial-era family reconstruction — inventories name household members, and administration records name heirs.

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — name-indexed
- **Physical/microfilm:** Original records held at **county probate courts** and the **Massachusetts Archives**. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records / Probate)

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** Plymouth Colony probate records (1620–1691) were kept by the Plymouth Colony court — they are **separate from** Massachusetts Bay County probate records. Plymouth Colony records have been published and indexed; search them independently.

---

#### 5. 🗺️ Land Records — **Physical / Microfilm; Limited Online**

Deeds were recorded at the **county level** from the **1630s** onward and survive in remarkably complete runs at **county registries of deeds**. For the colonial period, land records name grantors and grantees, describe property bounds using neighbors' names, and can establish residence, relationships, and chronology.

- The FamilySearch collections_search returned **no separate indexed land record collection** for Massachusetts 1620–1700. Land records for this period are largely in microfilm and physical repositories.
- **County Registries of Deeds** (e.g., Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex) hold the deed books — some early volumes have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- The **Massachusetts Archives** holds colonial-era land grants and General Court land records.

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** Plymouth Colony land records are held separately from Massachusetts Bay county deed books. Published transcripts and indexes exist for many Plymouth Colony land transactions — check NEHGS.

---

#### 6. 🏛️ Colony Court Records — **Physical / Published Transcripts**

The **General Court** (legislature and court) and inferior courts generated records of enormous genealogical value: land grants, freeman admissions, disciplinary hearings, petitions, and criminal cases.

- **Massachusetts Archives (Boston):** Holds original colony records, Governor's correspondence, and General Court records from the **1620s onward**. (Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- Many records published in:
  - *Records of the Governor and Company of Massachusetts Bay* (Shurtleff, 5 vols.)
  - *Plymouth Colony Records* (Shurtleff & Pulsifer, 12 vols.) — published and indexed separately for the Plymouth side

---

#### 7. 🚢 Passenger / Immigration Records — **Background Context Only**

The great Puritan migration occurred roughly 1620–1643. The FamilySearch *Passenger Lists* collection (id: 1784312) begins in **1820** — it does not cover the colonial period. For 17th-century arrivals, use:

- **The Great Migration Study Project** (NEHGS): Documents every known settler who arrived in New England 1620–1643, with evidence citations and family reconstructions. Published in multi-volume sets; accessible at NEHGS and many research libraries. This is the **essential starting point** for any 17th-century Massachusetts family. (Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Ship passenger lists** from English port records (e.g., Bristol, Southampton) — some survive and have been published.

---

#### 8. 🪖 Military Records — **Published Transcripts**

Colonial-era militia service (especially King Philip's War, 1675–1676) is documented in colony court records and published muster rolls. NARA federal military records begin in 1775 and are not applicable to the 1600s. Check:

- Published muster rolls and pension records in the Massachusetts Archives
- *Soldiers in King Philip's War* (Bodge, 1891) — a standard reference

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Colony records, General Court, court files, military, land grants — 1620s onward | In person; some records on microfilm at FamilySearch |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** (Boston) | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration series; manuscripts; published genealogies | Member access; some digital via AmericanAncestors.org |
| **County Registries of Deeds** (Essex, Suffolk, Middlesex, etc.) | Deed books from 1630s | In person; some microfilmed |
| **County Probate Courts** | Probate files from 1630s | In person; some indexed on FamilySearch |
| **Congregational Library & Archives** (Boston) | Early New England church records | In person; online catalog |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Indexed collections + digitized volumes listed above | Free online |
| **AmericanAncestors.org** (NEHGS digital) | Great Migration, vital records, compiled genealogies | Subscription |

---

### Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Access Level |
|---|---|
| Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Church Records, 1630–1920 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Church admissions/baptisms, Suffolk, 1630–1700 | ⚠️ Full-text searchable — NOT name-indexed (browse or full-text search) |
| Town meeting & proprietors' records, 1620–1698 | 🔍 Browse-only (image by image, no search) |
| Probate Records, 1635–1991 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Land/deed records | 📦 Largely physical / microfilm only |
| Colony court records | 📦 Physical (Massachusetts Archives) + published transcripts |
| Passenger records (colonial period) | 📦 Published compilations (Great Migration series) |

---

### Research Quirks to Know

1. **Two colonies, one territory.** Any family before 1691 must be placed in either Plymouth Colony or Massachusetts Bay Colony — they had separate courts, land records, and vital registration. Search both if the town location is uncertain.
2. **Town-level vital recording from 1639** — recording was at the town clerk level, not centrally. Identify the town first, then search that town's records.
3. **The Tanner–Corbin "Vital Records to 1850" series** covers 200+ towns and is the fastest path to published, indexed vital records — check NEHGS and WorldCat before searching microfilm.
4. **The Great Migration Study Project (NEHGS)** is the definitive prosopographical tool for 1620–1643 arrivals — start here before diving into primary records.
5. **No federal census for this period** — the federal census begins in 1790. Colonial-era "censuses" are actually tax lists, militia musters, or freeman lists in colony records.
6. **Church membership ≠ church attendance.** Many colonists attended church but never achieved full communicant membership. Baptism records survive separately from membership lists.
7. **FamilySearch wiki pages for Massachusetts** (Vital Records, Church Records, Probate, Land, Genealogy) returned generic content in this survey session rather than Massachusetts-specific detail — consult them directly at FamilySearch.org/wiki for the most current guidance, as the pages exist but did not surface here.

**Step 5 — Compiling the guide.**

Here is what the tools returned and what they did not, grounded strictly in the results:

---

# 🏃 Oklahoma Land Run of 1889 — Locality Research Guide
**Place:** Oklahoma Territory / Indian Territory → Oklahoma (state 1907)
**Period:** 1889–c. 1910 (pre-statehood through early statehood)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

This period spans **two separate territories that did not merge until statehood on November 16, 1907**:

| Territory | Dates | Coverage | Capital |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Unassigned Lands** | before May 2, 1890 | The 2 million acres opened April 22, 1889 | (none) |
| **Oklahoma Territory** | May 2, 1890 – Nov. 16, 1907 | Western Oklahoma; created by Organic Act | Guthrie |
| **Indian Territory** | concurrent | Eastern Oklahoma; Five Civilized Tribes | Tahlequah/Tishomingo etc. |
| **State of Oklahoma** | Nov. 16, 1907 → | Both territories merged | Oklahoma City |

Records created before 1907 were filed under **one of two entirely separate systems** — which one depends on whether your ancestor settled in Oklahoma Territory (western lands opened by land runs) or lived in Indian Territory (Five Tribes country to the east). Determine which territory first, then find the right record set.

---

## ⭐ Record Type 1 — Land & Homestead Records
*The single most important record class for Land Run families.*

Land Run participants filed homestead applications at federal **General Land Office** offices in **Guthrie** and **Kingfisher**. Each homestead file typically contains the original application, proof of settlement (naming witnesses), and the final patent. **Rejected applications also survive** and often contain detailed family information.

| Where to search | What's there | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection 1541872** — "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" | 234,567 records / 117,283 images | Indexed + images online |
| **FamilySearch digitized volume IGN 005221388** — "Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs, 1889–1907" | 402 images, **74% name-indexed** | Searchable by name via FamilySearch record search |
| **NARA, Record Group 49** (General Land Office) | Full homestead case files | Physical at NARA Washington, D.C.; partial digitization |
| **BLM General Land Office Records** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents (partially indexed) | Free online |

> **Tip:** The BLM GLO site lets you search patents by name and download scanned patent documents. A patent confirms a claim was proved up; the full homestead file at NARA has far more family detail.

---

## ⭐ Record Type 2 — Indian / Five Tribes Records
*Essential even for non-Native families — the Dawes rolls document neighbors, employers, and intermarried whites.*

The Dawes Commission (1898–1906) enrolled citizens of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) for allotment purposes. Enrollment jackets can contain ages, family relationships, physical descriptions, and testimony.

| Where to search | What's there | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection 1987432** — "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" | 567,890 records / 283,945 images | Indexed + images online |
| **FamilySearch digitized volume IGN 005221389** — "Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910" | 176 images, **0% indexed** | ⚠️ **Browse-only — must be paged through image by image; no name search** |
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Full Dawes case files (RG 75) | Physical; some digitized on Fold3 |

> ⚠️ The Dawes enrollment jackets volume is entirely un-indexed and not full-text searchable. To use it you must browse each image manually.

---

## Record Type 3 — Marriage Records

Oklahoma Territory counties began recording marriages upon their formation in 1890. These are county-level records — identify which county your ancestor lived in before searching.

| Where to search | What's there | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection 2134789** — "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" | 456,789 records / 913,578 persons / 228,394 images | Indexed + images online |
| County courthouses | Original registers | Physical; some counties have not transferred records |

---

## Record Type 4 — Church & Mission Records

Denominations established congregations in the new towns beginning sporadically in 1889, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)). Mission churches serving Native communities predate the Land Run by decades.

| Where to search | What's there | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection 1654321** — "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" | 123,456 records / 61,728 images | Indexed + images online |
| Denominational archives | Local congregation registers | Physical; contact individual denominations |

---

## Record Type 5 — Census Records

The **1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed** by fire, making Oklahoma's pre-statehood population particularly difficult to document. However, a rare exception exists:

| Record | Coverage | Where held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Oklahoma Territory Special Census, 1890** | Settlers in the new territory — one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation | **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)**, Oklahoma City | Physical; partially available on microfilm |
| **Federal Census 1900** | All of Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory | FamilySearch / Ancestry.com | Fully indexed online |
| **Federal Census 1910** | State of Oklahoma | FamilySearch / Ancestry.com | Fully indexed online |
| **County tax rolls, 1890s** | Property owners by county | Oklahoma State Archives / county records | Partially available |

> ⭐ The 1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census is exceptional — do not skip it. It can document settlers before the 1900 federal census.

---

## Record Type 6 — Vital Records (Births & Deaths)

> ⚠️ **Coverage gap:** None of the FamilySearch-specific Oklahoma wiki pages returned Oklahoma-specific content in this survey (all resolved to a generic page). No statewide vital registration start date was returned by the tools. Civil birth and death registration for Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) did not surface in any indexed FamilySearch collection. **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly** at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records) and the **Oklahoma State Department of Health** for registration dates. Church records (collection 1654321 above) are likely the primary substitute for vital events in this period.

---

## Record Type 7 — Territorial Court Records

Oklahoma Territory district court records (1890–1907) include civil and criminal cases, **probate filings**, and **pre-1906 naturalization petitions** (before 1906, any court of record could naturalize).

| Where held | What's there |
|---|---|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** (NARA Southwest Region) | Oklahoma Territory district court records |
| **Oklahoma State Archives**, Oklahoma City | Territorial and early state court records |

> **Naturalization note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court — territorial district courts, county courts, even probate courts. Search all court levels.

---

## Record Type 8 — Newspapers

Booming new towns (Guthrie, Kingfisher, Norman, Oklahoma City, Stillwater) launched newspapers almost immediately after the April 22, 1889 Run. Local papers published land claim notices, homestead proofs, and social items.

| Repository | Access |
|---|---|
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Oklahoma newspapers online (subscription) |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** digital newspaper collection | [Gateway to Oklahoma History](https://gateway.okhistory.org) — free |
| **Library of Congress Chronicling America** | Some territorial-era Oklahoma papers free online |

---

## Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | Holdings | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Collections 1541872, 1987432, 2134789, 1654321; digitized volumes | Free online |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)** | 1890 special census, territorial records, newspapers, photos | Oklahoma City, OK |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** | State and territorial government records | Oklahoma City, OK |
| **NARA — Washington, D.C.** | RG 49 General Land Office homestead files | In person or digitized portions |
| **NARA — Fort Worth** (Southwest Region) | Oklahoma/Indian Territory court records, RG 75 Five Tribes | In person |
| **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents | Free online |
| **County courthouses** | Marriage registers, deeds, probate | County seats, western Oklahoma |

---

## Tracing Ancestors Back to Origins

Land Run settlers came overwhelmingly from **Kansas, Texas, and Missouri**, per the [FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). Once you confirm a Land Run family in Oklahoma records, trace backward into those states' records — Kansas homestead records, Texas county courthouses, and Missouri deed books — to find the family before 1889.

---

## Key Research Quirks

1. **Two-territory split is not optional.** Oklahoma Territory (west) and Indian Territory (east) had completely separate court, probate, and land systems. Determine which territory before searching.
2. **The 1890 federal census is gone** — the Oklahoma Territory Special Census at the Oklahoma Historical Society is the replacement for that decade.
3. **Homestead case files at NARA** contain far more genealogical detail than the patent alone. Always request the full file, not just the patent record.
4. **Dawes enrollment jackets (IGN 005221389)** are browse-only — zero indexing — and must be paged image by image.
5. **Pre-1906 naturalizations** appear in territorial district courts, not just federal courts — search court records at NARA Fort Worth.
6. **"Sooners"** who entered before the official start were disqualified and many had their claims contested. Contest records (at NARA RG 49) can be genealogically rich.
7. **No specific vital registration start date** for Oklahoma Territory was returned by the tools — verify at the FamilySearch Wiki or Oklahoma State Department of Health before assuming birth/death certificates exist for this period.

---

# Locality Research Guide: The Alabama Region, c. 1780–1820 (Pre-Statehood)

**Jurisdiction surveyed:** Alabama region as Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) → Alabama Territory (1817–1819) → State of Alabama (1819–)
**Period of interest:** approximately 1780–1820, with emphasis on the territorial era around 1800

---

## Jurisdictional History — the essential first step

This is one of the most important things to understand before searching any record:

| Period | Controlling Authority | What that means for records |
|--------|----------------------|----------------------------|
| 1702–1763 | **French** (Mobile/coastal) | French colonial registers; archives in France |
| 1763–1780 | **British** (Mobile/coastal) | British colonial administration |
| 1780–1813 | **Spanish** (Mobile district) | Spanish civil and church registers |
| 1798–1817 | **Mississippi Territory** (interior/eastern Alabama) | Territorial government — records filed under Mississippi Territory, *not* Alabama |
| 1817–1819 | **Alabama Territory** | Territorial records transition |
| 1819– | **State of Alabama** | State and county-level records begin |

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk:** Around 1800, the Alabama interior was part of the **Mississippi Territory** — there was no "Alabama" jurisdiction yet. Records from this era are filed under Mississippi Territory or its predecessor counties, not under Alabama. Search Mississippi Territory record sets alongside Alabama ones. Meanwhile, the **Mobile area remained under Spanish control until 1813** — a completely separate record system requiring separate searches in Spanish archives.

---

## Record Types Available for This Period

### 1. Territorial Censuses — **best substitute for vital records**

The Mississippi Territory conducted population enumerations in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810**, which covered present-day Alabama settlers. These are among the most valuable pre-statehood records available.

- **Held at:** Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890* (collection [2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756)) — covers from 1810; 287,634 indexed persons, no images
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890* (collection [1927171](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171)) — covers from 1792; 198,340 indexed persons, no images. **Search this for pre-1810 enumerations of Alabama settlers.**
- The 1800 and 1810 **federal census** also covered Mississippi Territory, but the 1800 schedules for this region are mostly lost.

---

### 2. Land Records — **the richest pre-statehood source**

Alabama is a **federal land state**: all original settlers received their land through the federal General Land Office (GLO), producing patents and grants that survive well.

- **BLM General Land Office website** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) — searchable database of federal land patents, many with images. This is the single most important resource for tracing territorial settlers.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection (Mississippi scope):** *Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907* (collection [1919694](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694)) — 312,450 records with images; covers the territorial era from 1798. ⚠️ Search this for Alabama-area land transactions under the territorial government.
- **Earliest land records in the Mobile area** are Spanish and British colonial grants, not federal patents. Source: [FamilySearch Wiki, Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).

**Also search:** Tax lists and militia rolls from the territorial period, noted in the FamilySearch Wiki as surviving for this era (ADAH holdings). These function as census substitutes and property records for years when no census was taken.

---

### 3. Court Records

- **FamilySearch indexed collection (Mississippi scope):** *Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920* (collection [1855293](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293)) — 245,670 records with images; starts 1799. Covers territorial-era court proceedings that included present-day Alabama counties.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985* (collection [1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764)) — 438,210 records with images; starts at the very beginning of Alabama's county system (1809). Probate records name heirs, ages, and relationships.
- Territorial court records also held at **NARA** (Southeast Region, Morrow, Georgia).

---

### 4. Vital Records — **no civil registration; church records only**

There was **no civil vital registration** in the Alabama region around 1800. Births, marriages, and deaths were recorded only by churches — and sparsely at that, given the frontier character of most settlements.

- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950* (collection [1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396)) — 156,789 records with images; the earliest Alabama church records on FamilySearch begin 1803.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950* (collection [1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408)) — 612,345 records with images; county marriage bonds and licenses begin 1809 when Alabama's county court system was established.
- For the **Mobile area under Spanish rule**, Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) survive in Spanish archives. See §6 below.

---

### 5. Military Records

- **Militia rolls** are mentioned in the FamilySearch Wiki as a territorial-era source for the Alabama region ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)).
- **War of 1812 and Creek War (1813–1814) service records and pensions** — many Alabama-area men served; records held at **NARA** and searchable on **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)).
- **NARA** holds the principal repository for federal military records of this period ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)).

---

### 6. Colonial Records (Mobile Area — French, British, Spanish)

This is a completely separate research trail for families in the coastal/Mobile area.

| Era | Records | Repository |
|-----|---------|-----------|
| French (1702–1763) | Census returns, church registers | Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| British (1763–1780) | Colonial administration records | UK National Archives; Library of Congress |
| Spanish (1780–1813) | Census returns, Catholic church registers, land grants | Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain; copies at Library of Congress |

Source: [FamilySearch Wiki, Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

---

## Digitized Browsable Volumes — Honest Assessment

You specifically asked about **digitized but non-indexed, browse-only volumes**. Here is what the survey found:

> **`volume_search` returned 0 results** for both `Alabama, United States` and `Mississippi Territory, United States` in the 1780–1820 window. This means **FamilySearch currently has no digitized image volumes indexed for this place and period that are surfaced through their Records Management Service** for browse-by-image access in the way that, say, a microfilm roll of county registers would be.

This is a genuine digitization gap for this early, frontier period — not surprising given the sparse documentation of the era. What *does* exist on FamilySearch for this period is in **indexed collections** (name-searchable, listed above) rather than unindexed browse-only rolls.

**Where to look for browsable digitized materials outside FamilySearch:**
- **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** ([archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov)) — has digitized selected territorial-era records, including some tax lists and county records
- **Ancestry.com** ([ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com)) — has Alabama and Mississippi Territory collections, some of which include browsable images
- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) — military and pension records for the War of 1812/Creek War period

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What's there | Access |
|-----------|-------------|--------|

# Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide

**Counties:** Schuylkill · Luzerne · Carbon · Lackawanna · Northumberland
**Period:** 1860–1890 | **Focus:** Irish immigrant ancestors, coal mining community

---

## Jurisdictional Overview & Critical Boundary Change

The five anthracite counties span two coalfields:

- **Southern/Middle field:** Schuylkill (est. 1811 — confirmed by place_search), Carbon, Northumberland
- **Northern/Wyoming field:** Luzerne, Lackawanna

**🔴 Lackawanna County did not exist until 1878 — carved from Luzerne County.** Every record for the Scranton, Carbondale, and northern coal-patch area before 1878 is filed under **Luzerne County**. Search Luzerne first for all events before 1878, then Lackawanna for 1878 onward. This is the single most consequential jurisdictional fact in this region.

**Schuylkill County population** (confirmed by FamilySearch place_population):

| Year | Population |
|------|-----------|
| 1860 | 89,510 |
| 1870 | 116,428 |
| 1880 | 129,974 |

This rapid growth reflects mass Irish immigration into the collieries, making this one of the densest immigrant communities in 19th-century America.

---

## ⭐ Specialized Coal-Region Indexes — Read This First

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records). The wiki_search also confirmed this page covers colliery employment indexes, Catholic parish survival, and triennial tax assessments unique to the anthracite field.*

### 1. Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898
The most important coal-specific finding aid. Names approximately **41,000 colliery workers** across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Each entry may include:
- **Occupation** (loader, breaker boy, mule driver)
- **Wage rate**
- **Parish of origin**, where recorded — this is potentially your direct link back to the Irish townland

Note: This index spans years before Lackawanna County existed; pre-1878 workers were legally residents of Luzerne County. The payroll records cross that administrative boundary seamlessly, making this index especially valuable.

> *The FamilySearch Wiki notes that payroll-derived indexes are the more direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records — miners with anglicized, phonetically spelled, or truncated names in the census may appear more reliably under a payroll-book spelling.*

### 2. Pennsylvania Triennial State Tax Assessments, from 1853
State assessors enumerated coal-region residents **every three years from 1853**. Ledgers record householder name, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity. These assessments fill the gaps between census years — critical given the destroyed 1890 census — and can document a miner's presence in a specific patch town across the entire 1860–1890 window. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)

---

## 1. Vital Records — Major Coverage Gap for 1860–1890

**Pennsylvania had no effective statewide civil vital registration during the 1860–1890 period.** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content in this session, so specific registration start-date details could not be confirmed from tool output — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records directly. For practical research purposes: **do not assume civil birth or death registrations exist** for coal-region miners in this window. Church records and mortality schedules are your primary substitutes.

**Substitute vital sources for 1860–1890:**
- Catholic parish baptismal, marriage, and burial registers (see §2 below)
- Federal census mortality schedules (1860, 1870, 1880) — record deaths in the year preceding the census; often capture mine-accident victims
- Mine accident reports and coroner's inquests (physical records at county courthouses)
- Newspaper death notices (*Miners' Journal*, Pottsville; *Scranton Tribune*)

**Civil marriage collections that do overlap the window:**

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Date Range | Access |
|-----------|-----------------|-----------|--------|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages | [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | 1885–1950 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | ⚠️ Indexed, no images |

---

## 2. Church Records — Primary Source for Irish Coal-Region Families

For Irish immigrants in 1860–1890, Catholic parish registers are more reliable than any civil record class. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms: many Catholic parishes in the coal region were **established between 1840 and 1870** specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)

### Diocesan Archive Split — Critical Research Quirk
Which diocesan archive holds a parish's registers depends entirely on when the Diocese of Scranton was created:

- **Diocese of Scranton** (established 1868): holds baptismal registers for parishes in the **northern field** (Lackawanna/Luzerne counties) **post-1868**
- **Diocese of Harrisburg**: holds registers for parishes in the **southern field** (Schuylkill, Carbon, Northumberland) and for all coal-region parishes **pre-1868**

### Digitized Church Records on FamilySearch

**Schuylkill County Church Records:**
- Image Group **007936751** | 187 images | Coverage: 1842–1895
- Languages: **English and German** ⚠️
- **Access: Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image. Some records are in German (German Catholic parishes shared the region with Irish ones); original-language reading required for those entries.

County-specific digitized church volumes for Luzerne, Carbon, Lackawanna, and Northumberland were not returned by volume_search; physical and microfilm holdings at the diocesan archives and Pennsylvania State Archives should be assumed for those counties.

### Other Denominations
Irish Protestants may appear in Episcopal or Presbyterian registers. Welsh miners (often neighbors to Irish workers) had strong Nonconformist records — Calvinist Methodist, Congregational. These are typically held at regional historical societies, not confirmed as digitized for this period in FamilySearch.

---

## 3. Census Records

From FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records)):

| Census | Key Features for Coal-Region Research |
|--------|--------------------------------------|
| **1860** | Lists all household members; birthplace by country — "Ireland" |
| **1870** | Post-Famine immigration peak; records parents' birthplaces separately |
| **1880** | **First to record relationship to head of household** — proves family structure; records both parents' birthplaces |
| **1890** | ⚠️ **Virtually destroyed** — almost no population schedules survive for Pennsylvania. A critical 10-year gap. |
| 1900 | Outside target window, but valuable to anchor backward into the 1890s |

**Mortality schedules** (1860, 1870, 1880) record individuals who died in the year preceding each census, effectively serving as death certificates for that sub-period. Mine explosions and roof-falls made these schedules unusually rich in the coal counties.

---

## 4. Naturalization Records — Key to Irish Origins

From FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Naturalization Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records)):

> *"Pennsylvania naturalization records before 1906 are scattered among county courts — Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts all had jurisdiction. Declarations of intent and petitions for naturalization name the applicant's country of origin, which can identify Irish, German, or other immigrant ancestry. After September 1906, naturalization centralized in federal courts (NARA Philadelphia for eastern Pennsylvania)."*

Pre-1906 naturalizations are **court-specific and county-specific** — search each coal county separately.

### Digitized Volumes on FamilySearch

**Schuylkill County Naturalization Records:**
- Image Group **007936750** | 298 images | Coverage: 1849–1915
- **Access: Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image. ⚠️ This is a high-priority browse target: Irish miners who naturalized in Schuylkill County courts are here, unindexed.

**Pennsylvania State-Level Naturalization Records:**
- Image Group **008120443** | 351 images | Coverage: 1790–1915 | Languages: English & German
- **Access: 15% name-indexed** — search by name first for the indexed portion; browse the remainder (85%) image by image.

County-specific digitized naturalization volumes for Luzerne, Carbon, Lackawanna, and Northumberland were not returned — physical records at those county courthouses and at the Pennsylvania State Archives should be assumed.

**Post-1906:** NARA Philadelphia Region (900 Market Street) holds centralized naturalization records for eastern Pennsylvania federal courts.

---

## 5. Probate Records

| Source | Image Group | Images | Coverage | Access |
|--------|------------|--------|----------|--------|
| Schuylkill County Probate | 007936749 | 412 | 1851–1930 | ❌ Browse-only |
| Pennsylvania (state-level) | 008120441 | 1,180 | 1683–1994 | ❌ Browse-only |
| PA Probate Records collection | [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | — | 1683–1994 | ✅ Indexed + images |

Miner families had modest estates, but wills and estate inventories can confirm family members, name property in Ireland, and identify executors/administrators (often neighbors or co-workers from the same Irish parish).

---

## 6. Death Records

**Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968** (collection [2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317)) — begins in 1906, **entirely outside the 1860–1890 target window**. Useful only for miners who lived into the 20th century.

**Pennsylvania State-Level Death Records:**
- Image Group **008120442** | 674 images | Coverage: 1852–1968
- **Access: Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.

⚠️ **Coverage gap:** No indexed death collection covering 1860–1890 was returned by tool results. Substitute with mortality schedules, Catholic burial registers, coroner's inquests, and newspaper notices.

---

## 7. Land & Property Records

**Schuylkill County Deed Records:**
- Image Group **007936752** | 543 images | Coverage: 1815–1900
- **Access: 22% name-indexed** — partial; browse the unindexed 78%.

Coal-region miners typically rented company ("patch town") housing and rarely held deeds. Deed records are more useful for mine operators, merchants, and tradespeople. **Triennial tax assessments** (see Specialized Indexes) are the more consistently productive source for locating working miners in property-related records.

---

## 8. Marriage Records

**Schuylkill County Marriage Records:**
- Image Group **007936753** | 94 images | Coverage: 1870–1910
- **Access: Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.

Also search the indexed PA marriage collections (§1 above): County Marriages 1885–1950 and Civil Marriages 1677–1950.

---

## 9. Military Records

The Civil War (1861–1865) falls within our window. Many Irish coal miners served in Pennsylvania volunteer units. Key sources:
- **1863 Draft Registration (Conscription Act)** — lists occupation ("miner") and birthplace (Ireland); NARA microfilm
- **Pennsylvania Civil War Veterans Card File** — Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg
- **NARA pension files** — widow's applications often name children, marriage witnesses, and corroborate vital dates

These are primarily physical/microfilm records; search NARA Ancestry.com partnership and the PA State Archives.

---

## 10. Chain of Evidence for Irish Origins

For each Irish miner, work this sequence toward the old country:

1. **Naturalization petition (county court, pre-1906)** → county/townland of origin in Ireland often stated
2. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** → parish of origin sometimes noted for northern-field miners
3. **Catholic baptismal register** → godparents (sponsors) often came from the same Irish parish as the parents
4. **1880 census** → father's and mother's birthplace recorded separately
5. **NARA passenger arrival records** → Castle Garden (pre-1892) / Ellis Island (post-1892)
6. **Griffith's Valuation (Ireland, 1847–1864)** → cross-reference the surname + county of origin to locate the townland

---

## Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|-----------|---------|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Statewide collections, triennial tax assessments, military, some court records |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | Local records, *Miners' Journal* archives, photograph collections |
| **Lackawanna County Historical Society** (Scranton) | Northern-field records post-1878 |
| **Luzerne County Historical Society** (Wilkes-Barre) | Northern-field records pre-1878 and ongoing |
| **Diocese of Scranton Archives** | Catholic parish registers, northern coal field, post-1868 |
| **Diocese of Harrisburg Archives** | Catholic parish registers, southern coal field; all coal-region parishes pre-1868 |
| **NARA Philadelphia Region** | Post-1906 naturalizations; federal court records; passenger arrivals |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Digitized volumes listed throughout this guide |

## Key Quirks & Warnings

The payroll-derived index is the genealogical finding aid; inspection reports are context, not a personal-name index.

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood Period, c. 1760–1791)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Status during target period:** Vermont was **not a state** during 1760–1791. The territory existed as contested land between the Province of New Hampshire and the Colony (later State) of New York. From 1777 it operated as the **Vermont Republic**, a de facto independent republic, until admission to the Union.
- **Admitted to statehood:** 1791, as the **14th state** — per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))
- **Jurisdictional dispute:** New Hampshire granted townships in the region from the 1740s onward (the "New Hampshire Grants"). New York disputed and **refused to recognize** those grants, exercising its own colonial authority and conducting a 1771 survey of approximately 1,800 disputed-grant holders — per [Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Population:** The `place_population` tool returned no data for this period (coverage gap). Vermont's population grew rapidly in the 1760s–1780s as settlers moved in primarily from southern New England.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture; settlers clearing forested land for farms.
- **Ethnic/religious composition:** Predominantly English Protestant settlers from Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island.
- **Key historical event:** The American Revolutionary War (1775–1783), including the **Battle of Bennington (1777)** fought in Vermont; Vermont declared independence from both New York and Britain in 1777.

## Boundary Changes

This jurisdictional tangle is the defining complication for pre-statehood Vermont research:

| Period | Controlling Authority | Implication for Records |
|---|---|---|
| c. 1749–1764 | Province of New Hampshire grants land | NH-issued township grants held at NH State Archives |
| c. 1764–1777 | Colony of New York asserts authority; disputes NH grants | NY colonial land records, court records may name your ancestor |
| 1777–1791 | Vermont Republic (de facto independent) | Vermont's own governmental records begin; held at Vermont State Archives |
| 1791– | State of Vermont | State-level civil infrastructure builds out post-statehood |

**Critical research implication:** A single ancestor could appear in New Hampshire grant records, New York colonial land or court records, *and* Vermont Republic records — all for the same parcel of land. All three record sets must be searched.

---

## The Key Pre-Statehood Finding Aid: The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule

The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) specifically identifies this as the earliest systematic resident list for the future state:

> "The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule, prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood, enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry lists grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status."

This record predates any Vermont civil registration and is your first stop for identifying landowners in the territory before 1771.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Statewide registration:** The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki states statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in **1857** (state level) — decades after the target period closes. ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))
- **Town clerk records:** Earlier vital records were kept at the **town level** by town clerks. The wiki notes some town clerk records survive back to the **1770s**, but survival is **uneven** — coverage varies greatly from town to town. ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices (still the first call for pre-1857 Vermont vital records); some records microfilmed by FamilySearch and the Vermont State Archives.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary substitute for 1760–1791; family bibles; town histories that transcribe vital data.
- **Coverage gap:** FamilySearch's dedicated Vermont_Vital_Records wiki page did not return Vermont-specific content during this survey (redirected to a generic overview). The primary FamilySearch guidance is on the Vermont Genealogy overview page linked above.

### Church Records

- **Denominations:** Settlement patterns from southern New England brought **Congregationalist** congregations earliest and most numerously; **Baptist**, **Methodist**, and **Quaker** congregations also established early footholds during the target period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership rolls, and dismissal letters (documenting members who moved to new congregations — useful for tracking migration).
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Where held:** Local congregations; denominational archives; the Vermont State Archives; FamilySearch microfilm. Many 18th-century Vermont church records have not been digitized and exist only as physical volumes.
- **Coverage gap:** FamilySearch's Vermont_Church_Records wiki page redirected to a generic overview — no Vermont-specific indexed collections were returned.

### Census Records

- **Federal census:** The **1790 federal census** is the only federal enumeration within the target window. Vermont was included. It captures heads of household with tick-marks for free white males, free white females, and other persons — no names below the head of household.
  - **Access:** Indexed on both Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). The 1790 Vermont census survives intact.
- **Pre-1790 alternatives:** No federal census before 1790. For the period 1760–1789, the following substitutes establish who was present:
  - Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (~1,800 named grantees)
  - Town and state tax lists
  - Town proprietors' records
  - Church membership rolls
- **Coverage gap:** FamilySearch's Vermont_Census wiki page did not return Vermont-specific content.

### Land Records

**Land records are the single most important record class for pre-statehood Vermont.** Land tenure was the central legal controversy of the entire 1760–1791 period.

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New England township system). Vermont is a **state-land state** — land was granted by colonial/state authority, not the federal government; there are no Bureau of Land Management (GLO) records.
- **Three parallel grant systems to search:**
  1. **New Hampshire grants** (pre-1764): NH-issued township grants held at New Hampshire State Archives, Concord, NH
  2. **New York colonial grants and surveys** (c. 1764–1777): New York State Archives, Albany, NY. The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is part of this body of records.
  3. **Vermont Republic grants** (1777–1791) and early state grants (post-1791): Vermont Secretary of State and Vermont State Archives, Montpelier, VT
- **Town proprietors' records:** In the New England tradition, Vermont towns kept proprietors' records documenting original land grants and subdivisions among founding settlers. These are among the very earliest records for each town and are held at town clerk offices.
- **Town histories as surrogate access:** The Vermont Genealogy wiki specifically notes that 19th-century town histories (most published **1860–1900**) "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) — **treat these as high-priority sources for 1760–1791.**
- **Coverage gap:** FamilySearch's Vermont_Land_and_Property wiki page redirected to a generic overview; no Vermont-specific land record collections were returned by the tools.

### Probate Records

- **Jurisdictional structure:** Vermont probate is administered at the **probate district** level (not county) — a structure unique to Vermont established after statehood. For the period before 1791, probate would fall under New York or New Hampshire courts, or under early Vermont Republic courts.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives (post-1777 Vermont Republic courts); New York State Archives and New Hampshire State Archives for pre-1777 probate.
- **Coverage gap:** FamilySearch's Vermont_Probate_Records wiki page redirected to generic content; no Vermont-specific probate collections were identified by the tools.

### Military Records

- **Dominant conflict:** The **American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)** is the central military event of this period. Vermont militia was active throughout; the Battle of Bennington (1777) is a landmark event.
- **Record types:**
  - **Federal:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files at NARA (archives.gov — confirmed in the external links search results). Pension files are especially rich in family detail: many include widow's pension applications naming children, marriage dates, and places of birth.
  - **Bounty land warrants:** Issued to Revolutionary War veterans; useful for tracing land acquisition.
  - **Vermont-specific:** Vermont militia records held at the Vermont State Archives, Montpelier.
- **Online access:** Fold3 (fold3.com — confirmed in external links results) holds digitized Revolutionary War records. NARA's online catalog also offers some digitized pension files.
- **Coverage gap:** FamilySearch's Vermont_Military_Records wiki page redirected to generic content.

### Tax Records

- **Substitute value:** For 1760–1789 (before the 1790 federal census), Vermont town and state tax lists are critical substitutes. They name adult male property holders and establish presence in a specific town in a specific year.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives; individual town clerk offices.
- **Digitization level:** Largely physical or microfilm only; limited online availability.

### Cemetery Records

- **Online access:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com — confirmed in the external links results) is the primary online cemetery database and covers Vermont's 18th-century burial grounds, though volunteer-submitted coverage is uneven for very early graves.
- **Early burial grounds:** Many Vermont towns have 18th-century burial grounds predating formal cemetery organization. Some exist only as documented field-stone markers; transcription quality varies.
- **Physical records:** Formal sexton records are sparse for this period. Many burials are documented only by surviving gravestones and later transcription efforts by the Daughters of the American Revolution and local genealogical societies.

### Newspaper Records

- **Vermont's first newspapers:** Vermont's earliest newspaper, the *Vermont Gazette*, began publication in **Bennington in 1781** — giving an eight-year newspaper window within the target period.
- **Online access:** Newspapers.com (confirmed in external links results) and the Library of Congress *Chronicling America* project hold some digitized early Vermont newspapers, but coverage of the 1781–1791 window is thin.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, land dispute legal notices (especially relevant given the NH/NY grant controversy), and public announcements.

### Immigration/Emigration Records

- **Context:** Most Vermont settlers during 1760–1791 migrated **internally** from Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island. Transatlantic immigration to Vermont was minimal in this period.
- **Record types:** No formal records exist for internal colonial migration. Migration is reconstructed by:
  - Following neighbors and family clusters from origin communities using land records (deeds of sale in the origin town, followed by land grants in Vermont)
  - Church membership dismissal letters (a member leaving a congregation received a letter to present to the new congregation)
  - Chain-migration patterns identifiable in town histories
- **Nearest ports:** Boston and Providence handled what little transatlantic traffic there was to this region, but NARA passenger lists for the 1760s–1790s are fragmentary.

- **Jurisdictional dispute:** New Hampshire granted townships in the region from the 1740s onward (the "New Hampshire Grants"). - **Population:** The `place_population` tool returned no data for this period (coverage gap).

- **Key historical event:** The American Revolutionary War (1775–1783), including the Battle of Bennington (1777) fought in Vermont; Vermont declared independence from both New York and Britain in 1777.

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New England township system). Vermont is a **state-land state** — no BLM/GLO records.
- **Three parallel grant systems to search:**
  1. **New Hampshire grants** (pre-1764): NH State Archives, Concord NH
  2. **New York colonial grants and surveys** (c. 1764–1777): NY State Archives, Albany NY. The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is part of this body.
  3. **Vermont Republic grants** (1777–1791) and early state grants (post-1791): Vermont Secretary of State and Vermont State Archives, Montpelier VT
- **Town proprietors' records:** Document original land grants and subdivisions among founding settlers. Held at town clerk offices.
- **Town histories as surrogate access:** 19th-century town histories (1860–1900) "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." Per [Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Coverage gap:** Vermont_Land_and_Property wiki page returned generic content only.

### Probate Records

- **Jurisdictional structure:** Vermont probate is at the **probate district level** (unique to Vermont; established post-1791). Pre-1791 probate falls under New York or New Hampshire courts, or early Vermont Republic courts.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives (post-1777); NY State Archives and NH State Archives (pre-1777).
- **Coverage gap:** Vermont_Probate_Records wiki page returned generic content only.

### Military Records

- **Dominant conflict:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783). Battle of Bennington (1777) fought in Vermont.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files at NARA (archives.gov); bounty land warrants; Vermont militia records at Vermont State Archives.
- **Online access:** Fold3 (fold3.com) holds digitized Revolutionary War records. NARA's online catalog has some digitized pension files.
- **Coverage gap:** Vermont_Military_Records wiki page returned generic content only.

### Tax Records

- **Substitute value:** For 1760–1789, Vermont town and state tax lists name adult male property holders — critical substitutes for a census before 1790.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives; individual town clerk offices.
- **Digitization level:** Largely physical or microfilm only.

### Cemetery Records

- **Online access:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) is the primary online database; covers Vermont's 18th-century burial grounds, though coverage is uneven for very early graves.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records sparse for this period; many burials documented only by surviving gravestones and later DAR/genealogical society transcription.

### Newspaper Records

- **Vermont's first newspaper:** *Vermont Gazette*, Bennington, **1781** — giving an eight-year newspaper window within the target period.
- **Online access:** Newspapers.com and Library of Congress *Chronicling America*; coverage of 1781–1791 is thin.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, land dispute legal notices, public announcements.

### Immigration/Emigration Records

- **Context:** Most settlers during 1760–1791 migrated **internally** from MA, CT, NH, and RI. Transatlantic immigration to Vermont was minimal.
- **Reconstruction strategy:** Follow neighbors and family clusters from origin communities via land records (deeds of sale in origin town, then land grants in Vermont); church membership dismissal letters; chain-migration patterns in town histories.

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Coverage for Vermont, 1760–1791 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1790 federal census (indexed + images); microfilmed town and church records via FamilySearch Catalog | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 federal census (indexed); some early Vermont vital records; historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records, pension files | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Vermont cemetery records including 18th-century burial grounds | Free |
| NARA Online (archives.gov) | Revolutionary War pension files; 1790 census originals | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Some early Vermont newspapers from 1781 onward | Subscription |

**Coverage note:** The `external_links_search` tool returned 6 results for Vermont (1760–1791), all generic repository-level links rather than Vermont-specific, time-filtered collection links. Vermont-specific curated external links may exist beyond what was returned.

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives and Records Administration, Montpelier | Vermont Republic records (1777–1791); early state land grants; legislative records; town proprietors' records; militia records | In-person / online catalog at vermont.gov |
| Vermont Historical Society, Barre | Manuscripts, town histories (1860–1900), genealogical collections, maps | In-person; some digital |
| Individual town clerk offices | Town vital records (some back to 1770s); land records; proprietors' records | In-person / mail |
| New Hampshire State Archives, Concord NH | New Hampshire Grants records; colonial-era township grants for Vermont towns | In-person / mail |
| New York State Archives, Albany NY | New York colonial land records; 1771 Grant Survey Schedule records; colonial court records | In-person / mail |
| NARA (Washington DC and regional centers) | 1790 census originals; Revolutionary War service records and pension files | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT Online

- Town clerk vital records (1770s–1791): uneven survival, mostly not digitized — contact individual town clerk offices
- Vermont Republic governmental records (1777–1791): Vermont State Archives, largely physical
- Town proprietors' records: town clerk offices or Vermont State Archives, mostly physical (sometimes reprinted in town histories)
- Early church records: local congregations and denominational archives, largely physical or microfilm
- New Hampshire Grants records: NH State Archives, physical
- New York colonial land and court records for Vermont territory: NY State Archives, physical
- Vermont tax lists (pre-1790): Vermont State Archives and town clerk offices, physical or microfilm

## Known Record Losses

No specific courthouse fires or documented record destructions were returned by the FamilySearch tools. The inherent thinness of the record base reflects: (1) no civil registration existed during 1760–1791; (2) town-level record-keeping was newly established and inconsistent; (3) the multi-authority dispute scattered record creation across NH, NY, and Vermont Republic systems.

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.** ~1,800 named grantees with township, grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status — the earliest systematic resident list for pre-statehood Vermont. Per [Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

2. **Search all three grant systems.** The same ancestor may appear in NH grant records (NH State Archives), NY colonial land records (NY State Archives), and Vermont Republic/state records (Vermont State Archives) — all for the same land. Per [Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

3. **Town clerk records are the primary vital record source — contact each town directly.** Town-level records survive unevenly from the 1770s; identify the specific Vermont town and contact that town clerk or check FamilySearch's microfilm catalog for that town. Per [Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

4. **Mine the town histories.** Town histories (1860–1900) reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise difficult to access. Vermont Historical Society holds a large collection; many are also on Google Books and HathiTrust. Per [Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

5. **The 1790 federal census is your first federal anchor.** Use it to establish household composition at statehood, then work backward using land records, tax lists, church records, and the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.

6. **Search origin-state records before Vermont.** Most 1760s–1780s settlers came from MA, CT, NH, and RI. Records at the point of origin document the family before Vermont records begin.

7. **Revolutionary War pension files are genealogically rich.** Check pension files at NARA (archives.gov) and on Fold3 for adult males in Vermont 1775–1783. Widow's applications name children, record marriage dates, and cite witnesses.

8. **FamilySearch wiki coverage gaps.** All Vermont topic sub-pages returned generic content. All FamilySearch guidance for Vermont is effectively consolidated on [Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
